stories.Headline: States Don’t Have to Solve the AI Education Equation Alone. Tennessee Shows How
stories.Summary:
States across the country are taking different approaches to AI policy, with governors forming task forces, state education agencies issuing non-binding guidance, and legislatures requiring districts to adopt AI policies. A November 2025 survey found that 93% of 29 state education agency respondents had communicated or planned to communicate a vision for AI in K-12 education, but only 43% had assisted or planned to assist districts with implementation support. Among the 39 states and territories studied for a state early adopter database, just 11% had reached the "integrator" stage of moving past guidance into pilots, evaluation, procurement help, and implementation strategies. The authors, Bree Dusseault and Dana Harrison of the Center on Reinventing Public Education, argue that this gap leaves schools without the practical help they need. The authors say AI is a difficult policy area because both the technology and public opinion change quickly, so guidance and task forces alone fall short.

School and district leaders need state help with vetting products, generating evidence on what works, and building trust in how AI is used. States also need infrastructure that links policy to classroom practice and turns scattered local experiments into shared knowledge. The article notes that many state education agencies lack the funding or internal expertise to lead these efforts. Intermediary organizations, the authors write, can fill that role, and a majority of participants in their study reported pursuing partnerships for strategy development, implementation, or both.

The article uses Tennessee's State Collaborative on Reforming Education, known as SCORE, as its main example. SCORE is a statewide nonprofit without formal authority over district decisions, and its influence comes from long-standing relationships with state leaders, districts, colleges, funders, and technology providers. After Tennessee required districts to adopt AI policies covering safety, academic integrity, and risk mitigation, SCORE convened a working group that met regularly for roughly 18 months, and its recommendations were reflected in the state's Action Plan. SCORE also helps districts evaluate tools without endorsing products, and it helped fund a larger rollout of Coursemojo, an AI-enabled literacy tool, across seven districts, 20 schools, and more than 4,000 students in 2025-26.

The authors say participating leaders and teachers reported positive results, and districts later renewed the work, often with their own funds. The authors stress that the Tennessee model need not be copied exactly, since an intermediary could be a nonprofit, a university, a technical service provider, or a research group, as long as it has trust, staying power, and the ability to connect people who do not normally work together. They warn that without such coordinated support, better-resourced districts may experiment while smaller and higher-need systems struggle to evaluate tools, set safeguards, and provide training, which could widen existing inequities. They conclude that the next phase of state AI leadership will depend less on publishing guidance than on building infrastructure for continuous learning, so that policies set direction and partnerships provide the capacity to follow it.

stories.Headline: South Korea’s GDP growth beats forecasts amid AI boom
stories.Summary:
South Korea's economy grew much faster than expected in the July-September quarter, driven by strong global demand for chips used in artificial intelligence. Gross domestic product expanded 1 percent from the previous quarter, or 3.4 percent from a year earlier, according to advance estimates the Bank of Korea released on Tuesday. The central bank had forecast in August that growth would reach only 0.3 percent in the third quarter. The figures were published on October 27, 2026, by Al Jazeera, which reported them from the bank's data.

Exports, which make up about 45 percent of the country's GDP, rose 2.3 percent from the prior quarter, led by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment. Investment in facilities rose 4.1 percent and investment in intellectual property rose 2.3 percent, while construction investment edged up 0.7 percent. Private consumption, however, fell 0.2 percent despite the gains in exports and investment. Taken together, the quarter's results put the economy on course for its fastest expansion in more than a decade.

Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said earlier this month that he expected growth of 3.4 to 3.6 percent in 2026, which would be the strongest annual performance since 2011 excluding the COVID-19 pandemic. The economy had grown only 1 percent in 2025, its slowest pace since the pandemic. The article credits the rebound to a global shortage of memory chips, which has benefited South Korea's industry. South Korean exports in September jumped 83.5 percent from a year earlier to $120.9 billion, with chips making up nearly half of all shipments, according to the Korea Customs Service.

South Korea is home to two of the world's three largest memory chip makers, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. The two companies together control roughly 80 percent of the global market for high-bandwidth memory and 60 percent of the market for dynamic random-access memory. Asia's fourth-largest economy has therefore been well placed to profit from the surge in demand for AI hardware. The article does not describe any further policy steps or forecasts beyond the current estimates.

stories.Headline: RTX Spark: Local AI Coding Fails, I’ve Had (More Than) a Few ⭐
stories.Summary:
Thurrott.com and ZDNET have both published hands-on accounts of Nvidia's RTX Spark laptops, testing whether local AI can handle coding work. Paul Thurrott, writing on October 27, 2026, said he has spent many days trying to find a local AI coding setup on the RTX Spark that works consistently, and that he has only scored occasional small wins. He tested Llama Windows, a graphical front end to the llama.cpp inference engine, which Hugging Face timed to the launch of the RTX Spark computers earlier in the month. Thurrott described the setup as complex and said he had been repeating experiments with different tools and models almost every day for weeks.

David Gewirtz, writing for ZDNET on October 26, 2026, tested Lenovo's Yoga 9n 2-in-1, a 16-inch laptop priced at $4,000 with a 20-core processor, 64GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD. He compared it with his own 2025 Mac Studio, which has 128GB of unified memory and cost $5,300. In benchmarks, the Mac delivered about 1.3 times the CPU performance of the Lenovo, and the Lenovo was about three times faster at prompt processing. The Mac pulled ahead on token generation, however, running about 2.5 times faster on a 32-billion-parameter model, which Gewirtz attributed to the Lenovo's smaller memory pool. He ran a local coding agent, OpenCode, with an 80-billion-parameter Qwen coder model and a 32,768-token context window, the largest he could make work with Windows and the model loaded.

Gewirtz reported that the laptop was able to take Mac-only source code for an icon gallery app and, without a spec or screenshots, produce a rough Windows version within about four hours, though he noted much more work would be needed before it could be distributed. He said the constant context refreshes were tedious, and he credited the machine with staying cool during four hours of heavy work. In a battery stress test, the laptop ran a custom CPU and memory workload for one hour and 20 minutes from a full charge before shutting down, and its fan was loud enough to hear from the next room. Thurrott's account offers the more skeptical view, while Gewirtz's report shows that local coding can work on this hardware with real limits on memory and battery life.

stories.Headline: [PRNewswire] Guidewire Delivers Core Platform for Agentic Insurance
stories.Summary:
Guidewire, the insurance software company listed on the NYSE as GWRE, launched a new platform approach to agentic insurance on October 28, 2026, at its Connections conference in Las Vegas. The company says the platform gives insurers an open, secure, and complete foundation for using AI across the insurance lifecycle. It brings together applications, data, workflows, and controls so that insurers can move from isolated AI experiments to governed agents that improve the speed and precision of decisions. Guidewire presents this as a practical model for doing so.

The platform places agents on the same system that runs the company's core applications, so they can work with an insurer's current data and workflows. Controls define what each agent can know and do, with consistent security and an audit trail that stays current through ongoing updates. Guidewire describes its growing portfolio across underwriting, claims, and technical infrastructure, including Advanced Product Designer, PricingCenter, Risk Accumulation App, UnderwritingCenter, ProNavigator, Concierge, and Kaleidoscope. Several features, marked as early access or roadmap items, are available only to certain customers, and the company notes that some release features may not be available in all regions.

Mike Rosenbaum, Guidewire's chief executive officer, said that insurance is a business of decisions made in context and that embedding agents in core operations gives them the context and controls they need. Diego Devalle, the company's chief product development officer, said the scalability and observability that support the core now support agents as well, which lets insurers put them to work on live claims and policies. Amy Mollin, vice president of product management, said agents built into ClaimCenter capture losses, summarize files, and flag risk so adjusters have more time for important conversations. Karlyn Carnahan of Celent said the next challenge for insurers is making these capabilities work within existing systems. Tatjana Lalkovic, chief technology officer at Definity, said Guidewire's Developer Assistants help her company's teams move from idea to implementation faster.

The announcement comes as insurers face pressure from competitors to become more agile with products and pricing, and as many have moved past early AI experiments. Guidewire says it is also using AI in its own professional services, where it reports materially shorter migration and implementation timelines. The company is demonstrating the platform at Connections, where more than 3,000 insurers and partners from 36 countries are gathered for its annual customer conference. Guidewire will continue to expand its portfolio of agents, though the announcement itself does not specify a timeline for further releases.

stories.Headline: The Memory Bottleneck Divide: SK Hynix Sells out to Tier-1s, Micron Absorbs the Spills
stories.Summary:
SK hynix has reportedly sold out its AI memory capacity for next year, while Micron is locking in buyers through long-term agreements. According to the 24/7 Wall St. article, SK hynix posted second-quarter revenue of KRW 79.32 trillion, up 256.8% year over year, though that missed consensus of about KRW 84.12 trillion. Its operating profit reached KRW 60.54 trillion, up 557.2%, and it carries a 48.6% operating margin. Those figures point to strong pricing power in DRAM and NAND alongside a shift toward premium AI memory.

Micron, by contrast, reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion, beating the $50.97 billion consensus, with non-GAAP earnings per share of $33.42 against an estimate of $31.35. The article says Core Data Center led with $18.00 billion, which it reads as a sign that AI servers now set the company's pace. Micron has signed 26 strategic customer agreements, including 10 new ones this quarter, and it is co-designing an HBM4E product with NVIDIA. It has also raised pricing significantly for calendar year 2027, and management said it has no line of sight to when supply and demand will balance. Micron guided fiscal first-quarter revenue to $61.5 billion, plus or minus $1.5 billion.

The article's author, Alex Sirois, argues that both companies remain cyclical and that Micron carries more downside exposure because its HBM share is smaller and its commodity memory business is wider. He notes that a delay in data center spending or an inventory correction would likely hit Micron first, while SK hynix's sold-out HBM book gives him more comfort, though ADS holders still face currency risk. He also says his view would change if Micron's NVIDIA co-design turns into meaningful HBM4E share. Over the past month, SK hynix shares fell about 25.55% and Micron shares fell about 16.49%, and the author suggests cycle risk may already be weighing on both. SK hynix reports its third-quarter results soon, and the author plans to check whether its revenue catches up with consensus.

A separate Dr. Robert Castellano newsletter piece, dated October 26, 2026, adds context on Micron's technology strategy. It reports that during an October 21, 2026 webinar, Micron's chief technology and products officer, Scott DeBoer, said the company will not commercialize the 4F² DRAM cell design being studied by Samsung, SK hynix, and CXMT. Micron instead plans to keep scaling conventional DRAM while developing wafer bonding and eventually three-dimensional DRAM. The newsletter recalls that Micron was late to HBM, which trailed its two rivals, and asks whether this decision repeats that pattern. The rest of that piece is behind a paywall, so the outcome of that debate is not stated in the material available here.

stories.Headline: Lumion Highlights AI Agents for After-Hours Inquiries and Lead Follow-Up
stories.Summary:
Lumion, a technology company based in Salt Lake City, Utah, announced on October 27, 2026 that it is promoting AI agents built to handle customer inquiries, automated follow-up, and outreach to prospective customers. The platform combines AI-powered communication, workflow automation, and a unified inbox so organizations can manage calls, text messages, and website inquiries in one place. The company says the agents answer after-hours calls and other messages around the clock, and they can capture conversation details for employees to review later. The announcement targets a familiar problem, namely that inquiries often arrive when staff cannot respond, and delayed replies can cause prospects to move on.

The agents are meant to handle routine questions and record relevant context while leaving employees free to take over conversations that need more attention. A unified inbox gathers interactions from phone, email, and text so staff do not have to check several systems to see a customer's history. The platform also includes lead reactivation, which lets businesses reconnect with older prospects who never enrolled or completed a transaction. Lumion says businesses can start using the agents in as little as two weeks, configured around each organization's information and processes. Afterward, customers can extend the platform into application and onboarding workflows.

Lumion's chief statements come from Bilal Aslim, who is quoted in the announcement. He says a customer inquiry can arrive at any time, while a business team cannot always respond right away. According to Aslim, AI agents can help maintain continuity by responding to initial inquiries, capturing context, and supporting follow-up, so employees can concentrate on work that needs their judgment. The company presents the platform as a way to coordinate these tasks rather than to remove people from customer communication.

The announcement includes one customer example. At a career school, AI outreach to leads inactive for about two years produced two enrollments in the first week and 14 more over the following several weeks, with the first two generating a combined $10,000 in paid deposits. The articles stress that this reflects one customer's experience and that other organizations may see different results depending on lead quality and prospect responses. The company also says it has worked with more than 400 businesses and has managed and generated over $300 million in customer revenue through its platform. It further reports a $10.7 million seed round announced June 16, 2025, led by TTV Capital with participation from Tusk Venture Partners, intended to support market expansion and product innovation.

stories.Headline: Tsinghua University & NVIDIA Unveil New AI Video Model Ranking: Exposing Shortcomings of 38 Real-Time Generative AI Video Systems
stories.Summary:
Tsinghua University, NVIDIA and several other universities and research institutions have jointly released StreamEval, a new benchmark for streaming interactive AI video generation. The ranking covers 38 models, and the researchers presented it in late October 2026 as the first evaluation of its kind in the industry. Existing tools such as VBench and EvalCrafter judge a single prompt and the video it produces, which leaves them unable to test how these systems handle instructions that keep arriving during generation. StreamEval was built to close that gap by testing the systems under conditions closer to real use.

The benchmark spans five task types: digital human dialogue, virtual human performance, world generation, instruction editing and reference editing. Each type has 60 test cases, run at durations of 15, 30, 60, 120 and 300 seconds, and each case is run three times by the same model. The full dataset includes 1,347 online events released step by step along the timeline, so a model sees only the input available at that moment. Performance is scored across four dimensions and ten indicators, each rated from 0 to 100, and the five task types are ranked separately rather than merged into one overall list. All code, datasets and scoring rules are open source, and developers can submit their own models to the leaderboard.

The results show that a model producing stable video does not necessarily follow changing instructions. In digital human dialogue, Vidu S2-Avatar reached the top overall score among participating models that support custom images, at 93.98 after a 5-point bonus. In virtual human performance, the same system scored highest overall at 81.71, yet its instruction-following score was only 36.90, the highest value among seven models but still low. In world generation, the top overall scores were held by different models on different measures, which the researchers say shows that visual quality, instruction response and long-term continuity must be judged separately. The reference editing task was the hardest, with the best overall score at 39.02 and an edit success rate of only 15.00.

A separate report from the same period describes Cadence Design Systems and NVIDIA announcing a partnership and the Maestro AI model family, fine-tuned on NVIDIA's Nemotron models to work with Cadence's electronic design automation tools. Cadence's Paul Cunningham said that somewhere between 20 and 30 percent of chips under development are now designed with help from AI agents, a share he expects to keep growing. Cadence claims early testing showed up to a 30 percent gain in output quality and up to five times better token efficiency compared with general-purpose foundation models. The Maestro platform can be accessed through an API, run in a secure virtual private cloud, or deployed on premises, with customization on customer data offered as a managed service. The same report links this trend to the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, which has driven a series of new Nvidia-based supercomputers.

stories.Headline: Faculties of Education in Latin America address how to prepare future teachers for the age of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
On 14 October 2026, the UNESCO Regional Office in Santiago, together with the Network of Deans of Education of Latin American Universities (REDECANEDU) and the National Council of Deans of Faculties of Education of CRUCH Universities (CONFAUCE) in Chile, and in collaboration with CodeAI, held a regional round table on preparing future teachers for an age of artificial intelligence. The event, titled "Teaching and artificial intelligence: institutional challenges for initial teacher education," brought together 50 representatives of teacher education institutions from across Latin America. Participants examined how these institutions can incorporate AI into their work in ways that are critical, ethical and inclusive. Experiences from Mexico, Colombia and Chile were shared during the discussions.

The organizers stressed that teacher education must go beyond showing future teachers how to use digital tools. Felipe Fontecilla of CodeAI identified three key decisions for Faculties of Education: integrating AI into curricula, setting academic integrity criteria that require students to declare and justify their use of AI, and ensuring the time, resources and conditions needed to build the capacities of teacher educators. He also distinguished between the instrumental use of AI tools and AI literacy, which allows future teachers to understand how these technologies work, question their outputs and take part in shaping them. Francisca Díaz, Coordinator of the Regional Teacher Strategy at UNESCO, said the aim is to prepare teachers who can judge when and how to use AI while keeping their professional autonomy.

She called for institutional strategies covering curricula, assessment, academic integrity and the training of teacher educators, rather than isolated individual initiatives. Speakers from three institutions described their own approaches. Francisco Díaz Estrada of the Tecnológico de Monterrey in Mexico presented work on personalized learning, secure institutional environments for AI use, ethical governance and teacher professional development, stressing the evaluation of learning processes and the protection of data privacy. María Isabel Afanador Rodríguez, dean of the Faculty of Distance and Virtual Education at the Institución Universitaria Antonio José Camacho in Colombia, argued that AI should be linked to pedagogical knowledge, critical reflection and support for students facing inequality, while preserving essential human interaction in education.

Luis Alejandro Nitrihual Valdebenito, dean of the Faculty of Education, Social Sciences and Humanities at the Universidad de La Frontera in Chile, described the redesign of teaching degrees to integrate technology, pedagogical and ethical judgement, equity, inclusion and interculturality across the curriculum. The participants identified shared challenges despite the differences in their national contexts, including the need to strengthen institutional leadership, build the capacities of academic teams, and protect teachers' autonomy and professional judgement as AI use grows. UNESCO Santiago proposed a second regional meeting focused on concrete experiences that Faculties of Education are already implementing, so that progress, challenges and lessons can be shared. The proposal aligns with the work of the Observatory on Artificial Intelligence in Education for Latin America and the Caribbean, which supports evidence generation, knowledge exchange and regional cooperation.

stories.Headline: UnitedHealthcare Is Rolling Out Its AI Agent To 21 Million Members
stories.Summary:
UnitedHealthcare is expanding access to Avery, its generative AI companion designed to support care coordination for members, to 21 million people. The tool was first unveiled earlier this year, when it was available to about 6.5 million members in employer plans and 160,000 people enrolled in Medicare Advantage. The expansion is growing the tool's reach faster than the insurer originally expected, according to the reporting. The company says Avery has resolved 90% of member interactions, and in the remaining 10% of cases it can hand off to a human advocate.

Avery is built on what the company calls ground truth systems, a data foundation that sits on top of the information available through UnitedHealthcare. Craig Kurtzweil, the company's chief data and analytics officer, said that foundation is what lets members get better answers. Avery can provide details on deductibles, out-of-pocket maximums, provider networks, pricing and claims processing. Kurtzweil said accuracy is central to members trusting the tool and using it effectively. He described making the tool as accurate as possible as a major part of earning consumers' trust.

Kurtzweil told Fierce Healthcare that the expansion makes sense given the early results and feedback from users. He said Avery fits into a broader push to put more information in members' hands, including plan designs like Surest, which offer variable copayments that let members choose providers and care. The team is also building an option for Avery to call providers and schedule appointments on a member's behalf. Kurtzweil said the company intends to keep widening access until all of its enrollees can use the tool. He added that more and more people will be affected as the company works to reduce friction and make things easier for consumers.

stories.Headline: GDPR and CRM: What your customer data obligations mean
stories.Summary:
Article 1, published by HubSpot on October 27, 2026, explains how the EU General Data Protection Regulation applies to customer data kept in a CRM system. It says GDPR covers any CRM record holding personal data about people in the European Union or United Kingdom, wherever the company is based. The guide notes that this includes contact details, form submissions, emails, call logs, and behavioral data such as email opens. It stresses that a company must identify and document a lawful basis before processing that data, with consent and legitimate interest being the two bases that come up most often in CRM work. The article recommends tracking the lawful basis for each record separately rather than applying one setting to every contact.

The article describes what the rules require in practice. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous, so a pre-checked box or silence does not count, and subscription preferences should be granular so a person can opt out of marketing emails without opting out of other communications. Individuals hold rights of access, rectification, portability, restriction, erasure, and objection, and the article says each needs a repeatable process rather than an ad hoc response. For erasure, it warns that deleting a record from the core CRM is not enough if connected tools still hold it, since the data can resurface on the next sync. Objections to direct marketing must be honored immediately, and the objection itself should be logged so the status is not lost.

The article also addresses data minimization and retention, advising teams to collect only fields with a stated purpose and to review retention on a quarterly or biannual cadence. The article is written by Sam Lauron and presented as a guide from HubSpot, which sells CRM software and describes its own features as supporting compliant execution. It states that these features help with compliance but do not guarantee it, and it advises organizations to work with a legal advisor or data privacy expert. The article does not report any enforcement action or specific incident. It is a general explanation of obligations, and it does not indicate any further steps beyond what teams should do to set up their own processes.

Article 2, published by BusinessWorld Online on October 26, 2026, is the second part of a piece on how boards should govern data and artificial intelligence. It sets out several themes, including maintaining an inventory of reports, models, generative AI uses, and agents with assigned owners, and tiering controls by potential impact in line with risk-based approaches such as ISO 31000. It urges clear accountability, ongoing monitoring across the full life cycle, and treating vendors as part of the control environment. It also distinguishes binding law, such as the Data Privacy Act of 2012, from supervisory guidance and voluntary frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and it says personal data must be processed lawfully before it enters any model. The piece suggests that board committees can divide oversight among risk, audit, and governance matters while the full board keeps accountability, and it closes with questions directors should ask management.

stories.Headline: Modular builds back AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
A China Mobile data center expansion in Hohhot, in China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region, has passed its completion inspection after 211 days of construction. The work took place both on site and on factory production lines. Computing, cooling and backup power equipment was built into prefabricated units, which were then trucked to the site to form two server buildings and supporting power facilities. While site crews prepared foundations, factory workers assembled the equipment, wiring and pipework, so the units could be lifted into place and connected with little installation work left to do.

The contractor was China Construction Third Bureau First Engineering Co Ltd, and its chief engineer, Du Junzi, said that coordinating design, purchasing and production early lets tasks that normally happen one after another run at the same time. Planning starts on the drawing board, where teams check that connections match, delivery routes are clear and there is room for maintenance. Standardized connections also allow equipment to be added as demand grows. Du said the company chooses cooling systems to suit each project's conditions and uses technologies including natural cooling and heat recovery, with the aim of keeping facilities efficient throughout their working lives. In Hohhot, teams simulated power outages and cooling failures to confirm that backup systems responded as intended.

The flexibility matters to operators because large-scale artificial intelligence services need buildings that can host computing equipment and keep it supplied with electricity and cooling as workloads change. The International Energy Agency expects global data centers to use nearly twice as much electricity in 2030 as in 2025, and it names power supply, grid connections and equipment manufacturing among the constraints on expansion. China's "east data, west computing" initiative seeks to draw on regions with suitable energy and other resources to serve computing demand, including from eastern economic centers. The article adds that a facility's environmental performance depends on the electricity it uses, so energy supply and operating efficiency matter alongside the way it is built.

Elsewhere in the sector, conditions look tougher. Nscale, a London-based AI data center developer backed by Nvidia, is facing pushback over the roughly $30 billion valuation it is seeking in a U.S. IPO, according to a Bloomberg report citing people familiar with the matter. Some investors argue that a valuation of $16 billion to $19 billion would be more likely to draw buyers, pointing partly to the collapse of Australian AI data center company Firmus' IPO plan. Microsoft, both an investor and a client, has pulled out of a UK data center deal with Nscale after power constraints delayed the site, and construction at its flagship Norway facility is running six months behind schedule. Nscale filed publicly for the listing on September 18 and is still working through SEC comments before it begins marketing, after raising $3.36 billion last month in a pre-IPO round led by Third Point.

stories.Headline: Agentic AI Foundation expands with four new projects
stories.Summary:
The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) has grown from three projects to ten in its first year, adding four new initiatives at the AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026 event in San Jose on October 22 and 23. Mazin Gilbert, the foundation's executive director, announced the new projects along with three new governance committees. Alibaba contributed OpenSandbox, a secure sandbox for running agents, while OpenAI contributed Open Responses, a specification for interoperable large language model interfaces. Anthropic added its Agent Skills standard, and Hugging Face contributed OpenEnv, a framework for reinforcement learning environments. The event itself shifted much of its focus toward protocol features, security, and identity.

Open Responses already has support from AWS Bedrock, Databricks, Ollama, Nvidia, and vLLM, according to coverage of the event. Anthropic's Model Context Protocol received a stateless server mode in its July 28 specification, and about 70 percent of traffic on some platforms already uses it. Anthropic also announced support for MCP tasks in Claude Code, which lets tool calls run for minutes, hours, or even days. On the security side, cumulative SDK downloads for the protocol have reached 4.17 billion, up from about 3 billion a month earlier. About a third of the 116 conformance scenarios now test security, and enterprise-managed authorization is live in Claude.

Manik Surtani, the foundation's CTO, said the organization launched a year ago with a belief that agentic AI needed a neutral home to thrive. He compared the situation to Kubernetes, which succeeded after Google moved it into a neutral foundation. Surtani argued that a license alone does not keep infrastructure open and said the remaining open problems sit in identity, attestation, audit, and payments. Some outside observers were more skeptical, with one publication noting that Anthropic still defines its own Messages API and Google its Interactions API. Another warned that the rapid embrace of AI agents may be too fast for some industries.

Other speakers addressed practical and security concerns. Dawn Song, a UC Berkeley professor, warned that frontier AI could help attackers more than defenders in the near term, citing a benchmark in which one model produced about 230 working exploits against 869 targets in two hours. Her proposed response was secure-by-construction systems supported by AI-generated proofs. Chrome's Sarah Drasner presented WebMCP, a proposed web standard in origin trial that lets websites expose tools directly to agents, which she said can make some actions 2.5 to 7.5 times faster and complements MCP rather than replacing it. Block also demonstrated Buzz, an open source workspace where people and agents share channels, with version 1.0 expected in mid-November.

stories.Headline: Apple announces Siri AI will expand to these new languages soon
stories.Summary:
Apple released iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 on Monday, October 26, 2026, as the first major updates to the iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 systems that launched in September. The update expands Siri AI to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, which were not supported before, and it adds several other features. Apple also said four more languages, Chinese (Traditional), Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, will arrive by the end of the year. Siri AI was previously available only in English.

The Siri AI improvements in this release let the assistant recall earlier conversations, so a user can ask about a restaurant it suggested the week before. It can also draw on more sources, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, voicemails, and Safari history and Reading List. A new Excluded Apps setting lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can reach from one place. Other additions include Messages suggestions that help with tasks like adding a dinner invite to Calendar, and support for SynthID watermarking in Photos and Image Playground. The update also brings Simple Profiles to the Apple TV app and lets FaceTime calls include a third-party sign language interpreter or live captioner.

Apple did not describe who was responsible for the changes beyond the company itself, and the articles give no statement from any individual. The release notes say Siri AI is not available in the European Union or mainland China. Bloomberg reporting cited in one article says Apple plans to bring some initial Apple Intelligence features to China with iOS 27.3, but Siri AI is not expected among them. The articles expect the new Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese support to arrive with iOS 27.3, which is expected in December, with its first beta possibly appearing the following week.

The release also comes alongside other Apple announcements, including a new Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 with Siri AI announced on October 13. Users can get the update by going to Settings, then General, then Software Update. Apple also released iOS 26.7.2 with security fixes. Readers who have tried Siri AI in a language other than English have been invited to share their experiences in the comments.

stories.Headline: Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling
stories.Summary:
Investors who avoided AI-linked stocks have recently matched the broader market this year, after a sharp selloff in technology shares. A Goldman Sachs index that tracks the S&P 500 while excluding companies it considers enablers of AI was up 12.4% through October 22, which put it slightly ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The crossover came after the ex-AI index had trailed for most of 2026, and the S&P 500 tech sector fell about 7% during October while other sectors held up. Goldman launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, and it starts from the S&P 500 and removes those AI-related names before applying the usual index weighting.

The pullback in technology has been driven by investor doubts about the heavy spending on AI infrastructure. Shares of Meta Platforms fell almost 7% on Thursday after it outlined further plans for heavy capital spending and additional share issuance, and debt and equity tied to companies such as CoreWeave and Oracle have also lost favor. Power and equipment suppliers for the data-center buildout, including GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services, took steep losses. Separately, Axios reported that Meta's stock was hit last week despite stronger-than-expected third-quarter results, with the company's unspecified plans to spend aggressively on AI seen as the concern, and that Meta's quarterly free cash flow turned negative in the third quarter. Axios also reported that the 10-year Treasury yield, which hit more than 5.30% earlier in the month, fell to 5.00% by the end of the week as investors sought safety.

Analysts quoted by CNBC are recommending diversification away from AI exposure as protection against further weakness in technology. Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in an October 24 note that the pendulum had swung back toward non-AI holdings over the prior two weeks, and the firm upgraded commercial services and insurance to overweight, naming Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher. Berkshire Hathaway's Class B shares rose 8% this month, which CNBC attributed partly to its diversified holdings. Trivector Research pointed to non-tech companies such as Eli Lilly, whose stock is up 22% this year, and Viking Holdings, which said 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was booked for 2027. Barclays upgraded Viking to overweight with a $102 target, while the average Wall Street target is $109 against recent prices near $82.

Whether the rotation lasts remains uncertain, and the articles do not forecast how the AI trade will develop. Axios noted that the expenditures expected over the next year will need heavy financing from the corporate bond market, which is a source of investor anxiety. Investors also face economic, political and market turmoil that has encouraged a scramble for safety in both stock and bond markets. CNBC noted that some energy gains reflect the war in Iran rather than the rotation itself.

stories.Headline: Abu Dhabi's G42 brings AI expertise to the UAE and Greece
stories.Summary:
Abu Dhabi-based G42 has announced a series of memorandums of understanding that extend its AI work into the UAE and Greece. Emirates Petroleum Company, known as Emarat, signed one with G42 to explore AI, cybersecurity and advanced digital technologies as it moves into its next phase of transformation. The agreement covers AI applications for the energy sector, digital security and sovereignty, and next-generation service station concepts. The stated aim is to support innovation across the energy value chain through secure infrastructure and better customer experiences.

G42 has also signed agreements with Greek government and private-sector partners covering AI infrastructure, government services, life sciences and smart cities. With Greek infrastructure investor Copelouzos Group and UAE data centre provider Khazna Data Centres, along with Core42, the partners will explore an AI factory in Greece combining data centre infrastructure with cloud and compute capacity. Khazna is expected to lead the physical build, while Core42 will supply cloud and AI compute for sectors including banking, telecoms, shipping and government. Presight will work with Greece's Ministry of Digital Governance on AI urban analytics for public safety, starting with municipal waste management and water-network monitoring. Separate work covers applying agentic AI to government operations and education, and M42 has agreed a broad partnership with Athens LifeTech Park.

The announcements come from G42 and the companies named in them, and the articles present them as exploratory. Emarat's agreement is described as a plan to explore opportunities rather than a fixed programme with set costs or deadlines. The Greek arrangements likewise describe areas of focus, such as demonstrating potential use cases, without giving figures for investment or timelines. The articles do not report any statement from Greek officials beyond the existence of the agreements.

The wider context is G42's broader push to export AI services from the UAE. In a separate report, Group Chief Executive Peng Xiao presented AI services as a possible export business linked to a planned Abu Dhabi campus, Stargate UAE, a one-gigawatt computing cluster within a five-gigawatt UAE-U.S. AI campus. G42 expects the first 200 megawatts to begin operating in 2026, though it has not given a specific date that year. The articles give no cost figures, export revenue forecasts or named overseas customers for these plans. The next stated milestone is that first 200-megawatt cluster.

stories.Headline: 'This is a wow moment': T-Mobile has made the world's first AI-RAN call, and it could mean huge changes for the next generation of staying in touch
stories.Summary:
T-Mobile, Nokia and Nvidia say they have completed what they describe as the world's first AI-RAN call, routed through a commercial cell site in Bellevue, Washington. The call ran over T-Mobile's live production network using a Nokia Massive MIMO radio, Nokia's 5G anyRAN software, and servers built on Nvidia's Aerial RAN Computer platform. The companies stress that this was not a lab setup with test handsets, since the site connected to T-Mobile's existing 5G Standalone core and a commercial smartphone. The reported results, however, did not include any AI performance data.

The announcement came on October 27, 2026. The technology involved moves the radio access network, the antennas, radios and baseband computers that process signals at each cell site, away from custom chips and onto accelerated hardware. In this case that means Nvidia GPUs running Nokia's CUDA-based radio software, which allows AI models to fine-tune the radio link and could, in theory, rent out spare capacity to other AI workloads. The main goal is spectral efficiency, meaning more data carried through the same slice of airwaves.

Nokia's chief technology and AI officer, Pallavi Mahajan, wrote in a blog post about the call that the company is on a path to twice the spectral efficiency with AI-RAN. Nokia's July 2026 platform launch claimed efficiency gains of more than 20 percent so far, without saying where they were measured. Nokia has put its targets on a timeline, forecasting 50 percent gains in 2027 and more than 100 percent in 2028. Commercial AI-RAN equipment is due in 2027, according to the reporting, and 6G networks are expected around 2030.

The companies behind the call are the ones making these claims, and the articles present their statements as the basis for the milestone. Because no independent performance figures were published with the call, the efficiency targets remain company projections rather than measured results. The articles do not say when, or whether, consumers will see any of these changes on their devices. The first AI-RAN deployments are therefore still a matter of future commercial rollout rather than something customers can use today.

stories.Headline: AI4Research: a survey of artificial intelligence for scientific research
stories.Summary:
An AI research framework called AI4Research, described in a survey published on 27 October 2026 in Science China Information Sciences, maps how artificial intelligence is being used to carry out scientific research. The survey's authors, led by a group from Harbin Institute of Technology and other institutions, say that recent large language models such as OpenAI-o1 and DeepSeek-R1 have shown strong skill at logical reasoning and experimental coding. That progress has prompted many studies into systems that could run research workflows across many disciplines. Until now, however, no broad survey had pulled this work together, which the authors say has slowed understanding of the field.

The survey offers a classification of five mainstream tasks in AI for research and points to gaps and future directions, especially the rigor and scalability of automated experiments and the wider societal impact. It also compiles multidisciplinary applications, data corpora and tools, which the authors have made publicly available on GitHub. A separate report from 26 October 2026 describes a related evaluation framework called Agent4Sci, put forward by Anthropic researchers, which tests coding agents on 25 machine learning for science tasks across 11 scientific domains and 20 benchmarks. Those tasks were chosen from 497 candidate papers, with about 98 percent rejected, and each had to pass a baseline reproduction and standardized data splits, operating environments and training processes.

The Anthropic team ran the framework with a three-stage protocol that keeps the agent that improves a model, the agent that evaluates it on a held-out test set and the agent that audits the logs in separate roles. Four agents took part, namely Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Codex (GPT-5.4), each given eight H200 GPUs and a 12-hour budget with no human input on specific decisions. Average relative improvements were 10.4, 9.6, 6.8 and 4.4 percent respectively, and every one of the 20 benchmarks improved for at least one agent. The researchers say the gains came mostly from conventional machine learning engineering techniques rather than research-level insight, and that adding three lightweight plugin skills for research ideation, experiment management and timed checklists raised Opus's average improvement to 20.1 percent. The work was selected for the Evaluation and Datasets track at NeurIPS 2026.

The Anthropic researchers stress that independent evaluation and auditing do not rule out every covert form of gaming the benchmarks, even though cross-checks using auditing agents from the Claude, Codex and Gemini families found no flagged runs. The same article's headline framing, that AI still cannot conduct genuine real-world scientific research, reflects the conclusion that the observed gains were largely routine rather than scientific discovery. The survey's authors, for their part, describe the field as at an early stage and call for further work on rigor and social impact. The articles do not say what follow-up steps the authors or the Anthropic team plan beyond these publications.

stories.Headline: Entrepreneur wins $50,000 at University of Arkansas at Little Rock artificial intelligence pitch competition | The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
stories.Summary:
Kelvin Bell, founder and CEO of Stratos Digital, won the top prize at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock's second annual artificial intelligence pitch competition, which was sponsored by Amazon Web Services. The prize was $50,000 in technical development services, awarded for his project Victor AI. The competition took place on October 15, and the news was reported on October 26, 2026. Bell's project is a bilingual AI agent that helps restaurants answer phone calls, take orders, answer menu questions and suggest additional purchases. Victor AI is built to understand a restaurant's menu well enough to accept phone orders and try one up-sell per order, with the goal of raising the business's profit margins.

Bell said the prize will be crucial to developing the platform, which he said addresses an industry with high operating costs and low profit margins. He also said he has been interested in technology since he was seven years old. Bell already has two restaurants in Arkansas using the service, which lets staff focus on food preparation and other operations while the AI agent handles phone calls. Other winners were Ashley Franke, founder of The Rockin' Chair, who took second place and $35,000 in services, and James Hensley, whose company On Paper took third place and $25,000 in technical development services. Franke's platform gathers accessibility information about live event venues in one place for customers with disabilities, and she hopes to fund it through partnerships with venues so it stays free for fans.

Hensley's app lets people under probation or parole upload an image of their supervision conditions and receives reminders about responsibilities and appointments. Hensley said about 70,000 Arkansans are currently under supervision. The competition comes as UALR expands its AI offerings, including a bachelor's degree in AI launched this fall, which the university describes as the first of its kind at a public university in Arkansas. Laura Fine, state director for the Arkansas Small Business and Technology Development Center, said the pitches showed that Arkansas entrepreneurs have creative ideas and that the three winning companies will receive support to accelerate their work with AI.

stories.Headline: Liquid AI Releases LFM3: 6 Open-Weight 2B-Class Multimodal Models
stories.Summary:
Liquid AI has released LFM3, a new generation of its Liquid Foundation Models, consisting of six open-weight models in the 2-billion-parameter class that share one backbone. The family covers text, vision, audio, omni, and decision tasks, and Liquid AI says every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU and then deployed on phones, laptops, private servers, or in the cloud. The two articles report the release on October 27, 2026, with the Hugging Face post presenting it as the starting point for specialized models. Both are written around the same family of models.

The family includes LFM3-1.7B, a text model with 1.73 billion parameters and a 256K context window that can run in about 1 GB of memory at 4-bit precision. LFM3-VL-2B is the first LFM vision model to accept video input, sampled at 2 frames per second, and LFM3-Audio-2B handles speech in and out across 18 languages with tool calling. LFM3-Omni-2B combines vision, audio, and language, and two decision models, d1-2B and d1-Omni-2B, answer many questions in one forward pass. According to Liquid AI's own evaluation, LFM3-1.7B averages 49.37 across 29 benchmarks, ahead of Qwen3.5-9B at 47.24, with strong results on IFEval and AutomationBench but weaker ones on Humanity's Last Exam without tools and RULER at 128K. Checkpoints in GGUF, MLX, ONNX, FP8, and NVFP4 formats ship with the release.

The architecture uses a tri-hybrid layer mix across 24 layers, made up of 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers, with convolution kernels grown from 3 to 7. Liquid AI says it found this design through a hardware-in-the-loop architecture search covering 14 device and backend combinations, including a Raspberry Pi 5 and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. Other changes include head-wise sigmoid gates, partial RoPE on global layers, and sandwich norm. The base model was trained on 22 trillion tokens, with the final 3.5 trillion focused on agent-heavy mid-training that extended context to 256K, and post-training ran in four stages.

Liquid AI reports that LFM3-1.7B beats its own LFM2.5-2.6B with 35% fewer parameters, and that it scores 38.42 on WebArena-Verified against 28.94 for Qwen3.5-9B. Its comparison table lists the LFM Open License v1.0, which carries a $10 million revenue threshold, while several rivals use Apache 2.0. The Hugging Face post, written by members of the Liquid AI team, presents LFM3 as a basis for fine-tuning on private data and deployment at the edge. Neither article describes further releases or timelines beyond the current family.

stories.Headline: Akamai launches AI inference & agent sandbox tools
stories.Summary:
Akamai has launched two new artificial intelligence products, Akamai Inference and Akamai Agent Sandbox, adding managed model serving and isolated execution to its cloud platform. The company introduced the services on October 27, 2026, aimed at organisations moving AI systems from trials into production. These areas, which include model serving, latency, data access and agent security, have become harder for businesses to manage. The products sit on Akamai's existing cloud infrastructure.

Akamai Inference gives customers managed access to open-weight and custom models through APIs that work with existing OpenAI-compatible applications. Customers can choose serverless, pay-per-use inference or dedicated deployments. At launch the catalogue holds 12 open-weight models, with sizes from 8 billion to 2.8 trillion parameters, including NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, OpenAI gpt-oss-120b and Google Gemma 4. The service also connects to managed databases, object storage and private and public clouds so models can use enterprise data. Akamai also expanded its dedicated GPU fleet with NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra clusters, with each eight-GPU node carrying 288 GB of memory per GPU, or 2.3 TB in total.

Akamai Agent Sandbox targets AI agents that act for users or write and run code, and it places that generated code in a separate isolated environment. Agents run on Akamai Functions, while their code runs apart from the agent runtime. Delivered as an open-source component of the Spin framework, it uses WebAssembly isolation to limit compute, memory, outbound connections and system access. Developers can pick among dedicated CPU systems, NVIDIA-accelerated infrastructure, managed Kubernetes and serverless execution across edge and core environments.

Adam Karon, Chief Operating Officer and General Manager of Akamai Cloud, said customers had pushed the company to build a fuller AI offering and that they want to build, run and protect AI on one platform. Jon Alexander, Senior Vice President of Cloud Technology, said enterprises should not have to choose between speed and control when putting AI into production. Akamai said its infrastructure has secured multiyear contracts worth more than $14 billion collectively, and its cloud network spans more than 4,350 edge locations. Both products are available in beta, and Akamai plans to prepare its data centres for NVIDIA Vera Rubin systems in 2027.

stories.Headline: Deutsche Telekom Invests in Tandem Health's AI Healthcare Platform
stories.Summary:
Deutsche Telekom's strategic investment arm, T.Capital, has put money into Tandem Health, a Swedish company, as part of its Series B funding round. Tandem Health has built an AI-powered medical assistant that handles clinical documentation, coding and decision support on one platform. The system is already used at more than 10,000 healthcare facilities in 14 European countries, including Germany, and it is integrated into around 130 electronic health record systems. It holds a Class IIa medical device certification under the EU Medical Device Regulation. A second report puts the round at roughly $100 million (€90 million) and notes that the funding came last month.

The investment is meant to support Tandem Health's push toward an AI-native operating system for European healthcare providers. Beyond its current tools for documentation, coding and clinical decision support, the company is building applications for patient navigation, appointment management and administrative work. Deutsche Telekom presents the deal as part of its wider strategy to back artificial intelligence, digital platforms and sovereign cloud infrastructure in highly regulated industries. Staffing shortages and growing paperwork are putting heavy strain on European hospitals, and the companies argue that automating administrative tasks can help. Karine Peters, Managing Director at T.Capital, says AI will play a key role in addressing healthcare's challenges and that the firm sees Tandem Health as a fast-growing company that cuts administrative burden while meeting high standards for quality, safety and compliance. Gottfried Ludewig, Senior Vice President of the Health Industry and Head of Public Sector at T-Systems, says healthcare needs trustworthy, secure AI that can be deployed right away and that the partnership aims to speed up adoption of new care technologies. stories.Headline: Apple adds AI tools to Creator Studio in major update
stories.Summary:
Apple has added new artificial intelligence features and editing tools to its Apple Creator Studio suite, updating Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro, Pixelmator Pro, Keynote, Pages and Numbers. The update was announced on October 27, 2026, alongside new iMacs and a 14-inch MacBook Pro powered by the M6 chip. It will be a free App Store update for existing subscribers in November. The package brings MotionVFX content into Final Cut Pro, a new image-editing tool in Pixelmator Pro, video assets in the Content Hub, and beta assistants in Logic Pro and the productivity apps.

He also said the assistants in Logic Pro, Keynote, Pages and Numbers would change how people interact with and learn those apps. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has stepped up quality monitoring, and Gadkari said reported construction-quality problems had dropped by 30% since the monitoring began. He said he was personally reviewing hundreds of projects and urged the public to flag problem stretches on social media.

The surveillance vehicles are vehicle-mounted, multi-sensor platforms that assess road conditions and pavement quality at speeds of 40 to 80 kmph. The ministry has mandated their use, and the National Highways Authority of India is deploying them to monitor quality, plan repairs and feed data into AI-based systems such as the RAMS Data Lake. Gadkari said the ministry had already blacklisted several companies making bearings and expansion joints over quality concerns, and that it was taking a zero-tolerance approach to lapses. He also said AI-based Advanced Traffic Management Systems would be deployed first across about 1,000 km of highways, with real-time tracking of every movement. He stressed lane discipline as a way to reduce road accidents.

Gadkari is the official driving these measures, and he said he expects the remaining quality problems to be resolved over the next two years. Akhilesh Srivastava, co-chair of the CII National Taskforce on Road Safety and president of the India ITS Forum, praised the country's adoption of technology and said the next goal was how many lives could be saved on the road. MV Satish, chair of the CII National Committee on Roads and Highways, said the network needed greater durability, sustainability, safety and technological readiness, not just faster connectivity. stories.Headline: Will AI decide who wins the midterms?
stories.Summary:
Concerns about artificial intelligence are now tied to the November 3 midterm elections in the United States, and researchers at UC Berkeley and Stanford are studying whether AI tools will shape how voters get information and cast ballots. Surveys cited in the reporting show that half of U.S. adults use AI, with a quarter using it daily, up from roughly one-third two years earlier. At the same time, 82 percent of respondents in a CNN poll said they were more concerned than excited about the pace of AI development, and 71 percent wanted more government regulation. The Wesleyan Media Project counted 170 AI-generated political ads in the 2026 cycle, representing $80 million in ad spending, and more than two-thirds did not disclose their use of AI, even though lawmakers in 30 states have banned AI deepfakes in election communications.

The same reporting describes both risks and possible benefits. Berkeley political scientist Susan Hyde worries that voters may struggle to make informed choices when they cannot trust the information they receive, and she notes how easily politicians can speak to supporters through propaganda-style messaging. Her colleague Gabriel Lenz argues that false campaign claims are nothing new and that economic concerns such as inflation and unemployment usually weigh more heavily on voters. On the other side, Anthropic and OpenAI have partnered with groups such as Democracy Works and AP News to supply accurate election information, and a Stanford study led by PhD student Joe Mernyk found that participants rated a nonpartisan AI tool as trustworthy and reported stronger intentions to vote after using it. Lenz cautioned that the real question is whether chatbots will improve on voters' existing sources of information, and that this is hard to measure.

A separate analysis from Seoul Economic Daily looks at how the midterms could affect AI companies through regulation and cost. Republicans currently hold 53 Senate seats and a narrow House majority, and forecasts suggest Democrats have a strong chance of retaking the House while the Senate remains a toss-up. The Ratepayer Protection Act, which would have state regulators review how data centers pay for added grid expansion, passed the House 417 to 3 last month but failed in the Senate with 57 votes in favor and 43 against, short of the 60 needed. Democrats have introduced about six bills that would scale back tax breaks for data centers or tax AI use and excess profits, and a Reuters/Ipsos poll found 69 percent of registered Democrats supported limits on data center construction compared with 43 percent of Republicans. Industry-watching outlets say the outcome will determine whether these pressures on AI infrastructure costs grow, though the article notes that election results cannot be known until the votes are counted.

stories.Headline: AI Boom Deepens Youth Job Woes
stories.Summary:
The Bank of Korea released a report on October 26, 2026, arguing that the country's artificial intelligence and semiconductor boom is making it harder for young people to find good jobs. The central bank's analysis, titled "Sluggish Youth Employment and Policy Tasks," found that the industrial structure is being reorganized around information technology manufacturing, while companies increasingly prefer experienced workers as AI spreads. Although the youth unemployment and employment rates have not fallen to levels seen in past downturns, the share of young workers in temporary and daily jobs has clearly risen. The bank examined workers aged 15 to 29 and concluded that the trend reflects a shift toward the secondary labor market, where pay and job security are weaker.

The report says the problem cannot be solved through job programs alone, since those target only the supply of workers. It recommends pairing industrial policy with changes to the labor market, including spreading the benefits of IT manufacturing growth to related industries and domestic demand sectors and building closer links between education and industry. It also calls for a more flexible employment system so young people can enter and move between jobs more easily. The bank reported that the share of young workers moving from the secondary to the primary market fell from the 8 percent range between 2014 and 2019 to the 5 percent range in 2023 and 2024, which it described as a "secondary labor market lock-in effect." It also noted that Korea's employment protection for permanent workers ranks about 10th among 23 major countries, which it considers relatively high.

The Bank of Korea is the institution responsible for the findings, and its report was described in coverage by Businesskorea and JoongAng Daily. The bank said that existing youth employment measures focused on labor supply cannot fundamentally fix the problem, and that comprehensive reform is needed. It argued that IT manufacturing, including semiconductors, has driven recent growth but creates relatively few regular jobs compared with its output gains. The bank also warned that AI is taking over entry-level and basic tasks, which could become a structural barrier in finance and insurance, professional and technical services, and information and communications. It cautioned that even if demand recovers, youth employment could stay weak unless the gains from growth translate into quality jobs for young people.

stories.Headline: Korea should not sacrifice AI boom over chip dependence fears: IDB economist
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, October 27, 2026, Laura Alfaro, chief economist and economic counselor at the Inter-American Development Bank, told a press conference in Seoul that Korea should keep pursuing the artificial intelligence boom rather than slow growth out of worry about its heavy reliance on semiconductors. She made the remarks at the Global Financial Stability Conference 2026, hosted by the Ministry of Finance and Economy and the Korea Development Institute. Her position was that the country should instead cushion itself against swings through stabilization funds and greater structural flexibility. The comments were reported by the Korea Times and the JoongAng Daily, the latter with a wire contribution from Yonhap.

Alfaro compared Korea's exposure to chips with the "resource curse" that has affected Latin America, where economies dependent on minerals and oil suffer when commodity prices fluctuate sharply. To manage such cycles, she recommended a stabilization fund that would set aside part of the gains made during boom periods and draw on them during downturns. Such a fund could also limit excessive appreciation of the domestic currency and soften the effects of large, rapid capital inflows. She also called for more flexibility in labor markets and government spending, saying the core problem in boom-and-bust cycles is an inability to adjust in downturns. The JoongAng Daily reported that Korea has proposed a Future Fund, drawing on sources including windfall tax revenue from chipmakers, with a general account and four program accounts covering youth, growth engines, regional development, and education and talent development.

Alfaro said she was not familiar with the details of the government's proposed Future Response Fund but supported its underlying rationale, and the JoongAng Daily quoted her as saying the "spirit" of the Future Fund sounds like what needs to be done. Asked whether debt repayment should take priority over building assets, she said neither approach was necessarily superior, since both amount to saving. She also described herself as "AI positive" and argued that concern over volatility should not deter investment in the technology, since productivity gains from AI offer a route to growth in a region facing shrinking birth rates. Separately, she said Latin America's green energy and mineral resources, such as copper, could support mutually beneficial exchange with Korea in AI, given how energy-intensive the technology is. The reports do not indicate any formal government response to these remarks or what steps will follow.

stories.Headline: Risks & Rewards: How AI Is Redefining the CISO's Role
stories.Summary:
Mark Weatherford, Nvidia's head of cybersecurity policy and strategic engagement, spoke at the ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 in Denver, where he described how the chief information security officer role is changing around artificial intelligence. Security leaders are now expected to help their businesses gain a competitive edge with AI while also using the technology to manage cyber risk. Weatherford's remarks were reported by Jai Vijayan of Dark Reading on October 26, 2026. He said keeping up with the pace of change is the biggest challenge, noting that penetration testing four times a year, once considered adequate, is no longer enough and that testing should now run around the clock.

Weatherford said many organizations are deploying AI out of a fear of missing out, often without sufficient business due diligence or a clear understanding of the value they will get. He also observed that CISOs tend to default to "no" whenever there is any element of risk. He pointed to the Navy concept of command by negation, in which subordinates act on their own toward a goal unless a superior tells them to stop, and suggested security leaders should accept more risk on their own, calibrated to their company's risk tolerance. He urged CISOs to stay curious, step outside their comfort zones, and keep finding ways to improve their role, suggesting that one way to get up to speed on AI is to take up one new topic each week.

Weatherford argued that it is the CISO's job to make sure the board understands the risks and knows who owns each one, especially when another executive's AI deployment creates the risk. He acknowledged that such frankness can be career-limiting, but said CISOs often get blamed for decisions that are not theirs and should push back. In his words, the people taking a risk need to be responsible for it. On talent, he favors paid internships that bring AI-native young people into the company, and he has suggested interview exercises in which candidates use AI to solve a live business problem with no single right answer. He also said organizations should maintain career paths and upward mobility, and that simply paying people more while keeping them in the same roles is not an effective way to retain them.

stories.Headline: Businesses increasingly adopt AI for cybersecurity while individuals expand privacy protections
stories.Summary:
Businesses across the OECD are turning to artificial intelligence to defend against cyber threats, while individuals are using privacy tools to take more control of their personal data, according to new OECD data released in late October 2026. In 2023, 17.7% of enterprises in the OECD experienced ICT security incidents, a rise of 28.2% from 2018. In 2025, 5.3% of enterprises used AI for ICT security, roughly one quarter of all enterprises using AI. Uses include machine learning systems that detect and prevent attacks and AI-based user authentication. Adoption in 2025 was 23.2% higher than in 2024, 68.6% higher than in 2023, and more than double the 2021 level.

Use of AI for security depends heavily on company size and sector. In 2025, 26.7% of large enterprises used AI for ICT security, compared with 9.6% of medium-sized enterprises and 3.7% of small ones. Among industries, 18.1% of firms in information and communication reported using it, well ahead of professional, scientific and technical activities at 8.9%. Adoption in the ICT sector was about nine times higher than in accommodation and food services, at 2.1%. The OECD suggests these tools spread most in information-intensive sectors, where cyber risks and reliance on digital systems are greatest.

Individuals are also acting more on their own data. Between 2020 and 2025, the share changing browser settings to limit cookies rose by 26.8%, while those refusing personal data use for advertising rose by 17.2% and those restricting access to their location rose by 14.0%. Smaller increases were seen for limiting social media profile access (11.3%) and using anti-tracking software (7.0%). The OECD links these trends to more privacy controls in browsers, operating systems and online platforms, and to greater awareness of data protection. By 2025, more than half of individuals had either restricted location access or refused personal data use for advertising, while the share reading privacy policies before sharing data fell by about 8.4%.

Concern about privacy is rarely the reason people avoid generative AI, with only 4.5% of OECD individuals citing it as their main reason in 2025. Older adults aged 55 to 74 were more likely than those aged 16 to 24 to avoid AI over such concerns, at 5.8% against 1.9%, and less likely to take active privacy steps. Younger people reported fewer worries about AI but frequently used privacy controls and anti-tracking tools. Education also shapes privacy behaviour: individuals with higher attainment were far more likely to refuse personal data use for advertising (68.1% against 39.5%) and to restrict location access (65.8% against 38.9%) than those with low attainment, although concern about generative AI was similar across both groups.

stories.Headline: Why should Big Tech know what you're working on? Scale AI accused of spying on AI trainers
stories.Summary:
On October 27, 2026, the European Centre for Digital Rights, known as Noyb, announced that it was filing five legal complaints in Europe against San Francisco-based startup Scale AI. The complaints target the way Scale AI's training platform, Outlier, tracks its workforce, which the group says infringes on workers' rights. Two complaints are being filed in Austria, with others in France, the Netherlands and Italy. The filing comes as AI companies face closer scrutiny in Europe, where the EU's AI Office opened investigations into OpenAI and Anthropic earlier that month.

Outlier recruits freelancers and subject-matter experts to help train, evaluate and improve AI models, using a platform worker model similar to those used by Uber and food delivery services. Noyb says the platform relies on more than 900,000 freelancers to evaluate and correct the responses of AI systems, and its customers include Meta, OpenAI, Google and the US government. According to the group, workers are placed on the platform with trackers from companies such as TikTok, LinkedIn and Facebook installed on their devices, giving those firms access to personal data like IP addresses and contact details. The complaints also allege that workers must repeatedly complete a biometric verification process run by a company called Persona, which involves video recordings of their faces and uploading their ID.

Scale AI is the company the complaints are directed at, and Noyb is the organization bringing them. Lisa Steinfeld Leiser, a data protection lawyer at Noyb, said that such constant tracking goes against workers' reasonable expectations and questioned why companies like LinkedIn or Facebook should know which tasks people are working on. Noyb has also said that the platform's freelance contract model leaves workers without adequate protections. The group describes the arrangement as workers effectively giving their expertise to large technology companies. It calls the workplace surveillance a clear violation of workers' fundamental right to data protection in Europe.

The case sits within a wider debate over how AI should be governed. In the United States, President Donald Trump signed an agreement with the six largest American AI firms that allows them to regulate themselves, which highlights growing divisions over oversight of the technology. Concerns also persist that AI could displace jobs and be used for harmful purposes. The articles do not say how the European complaints will be resolved or when the relevant authorities will rule on them.

stories.Headline: Idris Elba's Akuna Group launches free Artificial Intelligence filmmaking programme for creators in five African countries
stories.Summary:
Akuna Learning, the education arm of The Akuna Group chaired by Sir Idris Elba, opened applications on 26 October 2026 for a free AI filmmaking programme called From Script to Screen with AI. The programme is open to aspiring creators in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone and South Africa, and it is delivered in collaboration with Google. Google.org is supporting it with US$1 million, and the curriculum was developed by Curious Refuge. Applications close on 15 November 2026, and the programme is free both to apply for and to attend if selected. Over fifty weeks, selected creators will move through a twelve-week academy, then mentoring, pitching and production.

Everyone takes a foundational course in AI filmmaking before choosing one of five pathways: fiction, documentary, animation, advertising or screenwriting. The stages run from applications and selection between October 2026 and January 2027, to learning and certification from February to April 2027, then mentoring, a pitch round in June and July 2027, and film production through October 2027. Funded films will be showcased in October 2027, and creators keep control of their work, with no ownership claim by the programme or its partners. Applicants must be 18 or older, live in one of the five countries, and have a laptop, reliable internet and power for the full programme.

The Akuna Group is responsible for the programme, and Sir Idris Elba, its chairman, said the initiative is about education and giving creators across the continent access to courses that help them tell their own stories. He said selected projects will receive production funding and that he hopes the training leads to employment and helps shape how Africa is portrayed. Khaled Gad, the group's chief executive, said training alone does not build an industry, so the programme takes creators from their first application through to a finished, funded film. He also said that no film school background or prior AI experience is needed, only finished work that shows what the applicant can do.

The release notes that women are strongly encouraged to apply. The Akuna Group describes itself as a pan-African creative economy organisation that builds skills, capital and platforms for African creators. The articles do not say how many creators will be selected, how the funding will be divided among projects, or what the programme will cost Google beyond the stated US$1 million. stories.Headline: Cosm by Cielo™ introduces an AI-native operating model for the next era of talent acquisition
