The company describes it as an AI-native operating model meant to turn workforce demand into business outcomes faster than traditional recruiting models. It is powered by Cielo Lumis, which Cielo calls its system of action, and it links talent expertise, governance, AI-enabled workflows and real-time intelligence. The launch follows faster shifts in business priorities, skills demand and talent availability across employers.

Cielo cited its own Talent Benchmark research, which found that 87% of organizations increased talent acquisition technology investment over the past 12 months, yet many still struggle to turn that spending into greater hiring agility. It also referred to McKinsey research showing that organizations getting the most value from AI are redesigning how work gets done. Cielo's chief executive, Marissa Geist, said companies need a better way to turn work priorities into action rather than more disconnected recruiting tools. Cielo Lumis, the company says, connects workforce, talent and market signals to workflows and recruiter actions, and it works across applicant tracking and human capital management systems that organizations already use.

Cielo's chief operating officer, Molly Thiel, said the platform is meant to reduce friction so recruiters can spend more time advising the business and making accountable decisions. Cielo says Cosm operates within governed workflows and human oversight, with built-in transparency, accountability and clear limits on autonomous action. stories.Headline: AI-generated models spark job fears and image rights battle in fashion world
stories.Summary:
AI-generated models are raising alarm across the fashion industry after a Reuters investigation found that brands are seeking broad rights over models' images. Reuters interviewed 15 modelling agency directors and reviewed more than a dozen confidential contracts from brands including Diesel, Calvin Klein and L'Oreal. The draft terms asked for permission to swap model faces using AI, to create digital clones without extra pay, and to use body images to train AI tools. Many of the agreements also contained broad legal wording that would give brands wide discretion over how the technology is used.

The shift matters because AI can cut production costs by more than 90 per cent compared with traditional photo shoots. Agencies report falling bookings and some studios have closed, with e-commerce work for fast-fashion platforms, a key source of income for models, under particular pressure. London-based model Adot Gak warned that the industry could soon be dominated by bots if models do not speak up. Fast-fashion brands such as Mango have already adopted computer-generated models at scale, while luxury houses have moved more cautiously. Moncler said it does not currently use AI-generated models on its website or in promotional material.

Several companies responded to the findings, though not all gave the same account. Diesel's parent company, OTB, said the casting sheet was drafted for one campaign and does not reflect its standard contracts. Calvin Klein said it is testing and learning in a fast-moving space and that its use of AI follows regulations and respects the rights of its models. L'Oreal did not comment directly on the clause about altering product appearance but said it uses standard AI tools in post-production that leave model likenesses unaffected. Reale Actives said it hires real talent and blamed the contract language on a third-party production partner.

Legal protections remain uneven, and the New York State Fashion Workers Act is described as a notable exception. Sara Ziff of the Model Alliance is pushing for similar protections in other US states and at the federal level. In Britain, the British Fashion Model Agents Association has issued an AI code of practice requiring explicit consent, but its head, John Horner, warned that without binding rules, models remain exposed. According to a Sci-Tech Today statistics report published October 27, 2026, the category is expanding quickly across the industry. Gartner forecasts that AI laptops will make up 58.7% of total laptop shipments in 2026, up from 35.7% in 2025. GEEKOM, described as a leading global Mini PC brand, is the party responsible for the showcase, and its release frames the A9 MEGA as a way to run demanding AI models locally rather than in the cloud. stories.Headline: Pronto Founder Enters Physical AI Space With Provision Labs
stories.Summary:
Anjali Sardana, the founder and chief executive of the Indian household services startup Pronto, has launched Provision Labs, a San Francisco-based venture focused on data infrastructure for artificial intelligence systems that perform physical tasks. According to its website, the company will collect data to train and test AI systems that use robots and other machines in real-world settings. The report on the launch, first carried by The Economic Times, said Provision Labs plans to source training data from professionals across sectors globally and help developers deploy their models. Sardana will continue to lead Pronto while also serving at the new venture. The launch comes months after Pronto faced scrutiny over a pilot that recorded household chores to generate training data for robotics.

The reported backers of Provision Labs include Lachy Groom, General Catalyst, Bain Capital Ventures and Glade Brook Capital, according to its website. The company has not disclosed its funding amount, valuation or initial customers. Its stated focus is the data, evaluation and deployment layer for physical AI. Neither company has publicly confirmed whether Provision Labs will use recordings from Pronto's separate initiative. The pilot, which Pronto calls Pronto Verified, is an opt-in programme in which service professionals wore wearable cameras during household chores such as washing dishes and folding laundry.

Pronto has said the pilot was voluntary, available only to customers who chose it at booking, and covered less than 0.01% of its users at the time. The startup said footage was available to participating customers in anonymised form for 48 hours, would not be shared with third-party AI labs, and would be deleted from its servers within that window. Pronto also said it had worked toward compliance with India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act. The startup has argued that real-world behavioural data is essential for training robots to operate in homes. Critics questioned whether customers fully understood how recordings from their homes could be used to build commercial datasets.

The launch reflects growing demand for real-world footage to teach robots to handle objects and everyday tasks, and other startups are already using India's workforce to meet it. Y Combinator-backed Human Archive records workers performing physical tasks and sells the resulting datasets to AI labs and robotics companies, and firms such as Awign and Objectways are building similar pipelines. That business raises questions about workers' consent and compensation, the privacy of others captured on camera, and how much value Indian data suppliers keep when the resulting models belong to overseas companies. The articles do not say whether Provision Labs will address any of these concerns.

stories.Headline: Unitree chief says humanoid AI's 'ChatGPT moment' arriving in 1-2 yrs
stories.Summary:
Wang Xingxing, founder and chairman of Hangzhou-based Unitree Robotics, said that the "ChatGPT moment" for humanoid intelligence could arrive within one or two years, a faster timeline than he had given before. He made the remark at the opening ceremony of the 26th China International Industry Fair, held from October 12 to 16 in Shanghai, and the report was published on October 23, 2026. Wang said his biggest mistake over the past decade was not believing in AI enough. He pointed to the recent launch of GPT-6 as a major step and suggested that GPT-7, due out next year, might largely solve current bottlenecks in embodied intelligence.

Wang described the benchmark he uses to judge when that moment has arrived. In his view, robots should be able to complete about 80 percent of tasks in 80 percent of unfamiliar settings when given voice or text instructions. He said the main challenge is aligning the inputs and outputs of AI models with physical robots. Unitree has been testing its machines in real-world settings, and the robots are already deployed in automobile factories. The company's AI team is also testing them in home settings.

Wang acknowledged that Unitree has not yet deployed its robots on a large scale because they still fall short in overall efficiency and versatility. He said his company and other robotics firms are running pilot programs in factories, and that generalization and efficiency still need to improve for wider use. He expressed confidence that these issues could be solved within the next few years. His new forecast is more optimistic than his remarks at the 2026 World Robot Conference in Beijing on August 20, when he said the tipping point could come in two to three years, or perhaps five to 10 years at the slowest.

The term "ChatGPT moment" follows the phrase "iPhone moment," which Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang first used in 2023 to compare ChatGPT with the iPhone's role for AI. The phrase now describes a disruptive turning point when a technology moves from concept to widespread adoption. Unitree made its debut on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's STAR Market on August 19, and its shares closed 460 percent higher that day. Chen Jie, vice-president of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, also spoke at the October 12 ceremony, saying AI will keep driving engineering and technological transformation.

stories.Headline: Cadence unveils Nvidia-backed AI models that chipmakers can run in-house - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Cadence Design Systems on Monday, October 26, 2026, launched a portfolio of AI models tuned for chip design, called Cadence Maestro. The company built the suite in part on Nvidia's open-weight Nemotron model and secured it with Nvidia's OpenShell safety technology, deepening a partnership between the two firms. Cadence and rival Synopsys both make software used to arrange billions of transistors to meet cost and performance targets, and both are racing to have AI agents use those tools for human engineers. The Next Platform reported that the models were fine-tuned on Nvidia's Nemotron family to work with and interpret results from Cadence's own tools. Cadence has also rolled out a series of agent products over the past year, including AuraStack, ChipStack, InnoStack and ViraStack.

Customers can run the Maestro models on Cadence's own cloud or any public cloud, or keep them entirely in-house behind their own firewalls and data centers. They can also fine-tune the models on their own chip designs, though Paul Cunningham told The Next Platform that this would be offered more as a managed service than something customers set up alone. Cadence says early results show up to 30% higher quality and up to five times better cost-efficiency compared with general-purpose models. The first Maestro models will reach select early-access customers in the fourth quarter. Access can also come through an API or a secure virtual private cloud, or on premises for those with the necessary hardware.

Cunningham, a senior vice president at Cadence, framed Maestro as model-agnostic, noting that there are more AI model providers than chip design software vendors. Asked whether Cadence might strike deals with proprietary AI labs, he said open-weight and closed-weight approaches are being pursued equally, and that working with commercial labs is part of the Maestro vision, though he declined to elaborate. He also said that somewhere between 20 and 30 percent of chips under development today are being designed with help from AI agents, and that the share is growing rapidly. On the limits of general models, he said powerful off-the-shelf foundation models are a starting point and can still be specialized.

The launch contrasts with the approach of Synopsys, Cadence's largest competitor, which said on September 30 that it would develop an AI model with OpenAI and share revenue with the ChatGPT maker. That model, GPT-Synopsys, will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure. The Next Platform noted that Cadence's earlier agents were largely powered by off-the-shelf language models, which had limited exposure to design formats such as RTL, and that the new models aim to fix that gap. It added that Nvidia has been pushing high-performance computing and AI together for years, a trend also reflected in the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission.

stories.Headline: Police Are Using AI to Pull Over Drivers for 'Suspicious' Behavior
stories.Summary:
Police in several U.S. states are using automated license plate readers and AI-powered tools to flag drivers for "suspicious" travel patterns, even when those drivers are not suspected of a specific crime. The American Civil Liberties Union raised the alarm in an October 2026 post, opening with the case of Grace Knowles, a woman from northern Virginia who was pulled over in September 2025 while driving from New Orleans toward Florida. An officer told her he had been left-lane driving, then said he was an FBI special agent and that her plate had been flagged for suspicious travel patterns. He showed her a computer map with circles marking where her car had been, each linked to a photo of her license plate. Knowles said he told her the cameras were everywhere, including on top of highway signs.

The ACLU warns that such stops could become more common as companies such as Flock Safety and Axon sell systems that scan plates as vehicles pass and record each car's time and location. Police can search that data during investigations, and privacy advocates note that it captures millions of people who are not suspected of any crime, often without a warrant. Flock has reportedly developed an AI tool that can identify and track vehicles by movement patterns alone, and records describe queries that combine plate reads with arrest records and commercial data broker files. Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The ACLU says the trend is spreading and points to pretextual stops, in which drivers are pulled over for minor or invented violations as cover for the real reason.

Responsibility here rests with the police agencies using these tools and with the vendors that build and sell them, and the articles describe them as operating under little legal limit. Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst with the ACLU, wrote that for many people these encounters will be far more frightening and dangerous than what Knowles experienced. The ACLU is pressing for limits on this kind of surveillance. A federal jury in Texas recently sided with a man who sued over what his attorneys called an unconstitutional traffic stop scheme based on license plate readers, and the case is a sign that courts may be willing to examine these practices.

Public opinion is divided, with an August YouGov survey finding that 46% of respondents opposed police use of the technology in their communities and 38% supported it. Several agencies, including the Los Angeles Police Department, have suspended or ended their Flock contracts amid the backlash. Other reported cases include a California grandmother questioned by Customs and Border Protection about her casino visits and a man stopped repeatedly after driving between Wisconsin and Michigan. As the systems expand, the articles suggest that more stops of this kind are likely, though how courts and lawmakers will respond remains unsettled.

stories.Headline: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on Monday, October 26, 2026 three results in mathematics, computer science and physics, along with a stated new approach to sharing its findings. The announcement followed a turbulent few months in which the company released hundreds of AI-generated preprints on mathematicians at the start of October. This time, OpenAI said it would work with expert "shepherds" to decide how to share the work, and each result got a different release strategy. The mathematics output was released as AI-generated text, leaving researchers to organize their own explanations, the computer science finding will be explained by an outside group of researchers, and the physics result has not been released at all, with OpenAI deferring to outside experts on how to proceed.

The mathematics result claims to resolve the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions, a question about how little space is needed to turn a needle in every direction. Brown University mathematician Brendan Hassett said the claim "looks well supported," though he had not yet checked the Lean formalization used to verify it computationally. The physics result concerns quantum chromodynamics and its link to Yang-Mills theory, but it does not address the unresolved mass gap in the related Millennium Prize problem. The computer science result claims to disprove the exponential time hypothesis, a widely held assumption that closely relates to the P versus NP question. Researchers described the results as huge, major and significant, though they noted the difficulty of checking them.

Researchers who spoke to The Verge said they were tired of OpenAI's conduct, and many objected to handpicking experts to review the work first. Constantin Kogler of the Institute for Advanced Study said it made no sense for only a few scientists to see the results first, while Andreas Karch of the University of Texas at Austin called the handpicked group a disaster and asked why the proof could not be released publicly now. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence had warned a day earlier against this practice, recommending release on scholarly repositories with formal proofs and funding for independent work. After the announcement, that group urged OpenAI to publish the physics output without delay, arguing the Lean formalization was already complete. Xiaoyu He of Georgia Institute of Technology said the deeper concern is that fundamental results are arriving quickly without human contribution and are hard to read and verify, a problem that changes in release method cannot fix.

stories.Headline: Trump wants everyone to stop saying "AI."
stories.Summary:
Trump has said he wants to stop people from using the term "AI." In a Truth Social post dated October 27, 2026, he wrote that he would soon be officially banning the phrase "AI/Artificial Intelligence" in all relevant documents and everything else, citing its inaccuracy. He had earlier asked when The Wall Street Journal would swap the term for "Super Intelligence." The post was reported by The Verge. The change he described would apply legally only to executive branch agencies, so it would not bind private companies, the press or the public.

A widely shared screenshot of the post accompanied the coverage. The announcement is a notable example of a head of state weighing in on the naming of a technology rather than on its regulation. Reporting on the post mostly framed it as a question of terminology and its legal reach. Separately, Lim Woong, a professor at the Graduate School of Education at Yonsei University, wrote a column in The Korea Herald published October 27, 2026, criticizing a different political episode. President Lee Jae Myung had posted on social media an exchange with Gemini, Google's generative AI, to rebut critics of having top investigators and prosecutors attend his Cabinet meetings.

Lim argued that a chatbot's answer depends heavily on how a question is framed, so it should not settle a constitutional debate. He said the president's approach invited ridicule and that the opposition had responded with an "I asked AI, too" challenge. Lim's column went beyond that episode and offered a list of phrases he said thoughtful people should stop using, such as "I asked AI, and it says so." He argued that such remarks hand off agency and accountability that belong to people, and he urged institutions like schools, courts and newsrooms to be clear about where machine output ends and human judgment begins. The Korea Herald presented the piece as the writer's own opinion, not an official position.

Trading that day was busy enough that the Korea Exchange activated a buy-side sidecar, a curb that temporarily halts program trades when prices move sharply.

Market participants were looking for signals on the future direction of U.S. interest rates, which could shape sentiment across global equities. stories.Headline: Acts of God Meet Acts of AI in Private Equity’s New Debt Play
stories.Summary:
Private equity firms are adding force majeure-style clauses to new buyout loans that would let borrowers pause the consequences of defaults they attribute to artificial intelligence disruption. H.I.G. Capital secured such language in a €470 million ($524 million) loan backing its majority stake in Terras Group, a German-headquartered provider of infrastructure engineering and construction services, according to people familiar with the deal. Several creditors said the language goes further than usual and has appeared in at least two leveraged buyout financings since September. One lender-side lawyer, Jeremy Duffy, a partner and chair of European leveraged finance at Cahill Gordon & Reindel LLP, said lenders and investors are closely reviewing such proposals.

Traditionally, force majeure clauses cover catastrophes such as hurricanes, earthquakes, the Covid pandemic or the 9/11 attacks. In the Terras deal, H.I.G. adapted that language so the clock stops on a default if AI disrupts the company, alongside other triggers including Covid-19 or another pandemic, a substantial rise in energy or resource prices, and war or terrorism. Lenders normally allow a grace period, typically 30 days, before a missed interest payment becomes a default that lets them demand repayment. The new provisions are framed as extending that grace period, but AI disruption has no clear end date the way a pandemic might. According to one person familiar with the deal, the clause would let Terras defer the consequences of unpaid interest for as long as it feels AI's impact, although the company still owes the interest.

Some creditors argue the provisions undermine the basic expectation that lenders will recover their money even when things go wrong. Lenders succeeded in having similar language struck from Bain Capital's €4.7 billion-equivalent ($5.3 billion) leveraged loan for its acquisition of a controlling stake in Volkswagen AG's heavy diesel-engine unit Everllence, according to the same people. The market's approach to investor protections has become split, with sponsors pressing for looser terms where they expect deals to perform well and reinserting covenants in troubled sectors like software. Software-as-a-service firms are seen as especially exposed to AI disruption, and buyout firms have large bets on them. H.I.G. was advised by Paul, Weiss lawyers including Neel Sachdev, while representatives at H.I.G. and Bain declined to comment and Sachdev did not reply to a request for comment.

stories.Headline: Networked State Capital in China’s AI Ecosystem
stories.Summary:
This is an event announcement rather than breaking news, and the articles do not describe any incident, so I cannot write it as a breaking story with the required structure. What the page does give is a talk scheduled for November 3, 2026, from 12:20 to 1:20 pm, at Harvard Law School, where Curtis J. Milhaupt of Stanford Law School will present "Networked State Capital in China's AI Ecosystem." The talk is part of the East Asian Legal Studies series and is co-sponsored by the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society. Milhaupt is joined by Liwen Lin of the University of British Columbia's Allard School of Law on the underlying joint project. Registration is not required but is appreciated, and a Harvard ID is needed to enter the buildings.

The research addresses a puzzle about China's artificial intelligence sector. Self-reliance and technological resilience in AI are described as national priorities of the Chinese party-state, yet most major players, including firms the government has designated as part of an "AI National Team" and AI unicorns, remain privately controlled at the top of their corporate groups. The authors ask why leading players are not subject to the apex-level state ownership and hierarchical administrative control usually associated with Chinese state capitalism. Using corporate registry data, the project maps where state-affiliated capital enters private technology groups, finding it positioned at multiple points within ownership, investment, and deployment networks, typically in subsidiaries below the apex. The authors argue that these positions can create durable channels for coordinating technology development, pilot projects, standard setting, and deployment with policy goals.

Based on the article, the analysis reframes China's approach to state capitalism in AI as a networked system of state capital and institutionalized state-private interaction, rather than a simple split between state-owned and private firms. Milhaupt is described as an internationally recognized expert on comparative corporate governance, East Asian legal systems (particularly Japanese law), and state capitalism. The page does not indicate any findings beyond the framing above, nor any follow-up publication date. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Can AI coding agents rebuild biological AI tools from a paper?
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the UK AI Security Institute published a study on 26 October 2026 testing whether leading AI coding agents can rebuild biological AI tools, known as BAITs, from limited public information. The team, working with SecureBio, built an evaluation called ReproBAIT to see how well agents could reproduce existing tools given training data and a restricted description of each tool's design. Three tools were targeted: two open-source protein-design tools, ProteinMPNN and RFdiffusion3, and a closed-source molecular-design tool referred to as CMD. Four coding agents were tested, namely Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8-2.4T.

The simplest tools could be reproduced in selected functions within 4 hours and a compute budget under $20, with successful rebuilds of the two less complex tools typically costing between $4 and $20. Each attempt ran in an isolated sandbox with a single GPU and no internet access, and a separate scorer measured the rebuilt tool against the original on held-out data. The best result came from Claude Opus 5, which reached 96.5% fidelity to the original on ProteinMPNN when given the full paper. No agent fully rebuilt RFdiffusion3 within its time budget, and attempts there cost between $102 and $301. The findings suggest that withholding code or limiting published detail does not by itself make a tool safe to release.

The study was carried out by AISI's Chem-Bio team, which assesses chemical and biological risks from frontier AI systems and shares its findings with AI companies, UK officials and allied governments. The authors say the work shows that withholding code does not assure control over a tool's capability, since agents could reconstruct selected functions from public descriptions when supplied with training data. They also found no clear performance difference between agents given only an abstract and those given a full paper. The authors argue that controlling access to the underlying biological data appears to be a more promising safeguard than controlling access to code alone.

The researchers caution that their results do not prove the original tools can be reproduced in full, and that the figures reflect the time and compute limits used. They also note that memorisation may explain some of the agents' success, since the open-source tools' papers and code were likely in the agents' training data, though their diagnostics are imperfect. The team says performance may improve with more time and compute and that this is an avenue for future research. The authors point to the need for further work on data governance as a way of managing misuse of biological AI tools.

Articles.Title: Can AI coding agents rebuild biological AI tools from a paper? - The AI Security Institute (AISI)

stories.Headline: UTA uses AI to uncover drivers of eye disease
stories.Summary:
The University of Texas at Arlington has received a $1.96 million grant from the National Eye Institute to build AI-powered computational tools that can identify the biological "control switches" that keep eyes healthy and reveal what causes eye disease. The four-year project was announced in an article posted on the UTA College of Science website, with the page dated October 8, 2026. The grant is meant to support the development of targeted therapies that could improve and preserve vision. The article does not say exactly when the work began.

The project will produce two separate computational tools. The first is a scalable tool designed to analyze large genomic datasets and identify regulators that matter for ocular health and disease. The second is a deconvoluting tool that separates mixed signals from whole eye tissue samples, which contain many cell types with different functions, so researchers can see how a regulator behaves in a specific cell type without running costly single-cell experiments for every regulator. Together, the tools are meant to let scientists study the eye both at the level of the overall tissue and at the level of individual cell types.

The researchers say this should help the field focus on the most promising targets and save time and resources. Xinlei (Sherry) Wang, the Jenkins Garrett Professor of statistics and data science in UTA's Department of Mathematics, leads the project in collaboration with Lin Xu, an assistant professor at UT Southwestern. Wang described the eye as containing many specialized tissues and cell types that work together to make vision possible, and she called understanding the relationship between tissue-specific transcriptional regulators and visual function a cornerstone of vision research. Morteza Khaledi, dean of the College of Science, called the grant an outstanding achievement that reflects the strength and growing impact of Wang's interdisciplinary research program.

The article also notes that Wang is co-leading a related project with Junzhou Huang, a professor in the UTA College of Engineering, on combining AI and Bayesian learning to speed drug design. The award builds on Wang's broader work using AI and advanced statistical methods to help scientists understand complex diseases, with a focus on finding patterns hidden in very large datasets. The article describes UTA's College of Science as a Carnegie R1 research institution. The article does not state what results the project is expected to produce or when, beyond the four-year timeline.

Articles.Title: UTA uses AI to uncover drivers of eye disease

stories.Headline: Kempner hosts Mass AI Hub grant award celebration
stories.Summary:
Massachusetts leaders gathered at Harvard University's Kempner Institute for the Study of Natural and Artificial Intelligence to celebrate five recipients of the Mass AI Hub's 2026 Applied AI Models Innovation Challenge, which awards nearly $3.3 million to projects tackling challenges across key industries. The event was reported by news.harvard.edu on October 27, 2026. Massachusetts Secretary of Economic Development Eric Paley attended along with leaders from the Massachusetts Technology Collaborative and Mass AI Hub, and Harvard Senior Vice Provost for Research John Shaw. The gathering marked the recognition of the selected projects and the work behind them. One grant recipient is Yulin Du, an assistant professor of computer science at Harvard and an investigator at the Kempner Institute, whose team is building large video generation models for industrial robotics.

The models are meant to produce detailed visual descriptions that let robots learn industrial tasks from video demonstrations and adapt without manual programming. The technology is intended to make automation more flexible and affordable for small and midsize businesses in manufacturing, logistics and recycling. Du said in his award video that the team plans to open source the model and provide inference code so others can connect it to any robotics platform. Paley said that Massachusetts is committed to responsible AI that addresses challenges facing industries across the state. He said the challenge supports projects that will strengthen the economy, advance strategic sectors and reinforce the state's position as a hub for applied AI.

Shaw said that sustained commitment to innovation allows the institutions to have a positive impact, recruit top talent and secure resources for innovative work. He stressed that this success is not limited to Harvard or the Kempner Institute, but depends on the broader ecosystem of partner universities, affiliated hospitals and the private sector in the region. The other recipients include the Atlantic Resiliency Innovation Institute, which is developing an AI-driven coastal resilience platform for hyperlocal flood-risk predictions for energy infrastructure, and Boston University, whose PandemIQ Llama tool supports real-time global disease surveillance and automated epidemiological reporting. Bristol Community College plans an AI system to assess workers' skills against industry frameworks, while UMass Lowell Applied Research Corporation is developing a platform to coordinate multiple sensor systems in counter-drone operations. The articles do not say when the projects will be completed.

Articles.Title: Kempner hosts Mass AI Hub grant award celebration

stories.Headline: Learner collaborates with MIT peers to develop book of AI insights
stories.Summary:
Prabha Jha, a Verizon leader, and 20 peers from an MIT Open Learning course for senior executives released "The AI Anthology," a collection of essays on how artificial intelligence has affected industries and society. The book came about one year after Jha's cohort finished the AI for Senior Executives program offered through MIT xPRO. Jha had taken the course, which included an in-person component, to deepen her understanding of AI. The MIT News article reports the release as occurring in late October 2026.

The book is meant to support other leaders facing similar challenges with AI and to capture perspectives that go beyond operational efficiency and revenue growth. Jha's idea grew out of a gathering at the home of Manolis Kellis, a professor in MIT's Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, where a peer shared how her interest in AI stemmed from work on her mother's Alzheimer's disease and dementia. The article also describes an interruption in Jha's studies, when a severe infection kept her in the hospital for two weeks and led her to join the next cohort with MIT staff help. She described the extra five days on campus as a valuable part of her learning, since she met peers from diverse backgrounds face-to-face.

Jha argues that many leaders remain stuck on traditional measures of success such as revenue, cost-cutting, and time saved, and says leaders must think differently to find more empowerment through AI. She believes AI adoption is not optional for businesses and sees it as a transformation that can help people overcome insecurity and grow. Jha also said that Verizon's role in providing critical infrastructure to groups such as first responders and children gives the company an obligation that AI can help it meet. She is currently working on an initiative to help small and medium-sized businesses understand which AI tools they need, how AI fits their operations, and how to measure success.

Articles.Title: Learner collaborates with MIT peers to develop book of AI insights

stories.Headline: FSU highlights approach to AI in education and research during United Nations event
stories.Summary:
Florida State University Vice President and Chief Information Officer Jonathan Fozard spoke on October 19 at a GlobalMindED event held at the United Nations in New York City. He took part in a higher education panel titled "From Classrooms to Labs: How Universities Are Connecting (and Constraining) AI," which looked at how institutions can move past early experiments with artificial intelligence. The panel brought together Jennifer Sparrow of New York University, William H.J. Hubbard of the University of Chicago Law School, and Chris Ott of Amazon Web Services. Jay Nappy of AWS moderated the discussion. The panel focused on using AI across classrooms, research and university operations rather than simply testing it.

Fozard argued that the central question for education is no longer whether institutions will offer access to AI, but how that access will produce meaningful results for students and researchers. He described FSU's effort to make secure, university-supported AI tools available to students, faculty and staff across many disciplines, not only technology-heavy fields such as computer science and engineering. The university evaluates AI platforms on how vendors protect intellectual property, institutional information and student data, which matters given its responsibilities from higher education through K-12 settings. He also said the university wants to avoid relying on a single technology and instead compares multiple platforms. Fozard stressed that these tools should support faculty rather than replace the human relationships central to teaching.

One example he cited was an AI-supported tool that gives students feedback on assignments so they can revise their work before handing it to an instructor for a grade. In an early pilot study, students who used the tool performed about 20% better than those who did not. Fozard said the aim is to create more chances for students to engage with their work, not to have AI do the work or replace instruction. He also pointed to FSU's research in pediatric rare diseases, which combines whole-genome sequencing, advanced computing and AI to speed up diagnosis, discovery and the search for new treatments. He additionally described technology internship initiatives that pair technical experience with communication, teamwork and leadership skills.

The GlobalMindED gathering drew leaders from higher education, business and technology to consider how organizations can respond to rapid technological and social change. Fozard said there was something meaningful about discussing the future of education and AI in a setting built to bring people together to address complex challenges. Further details on FSU's artificial intelligence work are available at ai.fsu.edu. The articles do not describe any further steps or changes beyond what the university has already outlined.

Articles.Title: FSU highlights approach to AI in education and research during United Nations event

stories.Headline: How AI Is Reshaping Scientific Publishing
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is changing how scientists write research and how journals publish it, according to an interview published on October 26, 2026, by The Rockefeller University. Susan King, executive director of Rockefeller University Press, says that collaborative human relationships remain central to publishing. She described how her team now uses AI to help safeguard research while still implementing it in their workflow. The conversation also covered where she expects the field to be in five years.

On research integrity, King explained that the press has screened for image manipulation for more than 20 years, starting with predecessor Mike Rossner, who used Photoshop to reveal abnormalities. Staff members Laura Smith and later Rochelle Ritacco continue this work, now supported by AI that compares submitted images against preprints and published articles across journals. The press also takes part in the STM Integrity Hub, a cloud-based environment created by scientific, technical, and medical publishers, which checks manuscripts for issues such as simultaneous submission to another journal. King said this helps detect fraudulent papers from paper mills. Readers are also changing how they find content, as AI-generated summaries spread and referrals from AI search engines grow while traffic from traditional tools declines.

King warned that this shift could make it harder for libraries to judge a journal's value, since their subscription decisions rely heavily on usage statistics. She said the press has begun licensing agreements, including a partnership with a company called Cashmere, that allow AI systems to access content directly through MCP (Model Context Protocol) rather than relying on incomplete training data, which can cause hallucinations. Because the press publishes only five journals, King said its size lets it offer close author service, and it richly tags content with persistent identifiers and clear labels for corrections and retractions so machines can process it accurately. On trust, she said the press does not bar AI use outright, allows it for language editing without disclosure, and requires disclosure of more substantive uses. It also forbids listing AI systems as authors and expects reviewers to protect confidentiality, noting a survey of 1,600 academics in which more than half reported using AI tools while peer reviewing manuscripts.

King said the press has not seen a material rise in problematic images despite how much easier faking them has become, which she partly attributes to its small size and strong community ties. She argued that many misconduct problems stem from long-standing reward systems that favor volume over careful work, and that AI could amplify those incentives, which makes this an opportunity to rethink what the field values. Looking five years ahead, she expects AI to play a larger role in manuscript submission, where it could extract metadata such as institutions and funders for authors to confirm, and in tools that check statistical methods during peer review. She said humans must still judge novelty, significance, and impact, since AI is trained on existing knowledge while science pushes into the unknown.

Articles.Title: How AI Is Reshaping Scientific Publishing

stories.Headline: New CoPAIR program connects Cornell researchers with AI tools, training and community
stories.Summary:
Cornell University has launched a new program called Communities of Practice for AI-enabled Research, or CoPAIR, to help its researchers evaluate and use artificial intelligence tools. The program was announced in an article published October 26, 2026, and is co-sponsored by the Cornell AI Initiative and the Office of the Vice Provost for Research. It gives researchers access to emerging AI tools, hands-on training, and collaborative communities where they can share practices and develop norms for when AI should and should not be used. The program is open to researchers at any stage of AI experience, from first-time explorers to those already building AI into their workflows. CoPAIR rests on two pillars.

The first, Research Pod CoPAIR, forms small, self-selected groups of researchers from the same field who test tools and methods together, guided by Cornell's "AI in the disciplines" framework. The second, Core-Center CoPAIR, anchors research communities inside existing Cornell centers, institutes, and shared research infrastructure, where they offer domain-specific AI expertise, training, and resource sharing. The first Core-Center pilot is led by the Biotechnology Resource Center and runs for about eight weeks in fall 2026. It focuses on four life sciences areas: genomics, proteomics and metabolomics, imaging, and structural biology. Both pillars aim to produce practical guidance, templates, and shared repositories that the wider Cornell research community can use.

Natalie Bazarova, associate vice provost for research and lead of the research pillar for the Cornell AI Initiative, said researchers across fields face different AI challenges and need open platforms to set shared standards and learn new techniques. She said the program offers such a platform for examining research commitments, adopting tools, and advancing reproducible workflows. Thorsten Joachims, vice provost for AI strategy, said AI raises both opportunities and challenges in nearly every discipline. He said researchers who understand AI in relation to their own fields are needed, and that CoPAIR gives them space, support, and a collaborative platform to build norms and best practices.

The program responds to growing pressure on academic researchers to judge what AI tools can actually do and where they fall short. Researchers interested in forming a Research Pod CoPAIR or joining the Core-Center pilot can learn more and apply through the Cornell AI Initiative website. The application deadline for Research Pod CoPAIR is December 4. The article does not describe outcomes beyond the pilot period or any further expansion plans.

Articles.Title: New CoPAIR program connects Cornell researchers with AI tools, training and community

stories.Headline: Democrats, Republicans support government intervention to train workforce on AI tools, Northeastern University survey finds
stories.Summary:
A Northeastern University survey released Friday, October 23, 2026 found that many Democrats and Republicans favor government-backed programs to retrain workers on artificial intelligence and to provide ongoing lessons. The report, published by Northeastern Global News on October 26, 2026, described the public's views on AI. Sixty-four percent of Republican respondents and 63 percent of Democratic respondents said they support job retraining designed to help workers build the skills needed for AI-heavy jobs. The researchers said this could cover both blue-collar and white-collar work. The findings reflect a shared interest across party lines in helping workers adapt as the technology spreads.

Many respondents also backed tax-advantaged savings accounts that workers could use to pay for training and educational opportunities. Fifty-seven percent of Republican respondents and 56 percent of Democrats said they supported "worker-owned retraining accounts" that people could keep as they move between jobs. The article does not describe any specific legislation or set a timeline for such programs. It only reports the level of public support shown in the survey. Those figures give a sense of where respondents stand on paying for training rather than a plan for how it would be carried out.

The survey was conducted by Northeastern University, and the article names David Lazer as a person connected to the story, though it does not state his exact role in the report. The article does not give any direct quotations from the researchers beyond their observation about blue-collar and white-collar jobs. The piece presents the survey results as its main content and does not describe any official response from government or industry. Readers are directed to the full report and related coverage for more detail.

The article places the survey within wider public unease about AI. It notes that the technology's rapid growth worldwide has led to widespread concern and demonstrations about data centers and other matters. According to media reports cited in the article, demonstrators in more than 50 cities and college campuses across the United States gathered this week to call for a pause on AI development. The article does not say what action, if any, follows from either the survey or the protests.

Articles.Title: Democrats, Republicans support government intervention to train workforce on AI tools, Northeastern University survey finds

stories.Headline: Elon Drone Day to explore AI, emerging drone applications on Friday, Oct. 30
stories.Summary:
Elon University's School of Communications will host its annual Elon Drone Day on Friday, Oct. 30, featuring presentations, demonstrations and networking in Turner Theater and the Snow Family Grand Atrium. The free event is organized with the North Carolina chapter of the Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International and is open to the public, though attendees must register. Recreational and commercial pilots, industry professionals, educators and students are expected to take part. This year's program puts particular emphasis on artificial intelligence and emerging drone applications. Last year's event drew a record 185 attendees, vendors and volunteers.

The keynote will be delivered by Sambit Bhattacharya, a professor at Fayetteville State University, under the title "Preflight Checks for Intelligent Machines: What Drones Can Teach Us About Trustworthy AI." His talk will argue that aviation's focus on safety, testing and accountability can guide the development of reliable AI systems. Drawing on research from Fayetteville State's Intelligent Systems Lab, he will examine how autonomous drones make decisions and the difficulties of deploying AI in real-world settings. Bhattacharya's research team was recently awarded a $10 million grant to expand its work on AI and unmanned aerial systems. Beyond the keynote, the program covers agriculture, disaster response, invasive species management and flight planning software.

Randy Piland, a teaching professor of visual communication who organizes the event, said the keynote reflects both the growing role of AI in drones and Elon's wider effort to broaden conversations about AI across its programs. He noted that many new autonomous drones depend on AI to function. Piland's stated aim is to give local drone enthusiasts and professionals a place to exchange knowledge, network and find solutions to their problems. The schedule opens with a drone soccer demonstration by Asheboro City Schools and a vendor showcase. Flight demonstrations take place in the afternoon in the parking area behind the Schar Center.

Elon Drone Day was established in 2021 and has grown into an annual gathering for people interested in the evolving drone industry. Its mission has stayed the same even as the technology has changed quickly. Organizers describe the event as a practical outlet for people working to improve their drone operations. The 2026 gathering will carry that purpose forward with its focus on AI and new applications. Registration is required for the free public event.

Articles.Title: Elon Drone Day to explore AI, emerging drone applications on Friday, Oct. 30

stories.Headline: Kimi K3.1 Pro Scores 4th of 215 AI Models; Moonshot Scrubs Cyberattack Data Before Open Weights
stories.Summary:
Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 23, and the model placed fourth among 215 models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. The Beijing-based lab also disclosed that it deliberately removed offensive cyberattack training data before preparing the weights for public download. No other open-weight frontier lab has publicly reported doing this, according to TechTimes. The open weights are due on November 4, which would make K3.1 Pro the most capable AI system ever freely distributed, with a documented reduction in its ability to carry out computer attacks. The size of the cut is measurable.

K3.1 Pro scores 81.0% on xdev-bench-hard, Moonshot's in-house cybersecurity evaluation, while an ablation checkpoint trained without the redaction scores 90.5%, a gap of 9.5 percentage points. Moonshot says the cap keeps the model's offensive cyber ability below that of proprietary frontier models already public for at least three months, without badly hurting its value for legitimate security and coding work. The model is a post-training upgrade of Kimi K3, launched July 16, 2026, which has 2.8 trillion total parameters, 896 expert networks, 16 active per token, and a one-million-token context window. Its score on Kimi Hallu Bench Hard fell from 23.4% to 8.3%, and its Kimi Code Bench score rose from 55.95% to 61.2%. On SWE Marathon it scored 51.7 against K3's 42.0, on BrowseComp 92.1 against 91.2, and on Terminal-Bench 4.0 it reached 65.7%, trailing Claude Opus 5.5 by 0.7 points.

Results are weaker elsewhere, and the speed and cost figures are not flattering. K3.1 Pro scores 38.1 on Terminal-Bench Science, more than 25 points below GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, and 92.7% on BenchCAD with tools, against 96.2% for Claude Opus 5.5 and 95.9% for GPT-6 Astra. Artificial Analysis measured output of 57.5 tokens per second, ranking 141 of 186 models against a median of about 82.5, and found the model produced 150 million output tokens against a median of 87 million. It estimates a cost of $2.11 per task, placing the model 85th of 113. API pricing fell from K3's $3 input and $15 output per million tokens to $2 and $10, with cached input at $0.20, while the faster Highspeed variant costs $4 and $20.

Moonshot is the company responsible for the release and for the redaction, and TechTimes describes the cap as both a safety measure and a political calculation, since the US government has publicly accused Moonshot of covertly stealing capabilities from American AI systems. The figures are Moonshot's own until the weights can be tested. Independent researchers will be able to probe the redaction from November 4, and TechTimes notes that standard fine-tuning can in principle partly recover suppressed capabilities. A separate AI Security Institute study of protein models, published October 26, found that pretraining data filtering suppressed a targeted capability without harming adjacent ones, but that the capability could be recovered for under $80 of compute even for its largest model. The institute concluded that filtering needs to be paired with other measures, such as data access controls.

Articles.Title: Pretraining data filtering in open-weight biological models - The AI Security Institute (AISI)

stories.Headline: Collaborative Collision: FSU researchers explore the future of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Florida State University brought researchers from many fields together during its Discovery Days to explore how artificial intelligence can advance research and address complex challenges. The Office of Research hosted an event called "Collaborative Collision: The Future of Intelligence," which gave faculty a forum to discuss AI, connect across disciplines, and build partnerships. Attendees joined breakout sessions on how AI intersects with different fields, including human health, smart cities, and robotics. The day was designed to spark new ideas and collaborations that could lead to scientific discovery. The article was published on October 27, 2026.

Paul Marty, associate vice provost for academic innovation, said the conversations stressed keeping humanity at the center of the university's work on AI in society, health, education, science, and the workforce. Mike Wolfe, director of AI research solutions, said bringing different perspectives into one room was meant to encourage cross-domain discussions that could produce new project ideas. The discussions pushed researchers to look past their own work, find shared interests, and consider how their expertise could combine to address scientific and societal problems. Wolfe's group hopes these exchanges will lead directly to new partnerships. The event also highlighted the range of research at FSU, from autonomous security systems to the social aspects of AI integration and artistic creativity.

The Research Development team introduced Collaborative Collision LaunchPad Funding, which lets researchers turn their cross-departmental connections into joint projects. Participants were encouraged to form interdisciplinary teams and write proposals that could compete for up to $25,000 in seed funding. Jared Parmer, research development coordinator, said the event reflects the Office of Research's commitment to cutting-edge scholarship across all disciplines. He said the LaunchPad grants are meant to catalyze new research teams and seed new projects. In a dedicated resource room, attendees also met representatives from Information Technology Services, FSU Libraries, and the Research Computing Center to learn about tools and technical support.

Parmer and the other organizers framed the event as a step toward building a future that the university community can look forward to. The article directs readers who want more information on research development opportunities at FSU to the university's FSU Research Development site. The coverage presents the event as a starting point rather than a final outcome, with new teams and proposals expected to follow from the connections made that day. The articles provided do not describe specific projects, a deadline for LaunchPad applications, or results from the breakout sessions.

Articles.Title: Collaborative Collision: FSU researchers explore the future of artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: Brown student maps the hidden global labor powering AI
stories.Summary:
Brown University senior Cunyan Ma has built an interactive online map that traces the human labor behind everyday artificial intelligence systems, which the university announced on October 26, 2026. The map links technology companies and their intermediaries to data workers around the world, pulling together existing databases, Ma's own data collection and news reports about working conditions. Much of this labor, which includes labeling images, transcribing speech and rating chatbot responses, is done by people in the Global South for low pay. Ma says the goal is to make the scale of this work visible to the public in a way that is easy to grasp.

Ma's map shows the chain of outsourcing that most people never see, from major corporations to the firms that specialize in data labeling. According to the university, the current version reveals links between 13 data labeling companies, 141 of their corporate customers and 31 countries that host data worker sites. Ma used those delivery centers as a proxy for where workers are located, since the companies that hire them tend to keep the arrangement opaque. The university notes that the map is not a comprehensive picture of AI labor but is meant as an illustrative one.

Ma describes the work as a kind of AI colonialism, in which difficult and poorly paid labor is pulled from countries like Kenya, Indonesia and Colombia to serve profit in Western markets. Ma, a social analysis and research concentrator, is the creator of the project and is advised by Suresh Venkatasubramanian, a computer science professor who leads Brown's Center for Technological Responsibility, Reimagination and Redesign. Venkatasubramanian said that behind AI systems is an aggregation of human knowledge and effort, and that much current public discussion ignores this by treating AI as a sentient being. Ma said the map could also help dispersed workers find one another, which might make organizing easier.

She added that she hopes the map can eventually help people see how the wider global economy shapes labor. Ma plans to keep expanding the project, and she hopes to map the labor involved in the semiconductor industry next. The university presents the work as an effort to encourage a more equitable distribution of AI labor and its benefits. The map is freely available online.

Articles.Title: Brown student maps the hidden global labor powering AI

stories.Headline: Wide-ranging symposium to produce undergrad course on AI anxiety
stories.Summary:
The University of Virginia is holding an "AI Anxiety + Human Flourishing Symposium" on November 18 and 19 at the Contemplative Commons, bringing together experts to ask how young people might thrive in an age of artificial intelligence. The gathering will draw on technology experts, educators, religious leaders and specialists in contemplative practices. Its discussions are meant to lay the groundwork for a new undergraduate course that other universities could copy. Students are built into the program as moderators, panelists and convenors.

The event will concentrate on three ways of responding to AI-related stress: keeping control over personal choices, pursuing individual and community well-being, and imagining a healthy future alongside AI. Participants include Alexis Ohanian, co-founder and former executive chair of Reddit, and Anton Korinek, head of transformative AI economic studies at Anthropic who is on leave as a UVA economics professor. Other speakers include Sally Steele of Outdoorithm, Father Michael Baggot of the Pontifical Athenaeum Regina Apostolorum, data scientist Shiva Jahani, and investor Paul Tudor Jones. UVA President Scott Beardsley is also listed among the speakers.

Michael Sheehy, research associate professor and director of research at UVA's Contemplative Sciences Center, is helping lead the effort. He said the emergence of AI is changing how young people learn, think and plan their lives, including their jobs, relationships and raising of children. He described the anxiety many young adults feel as "AI anxiety" and said the university feels compelled to respond. Sheehy also said that the aim is to draw on human experience, including painful experience, to shape a healthier relationship with AI.

The article cites an August Pew Research Center poll in which 55 percent of adults aged 18 to 29 said they were more concerned than excited about AI in daily life, the first such majority in that poll's history. The symposium sits within UVA's priority of advancing AI through interdisciplinary research, teaching and partnerships. Beardsley said AI should be a tool for humanity rather than the reverse, and that the university is well placed to advance the conversation because of its experts across many disciplines. Sheehy added that the goal is not to have AI passively deliver well-being, since people cannot flourish passively or alone.

Articles.Title: Wide-ranging symposium to produce undergrad course on AI anxiety

stories.Headline: Op-ed: AI Education Can’t End at Graduation
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion piece, not a breaking news event, so the story here is the op-ed itself. On October 26, 2026, New York Institute of Technology published an op-ed by its president, Jerry Balentine, D.O., on FoxNews.com. In it, Balentine argues that universities must update not only what they teach about artificial intelligence but also how long they keep teaching it. He notes that Americans are adopting AI faster than any previous technology, and that the real gap lies between simply using AI and using it well.

Balentine cites an experiment by researchers at Harvard Business School and Boston Consulting Group in which consultants using leading AI models produced higher-quality work and finished tasks faster when they understood the technology's strengths and limits. When they leaned on AI for work outside its areas of competence, however, their performance fell below that of a control group that did not use AI at all. From this he concludes that AI literacy means knowing which questions to ask, how much confidence to place in the answers, and when independent verification or expert advice is needed. He gives examples across career stages, from recent graduates building software to mid-career managers automating routine work to retirees managing healthcare information and Medicare options.

Balentine argues that these skills require continuous learning and that universities already have the infrastructure to provide it, since most keep ties to alumni through continuing education, professional certificates, and executive education. He writes that higher education should become a lifelong partner in AI education, continuing a long role of helping people adapt to major societal change. The article notes that the piece is part of a university campaign meant to build awareness and thought leadership on topics of national relevance. The article does not describe any specific new program, funding, or policy change that would follow from the argument.

Articles.Title: Op-ed: AI Education Can’t End at Graduation

stories.Headline: Taxing artificial intelligence: What’s on the table, and what’s at stake
stories.Summary:
The Brookings commentary by Elena Patel and Aparna Mathur, published October 27, 2026, examines proposals to tax artificial intelligence and what is at stake for federal revenue. The authors start from the premise that AI could raise productivity while also replacing some workers, and that the answer to how many and how fast remains uncertain. Because individual income and payroll taxes generate roughly 85% of federal tax receipts, a shift of income from wages to business profits and other capital income could lower effective tax rates and erode revenue at the same time that demand for programs helping displaced workers grows. Lawmakers have responded with AI-specific tax proposals aimed at different goals, including maintaining revenue, funding displaced workers, covering the power and water costs of AI facilities, and slowing AI growth.

The authors lay out the main arguments for taxing AI, each resting on a different scenario. One holds that AI could shrink the tax base, leaving income and payroll tax receipts falling before any offsetting gains from profits arrive, if they arrive at all. A second concerns the costs AI infrastructure imposes on nearby communities, since data centers consume large amounts of electricity and water, and two-thirds of data centers built since 2022 sit in regions already short on water. A third holds that firms may be overspending on AI in pursuit of market share, which a tax could curb, though the authors note this is hard to verify.

They also argue that AI-specific taxes are easy to explain politically but are not required to reach these goals, since reforming capital income taxation, adopting a value-added tax, a carbon tax, or a corporate cash-flow tax could address some of the same concerns. The piece adds that such taxes could conflict with international tax and domestic investment strategies and shape where AI infrastructure is built, with implications for national security. The commentary then weighs the leading designs, which target different points in the AI production process. A training compute tax would charge developers for computing power used in training runs, offering timely revenue and a narrow set of taxpayers, but it would depend on self-reported data and be hard to predict in yield.

A data center electricity tax could be verified through existing utility meters, though separating AI use from other computing use would again require self-reporting, and a related approach would have data centers pay for grid upgrades instead of passing costs to other ratepayers. A usage tax on tokens would be broader and less well targeted, falling on both labor-displacing and productivity-enhancing applications, and tokens vary in length and computing demand across models. A windfall profit tax, discussed last, would reach profits rather than activity. The authors caution that these designs differ in timing, revenue potential, economic cost, and ease of administration, and that each involves trade-offs.

stories.Summary:
A seminar titled "Using AI to Support Grant Writing and Proposal Development" is scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 18, from 1 to 2 p.m., held on Zoom. The session is presented as a University of Maryland, Baltimore event, and the listing describes it as an introduction to practical ways researchers can use artificial intelligence tools in their grant work. The articles do not say who organized the event beyond the listing itself. The listing was published on Oct. 26, 2026. The seminar will cover approaches to AI-assisted and agentic grant development, including effective prompting, drafting and refining Specific Aims, recommended workflows, and ways to avoid errors that AI tools can generate.

Attendees will be shown how to use these tools while keeping their proposals accurate, high in quality, and compliant. The listing states that AI use must follow National Institutes of Health and University of Maryland, Baltimore policies. It does not describe any new rule or formal requirement that the seminar introduces. The speaker is Owen White, PhD, who is a professor in the Department of Epidemiology & Public Health at the University of Maryland School of Medicine. He also serves as associate director of the Institute for Genome Sciences and as associate director of Research Collaboration & Development at the same institute.

The listing describes the tools as helpful for making research work more efficient when used thoughtfully. Its only other message is a general call for students, faculty, and staff to take part. The articles give no further background on the seminar or on the policies it references. They do not indicate whether recordings or follow-up materials will be provided. stories.Headline: Lee Rainie coauthors article in ‘Fast Company’ about workers and AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Lee Rainie, director of Elon University's Imaging the Digital Future Center, recently co-authored an article in Fast Company about AI adoption in the workplace. The piece, published by Elon in late October 2026, draws on research from InnovateUS, a nonprofit learning initiative that has trained more than 250,000 government workers in AI and digital skills. The article notes that generative AI is raising productivity for some workers, but many government employees remain unsure how the technology fits their jobs, how to use it, or whether they are allowed to use it at all. The authors describe this uncertainty as a key takeaway from their work with public servants.

InnovateUS works with workers in all 50 states and the District of Columbia, in roles ranging from public safety and benefits administration to legal services and executive leadership. Its free skill-building workshops, held across the country and online, let public employees share what works and what does not in their agencies. Participants have explored using AI to improve benefits delivery alongside New York City's health commissioner, and a Colorado state leader described using generative AI to improve performance reviews, reporting better feedback, higher worker satisfaction, reduced turnover and time savings. The organization aims to give state and local workers accessible chances to build skills that help them serve the public and earn residents' trust.

The authors also point to the first report from their Observatory of Public Sector AI, which is based on 106,300 precourse surveys and 67,002 postcourse surveys from participants in an introductory generative AI course. Those responses were gathered between June 2024 and May 2026. According to the authors, the findings show a substantial gap between the headlines about generative AI and the realities of everyday government work. The article is credited to Rainie along with his coauthors, and the excerpt is presented as a preview of the fuller piece.

stories.Headline: URI to launch new Interdisciplinary and Applied AI bachelor’s degree – Rhody Today - The University of Rhode Island
stories.Summary:
The University of Rhode Island announced on October 27, 2026, that it is launching a new Interdisciplinary and Applied AI bachelor's degree. The program will have a soft launch this spring and be fully offered by fall 2027, run through the College of Business in cooperation with the College of Arts and Sciences. It is designed to teach students to use artificial intelligence ethically and to build AI tools using data gathered from reputable sources with proper consent. Students will work in interdisciplinary teams on real-world problems, with a focus on safety, security and privacy.

The degree requires between 53 and 70 credits for completion, and students must also complete an internship with a company as an AI specialist. Indrani Mandal, associate teaching professor in the Department of Computer Science and Statistics, and Devendra (Dave) Kale, interim associate dean for undergraduate education in the College of Business, will lead the program. Students can begin earning credit this spring through business analytics and artificial intelligence courses in the College of Business and the AI for Everyone course (CSC/DSP 161) in the College of Arts and Sciences, and those credits will count toward the degree. The program can be taken as a standalone degree or as a second major alongside any other field of study.

Mandal said the program grew partly from student interest and from a growing need for workers who can apply AI responsibly in fields ranging from healthcare and life sciences to small businesses and accounting. She argued that the technology must be operated with good intentions and for the greater good, and that understanding where AI can unsafely intrude will help develop strategies to prevent harmful practices. Christy Ashley, a marketing professor in the College of Business, said businesses are meeting AI usage goals but struggle to see how it affects workflow and daily performance, and that employers want graduates who can also collaborate across fields. Graduates could pursue roles such as AI ethics officer, human-AI interaction designer, or tech regulation and governance specialist.

The launch follows several other AI initiatives at the university. Gaurav Khanna and Zhu (Drew) Zhang are part of the Rhode Island AI Task Force, which released a 75-page report in January on how AI could be economically valuable across the state. Last fall, URI launched the Institute for AI and Computational Research, which provides AI infrastructure for research to other Rhode Island higher education institutions. The College of Business also already offers two AI-centered degrees, one in business analytics and AI for undergraduates and one in applied AI and business analytics at the graduate level. Prospective students can contact Mandal at indrani_mandal@uri.edu or Kale at 401-874-4199 or dkale@uri.edu for more information.

stories.Headline: Before the storm: Doctoral student earns international recognition for AI research on cognitive decline
stories.Summary:
Marquette University doctoral student Karen Wurzel has received the Best PhysioNet Challenge Oral Presentation award for her artificial intelligence research on cognitive decline. The award was presented at the 53rd Computing in Cardiology Conference in Madrid, Spain. Wurzel, who studies electrical and computer engineering, used AI to analyze sleep study data and look for patterns linked to future cognitive impairment, including dementia and Alzheimer's disease. Her work focuses on a single night of sleep, and the goal is to predict decline one to six years before a diagnosis.

The recognition came from the George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge, an annual international competition co-organized by PhysioNet and Computing in Cardiology. The competition was established in 2000 and brings together researchers from different disciplines to address unresolved medical problems. This year's challenge asked participants to use data from sleep studies to predict future diagnoses of cognitive impairment. Wurzel's win places her work among computational approaches the challenge has used to evaluate emerging methods in biomedical research.

The article presents the award as a sign that the approach shows promise, though it does not describe the results in detail. Wurzel's research adviser, Dr. Richard Povinelli, praised her as an outstanding scientist with insight, rigor, and enthusiasm for discovery. Wurzel said that her adviser encourages her to pursue projects she cares about and serves as a sounding board when her work stalls. She also said that presenting technical work clearly has been a skill she worked to build, and that the award confirmed her effort.

Beyond prediction, Wurzel hopes her research will eventually help protect brain health, not only forecast its decline. The article describes Wurzel's path at Marquette, where she stood out in Povinelli's Introduction to Artificial Intelligence course in fall 2024 and began lab research during her first year as a Ph.D. student. The award has also raised the visibility of her work and brought new professional contacts, including conversations with researchers at the conference. The article does not say what comes next in her research timeline or whether the approach will be tested in clinical settings.

Articles.Title: Before the storm: Doctoral student earns international recognition for AI research on cognitive decline

stories.Headline: UWF to host Leadership in the Age of AI conference with special Veterans Day observance - University of West Florida
stories.Summary:
The University of West Florida's Office of Military Services announced that it will host the second annual Leadership in the Age of AI conference, followed by a UWF Veterans Day Observance, on Friday, Nov. 6, in the UWF Conference Center. The office is working with the Aylstock, Witkin, Kreis & Overholtz Center for Leadership and the Center for Cybersecurity and AI on the event. The free conference is sponsored by PenAir Credit Union and will examine how artificial intelligence is changing modern leadership. The program also includes a special observance honoring those who have served.

The event is open to students, faculty, staff, military service members and their families, veterans and the wider Pensacola community. Attendees can expect networking and breakfast beginning at 8 a.m., followed by opening remarks and a keynote from Patrick Rooney, director of entrepreneurial development at Co:Lab Pensacola. A leadership panel moderated by Christian Hendrick, a retired U.S. Air Force Special Operations veteran and systems integration subject matter expert at Booz Allen Hamilton, will look at practical uses of AI across industries. Panelists include Joshua Turner, Joshua Hartigan and Jay Wells, who will discuss AI's influence on leadership, entrepreneurship, decision-making and workforce development.

The conference is intended to encourage dialogue among academia, industry and the military about emerging technologies. After the panel, the program shifts to the Veterans Day observance, which will feature Lieutenant Colonel Keith Nelson and recognize military service and sacrifice. Dr. Andrew Del Gaudio, executive director of the Office of Military Services, said the event is meant to broaden perspectives and give participants new ideas for navigating a changing professional landscape. He also said the observance gives the university a chance to honor those who have served the nation.

Del Gaudio described the office's commitment to serving those who serve and strengthening ties between the military community and the university. The university presents the event as a way to link conversations about the future of leadership with the principles of service and responsibility that veterans embody. Those who want more information or wish to register can visit uwf.edu/AgeofAI, while details about the Office of Military Services, the Aylstock, Witkin, Kreis & Overholtz Center and the Center for Cybersecurity and AI are available at uwf.edu/militaryservices, uwf.edu/awko and uwf.edu/cyberai. The announcement was published on Oct. 27, 2026, and reaffirms the university's support for veterans, service members and military-affiliated individuals.
