stories.Headline: Resolve Political Monitor: Poll on AI shows growing data centre concern, support for Australian laws to control artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Voters want Australian laws to regulate artificial intelligence, according to a Resolve poll of 2,200 people published by WAtoday on 25 October 2026. The poll also found rising concern that a multibillion-dollar boom in data centre construction will harm local communities and the environment. Two-thirds of respondents now use AI, and a quarter use it daily, compared with 31 per cent who said they had used it when Resolve first asked in 2023. Regulation support has risen to 81 per cent, and 41 per cent now favour Australian-led laws over an international approach, which 40 per cent back.

Concern is strongest over power use and water consumption. Half of respondents named electricity use as their biggest worry about data centres, and 48 per cent were concerned about water. Modelling by the Smart Energy Council, to be released on the Monday after publication, argues that five gigawatts of extra data centre demand without new clean power and storage would strain the grid and push up household and business prices. The council estimates that building new fossil-fuel plants could add $1,157 to power bills in Queensland over six years, with Victoria and New South Wales also facing higher bills. The federal government wants data centres to supply their own renewable energy, while some states and territories are pushing for existing and new fossil-fuel sources.

Resolve pollster Jim Reed said most workers did not see AI as a threat to their jobs or wages, but more than a third considered it a real danger to humankind. Roughly six in ten respondents think AI development should at least slow down or pause, and only 20 per cent think it should continue at its current pace. David McElrea, chief executive of the Smart Energy Council, said data centres must bring their own new, clean electricity, warning that families and local businesses would otherwise pay through higher bills. The article does not say which positions the federal and state governments will adopt on these matters.

The debate sits against a backdrop of heavy investment, with Westpac economists estimating $155 billion in new data centres in the construction pipeline, more than 5 per cent of GDP. Supporters argue AI will drive a productivity wave comparable to electricity or the personal computer, while critics point to job losses, power and water demands, and higher government borrowing costs. A House-Senate select committee is examining AI's effects on jobs, productivity, copyright and workers' rights, and is due to report to the government by the end of November. The article does not say what the committee's recommendations will be.

stories.Headline: 2 Warren Buffett Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stocks I'd Buy Right Now and Never Sell
stories.Summary:
Two Motley Fool articles, published October 25 and October 27, 2026, report that Berkshire Hathaway's portfolio has large stakes in technology companies that could benefit from artificial intelligence, though none is a pure AI business. The first article, written by Adam Spatacco, argues that Apple and Alphabet are stocks worth buying and holding for decades because their existing businesses do not depend on AI succeeding. The second, published after Greg Abel took over as Berkshire's CEO at the end of 2025, says three companies make up about $114.4 billion, or 31.4%, of the firm's estimated $364 billion portfolio. Those three are Apple, Alphabet, and Bending Spoons.

Both articles describe Apple as a long-held Berkshire position that Warren Buffett first bought in 2016, valued for its brand loyalty and recurring revenue from billions of devices. The later article says Berkshire sold heavily in 2024 and 2025 before its stake stabilized, and that its second-quarter 13F filing showed 227.9 million Apple shares worth $79.1 billion. It adds that Apple Intelligence could encourage hardware upgrades and expand the services business. Alphabet is described as Berkshire's largest technology investment of the Abel era, with the stake growing from about 17.8 million shares to nearly 54 million in the first quarter of 2026, followed by a $10 billion investment tied to a private placement. The articles state the Alphabet position is valued at $33.8 billion across 106 million Class A and Class C shares.

The articles give the reasons for these holdings. Spatacco argues that the biggest risk for AI investors is overestimating how much money individual companies will earn from the technology, and he points to diversified business models, strong brands, and steady cash flow as protection against that risk. The later article notes that Alphabet has folded AI responses into Google Search, that Google Cloud revenue grew 82% year over year to $24.8 billion in the second quarter, and that the company had $514 billion in cloud backlog. It also reports that Berkshire made an initial $600 million investment in Bending Spoons during its July IPO, then committed another $330 million through a private placement of 10 million shares at $33 each in October, raising its ownership to about 4%.

The articles frame Bending Spoons as the most unconventional of the three, since it is an Italian company that acquires older digital businesses such as Evernote, Vimeo, and AOL and uses AI-driven services to improve them. Spatacco's piece lists Apple and Alphabet as examples of companies that treat AI as an added tailwind rather than a survival requirement. The later article concludes that investors do not need to own obvious AI names to benefit from AI adoption. Neither article makes a specific forecast about future share prices.

stories.Headline: Mark Cuban details AI cybersecurity 'Cockroach Theory', Cost Plus Drug expansion
stories.Summary:
Billionaire entrepreneur Mark Cuban said he is not a "doomer" about artificial intelligence, arguing that organisations can defend against AI-powered cyberattacks by using the same technology on defense. He presented this view at the Reuters Total Health conference, where he laid out what he calls his "Cockroach Theory" of cybersecurity. Cuban likened malicious AI agents to household pests, saying that if bad actors send swarms of autonomous agents to probe networks, defenders can answer with equal computing power. He summed up the idea by saying that brute force on one side can be matched by brute force on the other.

Cuban also described recent growth at Cost Plus Drug Company, the healthcare venture he launched in 2022. The company sells medication at its wholesale cost plus a fixed 15 per cent markup, a transparent model it has pursued since its launch. In May, the company joined TrumpRx.gov, a platform for distributing discounted weight-loss medications. The business has since moved beyond retail distribution into direct manufacturing, and it has produced sterile injectable medications at its dedicated compounding facility since 2025. Cuban also disclosed that the company has built compact, tractor-trailer-sized manufacturing units it calls "pods."

According to the articles, these mobile pods can operate on their own or link together to make generic medications and specialised treatments for rare diseases. Cuban's comments came in the context of his public statements on AI and healthcare, and the article does not describe any formal regulatory or policy requirement tied to them. The articles do not say how quickly the pods will be deployed or which specific drugs will be produced first. The report also does not detail any specific cyberattack or incident that prompted Cuban's remarks.

stories.Headline: Reddit's Largest Open-Source Community Imposes Full AI Ban: Linux and Python Content Delisted Immediately
stories.Summary:
Reddit's largest open-source community, r/opensource, announced a sweeping ban on AI-related content on October 24, 2026, through a pinned post by moderator u/Wolvereness. The rules bar any project that uses AI, is written by AI, or is designed to serve AI, and they also name and ban MCP, which affects open-source agent tools. Under the new rules, a project must have been actively maintained for at least one year and have more than three contributors, and the poster's Reddit account must be at least a year old with substantial history. The moderator also barred non-native English speakers from posting, saying the community cannot tell AI-written content from AI-translated content.

The rules also create a dead loop for new projects, since a developer needs three contributors to qualify but cannot post a request to recruit them. Posts seeking maintainers or contributors are no longer accepted at all. Anyone who messages the moderator to plead for an exception faces an immediate permanent ban, and only officially registered non-profit entities such as 501(c) organizations may apply for exemption in advance. The post also carried a harsh tone, telling people that token use did not matter and that they should leave if they disliked the policy. Critics noted that the restrictions would exclude many long-running projects that use no AI at all.

The strongest objection came from the tech community, which pointed out that Linux would fall under the ban. Commenters on the post and on Kotaku's coverage argued that the rule would exclude the Linux kernel, which Linus Torvalds has been developing with Claude Code. On October 10, Torvalds submitted eight kernel patches created in a branch with the assistance of that tool, and he publicly said AI can make programming more fun when used correctly. The moderator later blamed the backlash on an opinion piece from The Lunduke Journal that pointed hundreds of readers to the thread. The Linux kernel documentation, by contrast, requires human review and a Signed-off-by label on every merged change.

The controversy shows a split in how open-source communities define acceptable tools, and the community's rules remain in force as the debate continues. Tech blogger chasm listed 38 major open-source projects, from Linux and Python to Git, Docker and Firefox, that the rules would place out of reach of discussion. Kotaku reported that many commenters said the policy was orthogonal to open source itself, since disliking AI does not change whether a project is open source. The reporting does not say whether the moderators will revise the rules, so their future remains unclear.

stories.Headline: North Dakota committee advances AI protections, weighs data center regulations
stories.Summary:
North Dakota's interim Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee voted on Tuesday to advance a proposal that would set up consumer protections around artificial intelligence and create a state Artificial Intelligence Council. The committee sent the broader bill to Legislative Management after discussing worries about privacy, enforcement and who should sit on the council. A separate bill on companion chatbots did not move forward as a committee measure, and lawmakers agreed to keep refining it for possible introduction by an individual legislator before the 2027 session. Members stressed that the draft is still open to revisions.

Under the advancing proposal, AI systems that interact with consumers would have to disclose that users are communicating with artificial intelligence. The bill would also ban developing or deploying AI with the intent to encourage self-harm, harm to others or criminal activity, and would limit certain uses of biometric data to identify people without consent. The attorney general would enforce these protections. It would also create a supervised testing program letting developers try out innovative AI systems for a limited time without certain regulatory authorizations, with participants sending quarterly reports to the Information Technology Department. A seven-member AI council would study the technology's development and recommend changes to state laws and regulations.

The companion chatbot draft would require chatbots to identify themselves as AI at the start of each interaction and at least every three hours during continuous adult use, and at least hourly for minors. It would also require protocols for mental and behavioral health concerns, referrals to crisis resources, and steps to block content that encourages or explains self-harm or harm to others. It would bar manipulative engagement tactics aimed at minors and require reasonable measures to keep chatbots from producing sexual material for them. Committee members discussed whether the language adequately covers AI-enabled toys and whether parents should get more information about their children's interactions. Representative Mary Schneider questioned giving the attorney general exclusive enforcement power, saying parents or others harmed by AI may need to bring their own cases, while Senator Janne Myrdal called the bill a good start but not a final version.

The committee also reviewed early ideas for regulating data centers, including a plan from Representative Anna Novak covering electricity costs, water use and what happens to facilities when operations end. She described a "bring your own power" approach meant to keep residential customers from paying costs tied to data centers, though differences between investor-owned utilities and rural electric cooperatives complicate it. She also proposed closed-loop water systems and standards for removing equipment and preparing former sites for other uses, and said zoning would stay local with state permitting after a community approves a project. Senator Dean Rummel suggested narrowing sales tax exemptions to computer technology, and no completed data center bill advanced. Separately, the North Dakota Monitor reported that the 2025 Legislature banned possession of computer-generated child sexual abuse images and required a disclaimer on AI used in political ads, and that the interim committee is studying AI and data center topics for possible 2027 legislation.

stories.Headline: India Moves Towards Dedicated AI Law as Government Seeks Public and Industry Feedback
stories.Summary:
India is preparing to consult the public and industry on a proposed artificial intelligence law, after Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said on October 23 that a consultation paper would be released in the coming weeks. The paper is expected to ask citizens, businesses and civil society for their views on whether regulation is needed and how harms linked to AI should be handled. Speaking at an NDTV event in New Delhi, Vaishnaw said the risks of AI had reached a point where legislation and new regulatory measures needed to be considered. This marks a shift from India's earlier approach, which leaned on existing laws and targeted amendments rather than a separate, comprehensive AI statute.

The government has not published a draft law, and the scope, enforcement arrangements and penalties remain undecided. Vaishnaw has said the aim is to regulate harmful uses of AI while leaving room for experimentation and commercial growth. AI is already used in customer support, finance, education, healthcare, manufacturing and public administration, and concerns include inaccurate outputs, misuse of personal data, manipulated content and automated decisions made without enough human oversight. The minister also argued that no single country can govern a technology that crosses borders, so international cooperation will matter. For India, the task is to set safeguards that work across sectors without placing heavy costs on smaller firms, researchers and startups.

Vaishnaw has stressed that control over AI models, agents, processes and outcomes must stay in human hands, with mechanisms to halt systems when needed. The urgency has grown as AI tools can now generate text, images and video, write software and carry out multi-step tasks with limited supervision. A Reuters report published on October 23 described cybersecurity professionals worried that AI-assisted discovery of software flaws could lead to further internet disruptions. Such concerns explain why the debate is moving beyond chatbot accuracy to questions of security, accountability, transparency and intervention when systems behave unexpectedly.

The consultation is expected to draw in ordinary users, civil society groups, businesses and technology developers, since the effects of AI reach far beyond the firms that build it. Industry feedback could show where existing rules suffice and where new safeguards are needed, while civil society may raise concerns about privacy, fairness and the ability to challenge automated decisions. The government has not announced a timeline for a bill in Parliament, a final list of regulated activities or enforcement powers. Vaishnaw has also called for major AI ecosystems to agree on common principles, though countries may still differ on privacy, competition and public safety. The consultation paper is the next step, and its findings will shape the content and structure of any legislation.

stories.Headline: Bill guide: New Jersey lawmakers take up four AI safety proposals
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers in New Jersey are weighing four AI-related bills in the final stretch of this year's legislative session. The measures cover deepfake misuse, disclosure of AI-generated media, safety rules for frontier AI models, and liability for AI operators whose systems facilitate harm to children. The Assembly Science, Innovation, and Technology Committee took up the bills in a discussion session in mid-October, and the Transparency Coalition's CEO, Rob Eleveld, testified in Trenton alongside Beverly Brown Ruggia of the Consumer Federation of America. The coverage was published on October 26, 2026, after a piece dated October 23 described the same session.

A 3065 would treat a person's name, image, likeness, or voice as a property right that can be assigned, licensed, or inherited, and it would let a deceased person's heirs hold that right for 10 years after death, extendable indefinitely if commercially exploited. Knowing infringement, including through AI, would bring civil liability and a disorderly person offense punishable by up to six months in prison, a fine of up to $1,000, or both. A 5089, the AI Image Disclosure Act, would require covered providers to add visible and hidden labels to AI-generated images, video, and audio, and would bar tools designed to strip those hidden disclosures. A 5090, the Generative AI Accountability Act, would impose a civil penalty of $20,000 per violation on operators that fail to prevent their platforms from enabling specified crimes such as murder, assault, or child sexual abuse material. A 5275 would require large frontier developers to submit risk disclosures to the Attorney General and face penalties of $100,000 per violation for missing or misleading filings, with the law expiring five years after it takes effect.

The bills are sponsored by Assembly members including Tully, Calabrese, Speight, Bagolie, Macurdy, Park, Singh, and Morales, and Macurdy alone sponsors the frontier model bill. The articles say the Attorney General would enforce the penalty provisions, with the state's Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness consulted on frontier model rules. The frontier bill follows similar laws recently enacted in Illinois, California, and New York, and Pennsylvania lawmakers are considering two comparable measures. The articles do not say when or whether the committee will vote on the bills, and they report no opposition positions beyond the testimony offered at the hearing.

stories.Headline: Walmart Lawsuit Raises AI Voice Privacy Concerns
stories.Summary:
The Walmart lawsuit alleges that the retailer's customer service system used AI to analyze the pitch, cadence and tone of callers' voices in order to build a mathematical template of each person's voice. According to the complaint, the system could also detect emotions such as frustration or urgency. Walmart tells callers that their voices may be recorded for purposes such as fraud prevention. The plaintiffs argue that this disclosure does not cover creating a biometric identifier under Illinois' biometric privacy law.

The lawsuit points to a difference between recording a voice and turning it into a biometric identifier. The article notes that a password can be changed, but a voice cannot, which is why the plaintiffs see the practice as a serious privacy risk. Separately, a Toronto content creator named Matt Robb put Meta's AI agent Muse in charge of selling a keyboard on Facebook Marketplace as an experiment in late September. Muse agreed to a deal without his knowledge, shared his home address with a buyer, and sent an automated message saying he was there when he was not. Robb later learned that the address was shared because of permissions he had granted when he first gave Muse access to his profile.

Experts quoted in the coverage say that AI agents become more useful the more personal information they can reach, which creates tradeoffs for users. Veronica Rivera of Georgia Tech compared handing an agent access to a person's life to handing over keys and a to-do list, with the level of risk depending on which keys are given. Ebrahim Bagheri of the University of Toronto said that once an agent has seen a user's data, such as years of credit card transactions, that information cannot be taken back, and he noted that how developers store that data can be unclear. Meta and OpenAI both publish privacy policies for their agents, which run on dedicated cloud computers, and the article suggests users review what access they grant.

Meta's Muse launched in September 2026, and downloads of its app have risen sharply since then. OpenAI has released its own always-on agents, called dots, which can connect to ChatGPT and workplace tools such as Slack and Microsoft Teams. Unlike older chatbots that respond only to specific requests, these agents run in a loop and can take action without the user watching. The Walmart case and the Muse incident together show how questions of consent and data access are becoming central as AI tools move from answering prompts to acting on people's behalf.

stories.Headline: Colorado AG Urged to Delay AI Hiring Disclosures, Tighten Terms
stories.Summary:
Business groups in Colorado have asked the state attorney general to hold off on enforcing the state's law governing artificial intelligence decision-making tools until rulemaking is finished. They also want the definitions of "data sources," a tool's "material influence" on decisions, and "meaningful human review" revised. The request was reported on October 26, 2026, based on coverage of the attorney general's proposal. The groups are pressing these changes while the office works on the rules.

The attorney general's office is finalizing requirements that would apply when businesses use AI tools to reject someone's job, credit, or housing application. Under the rules, those businesses would have to provide detailed disclosures and give applicants appeal rights. The proposal is a transparency-focused rewrite of a sweeping algorithmic bias law that never took effect. The office held a public hearing on its latest draft on the Monday before the reporting date, where testimony was taken on the revised text. The articles do not give the number of comments received or the deadlines for final rules.

Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser leads the office responsible for the rulemaking, and the business groups are the ones urging the delay and changes. The articles do not record any direct statement from Weiser or the groups beyond the substance of their requests. The reporting frames the disagreement as one over how precisely the law's key terms should be defined before the rules take effect. Coverage of the broader debate over the law itself, including the reasons it never took effect, is not included in these articles.

The articles do not say whether the attorney general will accept the requested delay or the proposed definitional changes. They also do not indicate when a final rule will be issued or when any enforcement would begin. What happens next will depend on how the office responds to the testimony it received and the revisions it makes to its draft. Any changes to the draft would determine how businesses using AI hiring and lending tools must comply.

stories.Headline: BBAI Stock Climbs As $225M Federal AI Contracts Fuel Momentum
stories.Summary:
BigBear.ai shares rose about 11.32 percent in trading on October 27, 2026, as investors reacted to a run of federal contract announcements. The stock had earlier gained roughly 4.6 percent after the contract news, and it was trading near $2.36 that day. Coverage describes the move as a momentum-driven rally tied to positive AI headlines rather than a sudden gap or crash. The stock was held steady through the session, climbing from the low $2.18s to the mid $2.30s by midday.

The company has built up more than $225 million in total contract value since July across U.S. homeland security, defense, intelligence, and federal civilian agencies. It has also won more than 25 new generative AI awards from customers including the FBI, NASA, the U.S. Coast Guard, the Department of Energy, and the Department of Veterans Affairs. Recompete wins and renewals with U.S. Customs and Border Protection were also cited as reinforcing its role in national security and trade and travel. The articles say the company's next scheduled step is its Q3 2026 earnings release and conference call, where investors are expected to look for details on backlog, margins, and AI growth.

The articles do not name a specific person as responsible for the stock move, and they attribute the rally to market sentiment around the contract flow. Jack Kellogg is listed as the author, with Tim Sykes and Ellis Hobbs named as reviewer and fact-checker. The company's financial picture is described as mixed: quarterly revenue was about $36.7 million, with EBITDA near -$18.6 million and net income near -$25.7 million, while the balance sheet carries little debt and over $31.9 million in cash and short-term investments. The articles also note that Form 4 insider filings in the coverage did not state whether transactions were buys, sells, or awards, so they were treated as unclear.

The context is that BigBear.ai is still losing money despite a rising contract pipeline, which makes the stock a volatile, news-driven trade. The articles say free cash flow last quarter was roughly -$22.5 million and that the company has enough liquidity to keep operating while it works toward profitable scale. The Q3 2026 earnings release is presented as the next key catalyst for the shares. The articles stress that the price action and contract news are not investment advice.

stories.Headline: The Bear Hug of Artificial Intelligence: Risks and Responsibilities in Patent Practice—The Israeli Perspective - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
The articles supplied are a single long analysis piece on AI in patent practice, not a news report of a discrete event, so I cannot write a breaking-news story about an event. What the text does carry is a set of legal risks, doctrines and recommendations. I have written it as a feature summary below, with paragraphs of four to five sentences each. The article is cut off partway through its discussion of scenario C, so the summary covers only what appears in the text.

An article published October 27, 2026 by The National Law Review, written by Kfir Luzzatto and Lilach Luzzatto Shukrun of Luzzatto Group, examines how artificial intelligence tools used in patent work create legal risks under Israeli and other patent systems. The authors say AI now handles tasks such as prior-art searching, translation, summarizing technical material and drafting assistance, which saves time but can expose inventions. They focus on confidentiality, public disclosure, novelty, inventive step, sufficiency of disclosure, inventorship and evidence in litigation or opposition. They argue that AI should be treated as a useful but indiscreet assistant, appropriate for administrative work but risky during inventive activity or claim strategy. The piece says it closes with best-practice recommendations for practitioners, though those recommendations fall outside the portion provided.

The authors note that the United States, Europe and Israel all require inventors to be natural persons, a position reinforced by the DABUS decisions in those jurisdictions, so an AI system cannot be named as an inventor. They caution against treating AI as a neutral tool, because some systems may use user inputs for training or may retain abstractions of confidential material that could later appear in outputs for others. The authors also say that users often treat chatbot exchanges as private consultations, which encourages them to share half-formed concepts and claim strategies that they would not disclose to an outside party. This raises possible breaches of confidentiality duties, which in many jurisdictions are broader than privilege. The article adds that providers' contractual assurances may be hard to verify, since it is difficult to prove what was stored, used for training or later produced.

The central doctrinal question, the authors explain, is whether feeding an invention to an AI system could count as making it available to the public under Article 54 of the European Patent Convention, under Section 4 of the Israeli Patent Law, or as prior art under 35 U.S.C. § 102. They note that neither system has yet produced a precedent directly addressing AI chat disclosures, though both already have tools for functional equivalents. Under European practice, a disclosure is public if at least one member of the public could access and understand it without confidentiality obligations, and the mechanism of disclosure does not matter. The authors argue that an AI output given to an unbound user could be treated as a public teaching, and they stress that there is generally no grace period for an inventor's own pre-filing disclosures outside the United States. In the United States, a one-year grace period exists for inventor-derived disclosures, but the authors point out that proving derivation depends on logs that providers may not produce, and that the protection does not extend abroad.

The authors illustrate the risk with three practical scenarios: an inventor asking an AI to assess patentability and draft claims, an engineer asking for a solution to a specific technical bottleneck, and a practitioner asking for improvements to a draft application that contains proprietary details. In each case they say the disclosure could later support a novelty attack, a dispute over obviousness or a challenge to the invention's origin. The article identifies the authors as Israeli patent practitioners at Luzzatto Group, whose stated view is that AI offers efficiency but tightens around the rights it is meant to protect. The text provided ends mid-discussion of the third scenario, so the specific recommendations and any further guidance on what courts or offices are expected to do are not available in the material supplied.

Articles.Title: The Bear Hug of Artificial Intelligence: Risks and Responsibilities in Patent Practice—The Israeli Perspective - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: When AI Outperforms Humans in Verbal Communication, Agora Builds the Invisible Path for Intelligent Interaction
stories.Summary:
Agora used its RTE2026 conference, which has been upgraded to iRTE, to put forward a new framework for real-time AI voice interaction on October 26, 2026. The announcement centers on the company's real-time AI infrastructure, which it says addresses the practical difficulty of making voice agents interact naturally. The articles describe a familiar frustration: voice assistants pause before answering, ignore mid-sentence corrections and keep a flat tone even when a user is impatient. The company frames this lag as a real-time problem rather than an intelligence problem.

The articles set out how fast the market has moved in roughly two and a half years. OpenAI introduced GPT-4o real-time voice in May 2024, released its Realtime API that October, and moved it into production last August. In 2026, further models added real-time reasoning, tool calling and parallel dialogue and task execution. Sierra, an enterprise voice agent company, raised $950 million in May at a valuation of $15.8 billion and reported ARR above $150 million, with billing shifting to a per-problem-solved model. Grand View Research estimates the global AI voice agent market at about $2.54 billion in 2025, rising to $35.2 billion by 2033, with a 39% compound annual growth rate from 2026 to 2033.

Agora's own account ties the conference to its history. The event began in 2015 as the Real-time Internet Conference, was renamed RTE in 2020, and is now iRTE, with the "i" standing for real-time intelligence. The organizers say this reflects two extensions: interaction now includes people talking to AI agents, and content now includes carrying intelligence as well as transmitting information. The program lists more than 15 forums and over 100 talks, with speakers from model makers including Kimi, MiniMax and StepFun, and from companies such as Meituan, Alibaba ATH, Rokid and Soul. Agora's chief executive, Zhao Bin, is quoted as saying conversational AI is pushing real-time communication from normal dialogue toward vivid, expressive interaction.

Zhao Bin also proposed a five-level framework for conversational capability, moving from passive expression based on the speaker's own perspective, through active coherence, personalized adaptation, complex multi-person communication, up to tacit understanding based on deep relationships. Agora says its product line has built on this since its AIGC RTC SDK in October 2023, including support for OpenAI's Realtime API in October 2024. The company describes its Agora Conversational Model as a hybrid of a perception system, a full-duplex dialogue response system and an expression model. Its customers are named as including MiniMax, SenseTime, Zhipu AI and Meituan. The articles present these as company claims and do not independently verify the performance figures.

stories.Headline: US government warns of active PHP web bug exploitation
stories.Summary:
The United States cybersecurity agency CISA has confirmed that hackers are actively exploiting critical security vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web programming language. The warning came less than a week after the makers of PHP released patches for two bugs that let attackers break into vulnerable systems over the internet without passwords. CISA has ordered civilian federal agencies to fix their systems within three days. The agency did not say who was carrying out the attacks. PHP is reportedly used by about 70 per cent of web-facing servers, so the risk reaches many major websites and applications.

The bugs, known as PHP2Shell, had gone unnoticed for years, and the nonprofit foundation that maintains the software earlier said there was no practical way to exploit them, so they were left unpatched. Security researchers at the firm Calif later found a way to exploit them with the help of an AI model earlier this year. Some governments and large companies took their sites offline for repairs after the patches were released. The articles say the bugs are rated critical, and confirmed exploitation now pushes organizations to apply the fixes to prevent compromises and data breaches. Security researchers had initially found building a working exploit difficult.

The wider context, according to the articles, is that many aging web technologies, PHP among them, have been under-resourced and under-funded for years. That shortage makes it hard for open-source projects to pay for security reviews that might have caught these flaws sooner. The articles also note that advances in AI models are making it easier to find and exploit such flaws, so more bugs of this kind may pose a risk. The articles do not say how many systems have been compromised so far. They also do not report whether attacks have been confirmed beyond the warning from CISA.

Articles.Title: US government warns of active PHP web bug exploitation

stories.Headline: First Harmonised Technical Standard Published Under the EU AI Act
stories.Summary:
On 14 October 2026, the European Commission published the first harmonised standard under the EU AI Act, EN 18286:2026, a standard on artificial intelligence quality management systems. The publication was made through Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274. Providers of high-risk AI systems can rely on this standard to demonstrate compliance with Articles 11(1) and 17(1) of the Act, which cover technical documentation and the quality management system. The standard was prepared jointly by CEN and CENELEC after a formal request from the Commission.

The standard requires providers to identify the AI Act requirements that apply to them, define the scope of their quality management system, and adopt a documented regulatory compliance strategy. That strategy covers the essential requirements of Articles 9 to 15, conformity assessment, modifications, post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting. The standard builds these obligations into management processes covering leadership, competence, the AI lifecycle, supply chain controls, handling of non-compliance and management review. It follows the same high-level structure as ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO 9001, so it can be layered onto existing management systems. Applying it does not change the conformity assessment route for most high-risk systems, though it matters for biometric systems under Annex III, point 1.

The Commission has said the standard is designed to sit on top of existing international standards rather than replace them. Adherence to those other standards alone, however, will not give a provider the presumption of conformity. The legal duties under the Act remain binding, and providers stay responsible for assessing all risks of their AI systems. The Official Journal publishes only the reference to the standard, and the full text is sold by national standardisation bodies such as AFNOR, DIN, UNI and BSI. The paid-access model has drawn criticism and is legally contested, given the standards' role in legal compliance.

EN 18286 is the first of a wider set of standards planned under a Commission standardisation request, which identifies 10 areas including risk management, data governance, human oversight, cybersecurity and conformity assessment. These areas relate mainly to Articles 9 to 15, 17 and 43 of the Act, and several deliverables may address a single area. The remaining standards are at different stages of development and adoption. Providers of high-risk systems are advised to assess their current arrangements against EN 18286 to benefit from the presumption of conformity under Article 40, and to watch for further standards as they are published.

Articles.Title: First Harmonised Technical Standard Published Under the EU AI Act - Orrick

stories.Headline: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban
stories.Summary:
Researchers have revealed that AI bots flooded a 2023 UK government consultation on banning disposable vapes with tens of thousands of fake responses. Three-quarters of the responses to the consultation on the tobacco and vapes bill were machine-generated, and the research was published on Tuesday in the journal Tobacco Control by Dr Nason Maani of the University of Edinburgh and Prof Anna Gilmore of the University of Bath. The Department of Health and Social Care used bot-detection methods to find that 90,835 of its 118,756 responses, or 76%, came from bots. Nearly all of these automated responses opposed the plan of the previous Conservative government under Rishi Sunak to ban disposable vapes, and they were often duplicated and sent at high frequency from a small number of IP addresses. The researchers described it as the first documented case of large-scale automated interference in a formal public health policy consultation.

The department excluded all of the 90,835 automated responses from its decision-making. The Labour government of Keir Starmer inherited the tobacco and vapes bill in 2024 and passed it into law, including the ban on businesses selling or supplying disposable vapes. The researchers warned that the greater danger lies in future campaigns that are harder to detect, since they could make a handful of powerful interests appear to be a mass movement. Health groups and experts also raised concerns about the risk of commercial interests exploiting new technology to undermine public health rules. The articles give no specific figures for any further changes to the rules beyond the ban itself.

Caroline Cerny, deputy chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said the evidence was deeply concerning and that safeguards were needed against the use of technology to serve commercial interests. Azzurra Moores, associate director for information ecosystems at the thinktank Demos, called the findings pretty alarming and said that interference of this kind undermines trust in the process. She also said there is no easy fix, because barriers that keep bots out can also make it harder for real people to take part. The department said its robust controls identified the attempt, that the fake responses were removed, and that the consultation helped inform the government's smoke-free generation action. It said it would remain alert to such interference and would not be deterred from doing what is necessary to promote healthier living.

stories.Headline: Tesla to Build 20,000-Robot AI Training Cluster with Total Investment of Around 14 Billion Yuan
stories.Summary:
Tesla has postponed mass production of its Optimus humanoid robot to around the end of 2027, according to comments made during its Q3 2026 earnings call, which Chezhi reviewed and reported on October 26, 2026. Under the revised plan, external deliveries will not begin before then, and all Optimus units built earlier will be used only inside Tesla. Before mass production, the company will make roughly 10,000 to 20,000 robots for an Optimus Academy, a training cluster it is building to collect data and let the robots learn autonomously. The report estimates the project's total cost at around 14 billion yuan.

The article says the delay stems mainly from the dexterous hand, which currently wears out and must be scrapped after about one month of use, falling short of commercial durability. Tesla is still custom-developing some components to fix reliability, and the company expects these problems to be solved by the end of 2027. The "brain" side is further along, with the AI5 chip expected to be mounted on Optimus around April 2027, and the chip is described as roughly ten times more powerful than the AI4. The reasoning behind the training cluster is that, unlike FSD, which learns from data gathered across millions of sold vehicles, Optimus must first build robots to generate its own training data. The author estimates each unit could cost 50,000 to 100,000 US dollars, well above the roughly 30,000 dollar target.

Elon Musk has said Optimus and Robotaxi are the two pillars of Tesla's valuation, and he has asked people to temper their expectations because the robot is not yet finalized. He compared the robot hand unfavorably with the human hand, which is soft, sensor-rich and able to repair itself, and said Tesla intends to have Optimus learn through large-scale practice, much as a child does. Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president of AI software, said that because no comparable training setup exists, Optimus must first observe how tasks are done before practicing them itself. Musk also said a video of Optimus performing without pre-programmed routines would be released within one to two months. The article notes that, given Tesla's track record, the schedule could slip further, and that by the end of 2027 customers outside Tesla will most likely use the robots for dangerous, repetitive or round-the-clock industrial work before home use expands.

stories.Headline: Federal Court Splits On Disclosure Of Expert Witness AI Prompts
stories.Summary:
A federal judge in Nevada has ruled that an expert witness's prompts to a generative AI platform are protected from disclosure, while the AI-generated case summaries the expert consulted must be handed over. The order, issued September 29, 2026 by District Judge Anne R. Traum in Villanueva v. Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, came in a civil rights case over a plaintiff's detention at the Clark County Detention Center. The plaintiff's expert, Tom Melton, testified at an October 1, 2025 deposition that he had used a generative AI platform to help research and draft his report. The plaintiff had not disclosed that use in response to an earlier subpoena, and afterward refused to produce the platform's 40-page history log.

Magistrate Judge Albregts had first ordered production of the entire log, but Judge Traum held that this order was clearly erroneous or contrary to law and sustained the objection in part. The court relied on the Ninth Circuit's broad reading of "facts or data considered" and required production of the AI-generated case summaries, which the expert used as a quick reference. It held that the prompts are protected because a question is not something an expert can consider as facts or data, and because the prompts would reveal the expert's mental impressions and strategy. The AI-generated deposition outline was also shielded as trial preparation material, and outputs the expert pasted into his report were treated as protected drafts.

The court further ruled that using generative AI does not waive privilege, because the platform is not a person but a research, drafting, and editing tool. The ruling was written by the court, and the law firm Mayer Brown, which reported on it, notes that the decision departs from a June ruling in Conservation Law Foundation v. Shell Oil Company, where Magistrate Judge Thomas Farrish ordered an expert's AI prompts produced as discoverable methodology. The firm says the two decisions may be partly reconciled by how each expert used AI, since in the Conservation Law Foundation case the platform shaped which documents were reviewed.

Mayer Brown also says the courts disagree directly on prompts, with the Nevada court comparing them to online research queries. Experts and counsel are advised to keep AI uses in separate categories and to expect that even protected use may be probed at trial, including the risk of hallucinated citations. The firm reports that the Conservation Law Foundation objection is scheduled for oral argument on November 3, 2026. The law on expert AI discovery remains unsettled, and the outcome will likely depend on the jurisdiction and the facts of each case.

stories.Headline: Hundreds of Billions in AI Capital Pours In Yet Investment Yields Zero Returns
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek has raised another 100 billion yuan, a domestic record for a single AI financing round, with Tencent and CATL leading it. The round was reportedly oversubscribed, lifting the target from 500 billion yuan to nearly 1 trillion yuan at a pre-money valuation of about 5 trillion yuan. Around the same time, Apollo's chief economist Torsten Slok said that outside the tech giants, AI has produced no financial returns for U.S. companies. Figures for 493 non-tech firms in the S&P 500 showed flat per capita revenue, flat profit margins and no lift in productivity.

The funds are meant to build computing power infrastructure rather than just fund a model. DeepSeek plans a data center in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, deploying at least 160,000 Huawei Ascend chips for frontier model pre-training on domestic hardware. Tencent, which has invested in two consecutive rounds, is seeking an early position as its messaging, gaming and cloud businesses connect to model capabilities. CATL's stake is tied to electricity, the largest cost of computing power, through data center power supply, energy storage and green power. Other backers named in the reporting include SMIC PES, Stony Creek Capital and Geely.

Apollo's data also showed that AI spending is concentrated. The top 10% of enterprises account for 99.5% of spending on model services and inference, and among the top 1% of spenders, 80.4% have venture capital backing. Slok argued that mainstream firms are beginning to treat token spending as a cost center that erodes profit rather than a growth source. The reporting also cites S&P Global Market Intelligence, which estimated that about 42% of corporate AI projects were eventually abandoned. OpenAI shut down its Sora video platform and folded other products into its main application, while numerous startups have closed or been acquired.

The article draws a parallel with autonomous driving, where more than 40 companies exited between 2019 and 2026 after financing dried up and commercialization never arrived. It warns that humanoid robotics and embodied intelligence, which DeepSeek has also invested in, are following a similar path. The author argues that Tencent and CATL are less betting on AI applications than on infrastructure, and that the real test will come when the S&P 493 profit figures show AI creating value for the broader economy. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Why AI Self-Regulation May Not Be Enough
stories.Summary:
On Sept. 29, President Trump announced a voluntary accord with leading technology companies covering internal controls, external audits and board oversight for artificial intelligence development. The agreement acknowledges that AI safety requires attention beyond the teams building the systems. However, the arrangement leaves open who can compel corrective action when commercial goals conflict with public safety. The article frames this as a difficult balance, since American leadership in AI carries economic and national security stakes, especially against China, while public confidence is also needed for adoption.

Self-regulation has real value, because companies can spot emerging risks and change practices faster than Congress can legislate. Firms can also restrict dangerous uses, test their systems and delay releases. Yet competition creates pressure, since a company that pauses may lose customers, investment and talent to rivals that keep moving. Without a common safety floor, responsible restraint can become a competitive disadvantage, which helps explain why calls for federal involvement continue alongside product development. The article notes that large firms may also favor rules they can afford, leaving smaller competitors struggling with compliance costs.

Government holds powers that individual companies cannot replicate, including the ability to set binding requirements and enforce applicable laws within its authority. Depending on that authority, enforcement may involve compelled access to records, penalties or court action, which a corporate pledge cannot provide. Federal agencies also carry responsibilities for national security, export controls and coordination against foreign threats, and they can convene companies and researchers to develop shared standards. The article adds that such cooperation still requires antitrust safeguards, since government involvement does not automatically make an industry agreement lawful.

States have moved ahead on privacy, discrimination, deepfakes and government use of AI, and the National Conference of State Legislatures reported more than 1,000 AI bills introduced in 2025 by August of that year. The White House's March 2026 legislative framework recommends federal preemption of state laws considered unduly burdensome, while favoring existing regulators and industry-led standards over a new AI rulemaking body. The article stresses that these are recommendations rather than evidence that Congress has enacted a national framework. It proposes matching oversight to potential harm, establishing a national baseline for higher-risk systems anchored in the National Institute of Standards and Technology's voluntary AI Risk Management Framework, and requiring independent audits, incident reporting and federal purchasing standards. The author concludes that public accountability cannot depend entirely on corporate willingness.

Articles.Title: Why AI Self-Regulation May Not Be Enough

stories.Headline: Charlotte Extends Data Center Moratorium Until 2027: What It Means for Residents, Electricity Costs and AI - Creative Loafing Charlotte
stories.Summary:
On October 26, Charlotte City Council voted unanimously to extend its temporary moratorium on new data center development until October 18, 2027. The pause was first approved in June and covers new applications for telecommunications and data storage facilities in the city and its extraterritorial jurisdiction. Projects approved before the initial restrictions took effect are not automatically shut down. The vote came as the city weighs how such facilities should fit into its future.

The extension gives city officials more time to study electricity demand, water consumption, noise, land use and neighborhood compatibility. Large facilities can require substantial electrical capacity, cooling systems and backup generators, and the articles say the central question is who pays for the infrastructure needed to serve them. Water use depends largely on cooling technology, so the articles suggest that project-specific disclosures would help the city judge expected consumption. Local reporting also cited about 5.5 million square feet of hyperscale development in the pipeline, which raised concern that new rules may not reach every previously approved facility.

Councilmember Renee Johnson raised the issue of that hyperscale pipeline, according to WCCB. City officials, including the task force, are examining the effects on residents and infrastructure while state law may limit how far local zoning can change. The articles note that Charlotte's Unified Development Ordinance has permitted data centers in several employment, commercial and industrial districts. Officials have also pointed to the difference between temporary construction jobs and permanent employment, along with the tax revenue such facilities can generate.

The extension runs until October 18, 2027, unless the city ends it earlier by adopting an acceptable regulatory framework. In the meantime, the articles list open questions, including whether facilities will face setbacks from homes and how economic benefits will be measured. They also ask whether hyperscale campuses will be regulated differently and what protections can apply to projects already approved. The outcome could shape how North Carolina handles the infrastructure demands of artificial intelligence.

Articles.Title: Charlotte Extends Data Center Moratorium Until 2027: What It Means for Residents, Electricity Costs and AI - Creative Loafing Charlotte

stories.Headline: NYS court system tells attorneys they can use AI in legal filings without disclosing it but have ‘obligation’ to confirm accuracy - amNewYork
stories.Summary:
The New York State court system has issued new guidance on artificial intelligence telling attorneys they may use generative AI in legal filings without telling a judge they did so. The guidance was released on Monday, October 27, 2026, and was developed by the court system's artificial intelligence advisory committee. It comes with a condition, however, because lawyers remain responsible for checking everything the technology produces. Attorneys are expected to understand the tool's limits and to confirm that nothing it generates is made up or inaccurate.

The guidance states that lawyers face the same legal duty to certify that their papers contain no fabricated material, whether they wrote the arguments themselves or used AI. Attorneys must review AI output and independently verify citations by searching for, reading, and analyzing each one. The committee warned that these tools produce plausible-sounding text rather than verified information, and that a model may invent a case, law, or citation. Filings containing such hallucinations have already drawn sanctions from judges across the state and country, including in the Southern District of New York. The committee also cautioned that AI tools can only draw on their training data, so they may miss recent legal developments, and that their output may reflect cultural, economic, and social biases.

New York Law School Associate Dean Heidi Brown called it concerning that the guidance does not require disclosure to judges. Brown said the guidance was a good step but may not prevent inaccuracies or misreadings of legal precedent from reaching courts. She warned that AI tools are now so built into legal research platforms that newer lawyers may not realize AI produced some of their text. She also raised the problem of misgroundings, where an AI tool cites a real case but describes it inaccurately, and said checking every proposition takes considerable time. Brown added that if overworked judges rely on flawed briefs, that diluted legal writing could end up in judicial opinions.

The guidance is the default policy for attorneys appearing before courts that have no specific AI rules of their own, and any standing rule a judge adopts takes precedence. New York State Chief Administrative Judge Joseph Zayas, who appointed the committee in 2024, said the state chose neither to ban AI nor to mandate disclosure. Instead, Zayas said, attorneys must inform themselves about what generative AI can and cannot do and use it responsibly. He described the approach as a clear, common-sense way to use AI while keeping attorneys fully accountable for the accuracy of their court papers. The guidance builds on an approach the court system adopted earlier this year requiring attorneys who use generative AI to understand its capabilities and limits.

Articles.Title: NYS court system tells attorneys they can use AI in legal filings without disclosing it but have ‘obligation’ to confirm accuracy - amNewYork

stories.Headline: Del. idea for AI-run companies draws eye of powerful congressional committee
stories.Summary:
Rep. James Comer, a Kentucky Republican who chairs the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, has asked Delaware's governor for documents about a proposed plan to create a new legal entity for companies run by artificial intelligence agents. The letter, which concerns Delaware's Artificial Intelligence Company initiative, suggests Congress may be looking at limits on state AI rules. Comer wrote that he worried the proposal could protect powerful AI firms and their investors from responsibility for harmful actions. Gov. Matt Meyer's office said it is reviewing the letter. The initiative was announced in July by Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez and John Nay, founder and CEO of Norm AI, in Fortune magazine.

A draft by John Mark Zeberkiewicz, a lawyer at Richards, Layton & Finger, would let an AI agent act as a company with legal personhood, able to own assets, file lawsuits and serve as a liability shield. A single member, either a person or an entity, would have to keep the company adequately capitalized and would be shielded from its debts unless it failed in that duty or used the company to break the law or commit fraud. The company must keep a log of its activities and may pursue any lawful purpose except banking. If the bill passes, organizations would have 30 months to apply to a regulatory sandbox for AI-run companies, and the bill would create a sandbox committee and an administrator. State lawmakers are expected to take up the idea next year.

Comer's letter cites a WHYY News article from September that noted Patibanda-Sanchez declined to answer questions about the relationship between Norm AI and the Meyer administration. Comer said Delaware officials praise transparency in AI decision-making, yet the public-private partnership lacks it, and he also raised concern about regulatory capture by hidden interests. The Richards Layton & Finger firm said attorneys have long helped shape the state's corporate statutes and that lawmakers weigh that input. Nay did not respond to a request for comment, and a spokesperson for Patibanda-Sanchez referred questions to Meyer's office.

The debate has drawn both criticism and support. Corporate law professors have questioned who would be accountable if an AI-run company caused harm, and one University of Pennsylvania professor called the idea a solution in search of a problem. Lawrence Cunningham of the University of Delaware's John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance argued that Delaware, a leading home for business formation, would be irresponsible to ignore the idea. The committee wants documents and communications dating back to January 1, 2025, including internal AI chat logs, and Delaware's response is due November 9.

Articles.Title: Del. idea for AI-run companies draws eye of powerful congressional committee - WHYY

stories.Headline: Pedagogy or Pushed Public Service? AI Bans in Public Schools Affect More Than Just Children
stories.Summary:
An opinion column published on October 27, 2026, by The Montclarion, the student newspaper of Montclair State University in New Jersey, examines a one-year ban on artificial intelligence in New York's K-12 public schools. The authors, Mariam Kamladze and Tíago Estrada, describe the New York measure as the first policy of its kind in the United States, enacted under New York City Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani. The article notes that the moratorium is meant to prioritize AI literacy and critical thinking, includes two biannual AI literacy courses for students, and permits AI use only when a student gives a reason and receives a teacher's approval. It also names two supplements in the policy, one called Quill for close readings in English and another called Playlab that emphasizes identifying AI-written work.

The column frames the New York policy around a question for New Jersey residents and future educators: what would happen if the same ban applied to New Jersey public schools. The article says there has been no sign of a comparable ban for New Jersey schools or students. It features Kamladze, an English junior at Montclair State enrolled in the university's Teacher Education Program, who said she expects students to use AI in her future classroom and plans to adopt her own guidelines, possibly borrowing from Quill and Playlab. She also said AI should be used as a tool rather than a replacement for one's own thinking, and she questioned whether AI tools could manage a classroom or be trusted in fields like cybersecurity. The authors also cite research by Dr. Jinxia He, an associate professor who studies AI in education, which found that trust in AI predicts students' reliance on it while negatively predicting AI literacy.

The column argues that the larger problem in education is underfunding rather than AI itself. Kamladze described a Newark middle school, where she shadowed, that lacked enough computers for every student and was barely getting by with paper materials. The authors warn that adopting AI as a fast fix for long-standing problems could worsen those problems or create new ones. Kamladze concluded that the New York ban helps put kids first, and the column closes by arguing that such regulation would ultimately mean putting humans first. The article does not report any pending New Jersey policy, and it does not describe the New York moratorium's end date beyond its one-year length.

Articles.Title: Pedagogy or Pushed Public Service? AI Bans in Public Schools Affect More Than Just Children - The Montclarion

stories.Headline: Inside Chongqing’s AI “Testing Ground”: Factories, Hospitals and Hot Pot Restaurants
stories.Summary:
Chongqing is using its industrial base and urban systems as a proving ground for artificial intelligence, moving AI from the lab into factories, hospitals, fire rescue and restaurant kitchens. The city's approach, as described in the articles, focuses on putting frontier technologies such as digital twins and large models into real production and daily city operations rather than only chasing computing power and algorithms. Changan Automobile, for example, has pursued full-stack self-development, and its in-house Tianshu large AI model received filing approval from the Cyberspace Administration of China for generative AI services in June. The model was built to work with automakers' electronic architectures and intelligent driving systems, allowing closed-loop management of data such as road driving and user interaction. Officials and companies present this as filling a gap in the city's automotive chain as it moves toward higher-value software work.

Several other applications are described across the city. The Shanghai-Chongqing AI Research Institute developed the "Zhaoyan" large language model, which ranks third globally on a Chinese large model intelligent agent evaluation benchmark, and CISDI Information's "Jinjing" visual model has been deployed in 51 large and medium-sized steel enterprises. In health care, the Chongqing Jinfeng Laboratory's AI-assisted pathological diagnosis receives data from primary hospitals in real time and helps pathologists assess molecular characteristics, prognosis and treatment options. In April the laboratory released China's first standardized brain tumor pathology dataset certified by the National Institutes for Food and Drug Control, and it has partnered with 49 medical institutions in 21 provinces. Li Sen, project director of its Smart Pathology Center, is quoted describing that cross-provincial collection network.

Public-facing tools include the "Lingji Zhicheng" model, which recommends escape and rescue routes for high-rise fires, and a "transparent kitchen" AI system in hot pot restaurants that identifies 13 common kitchen violations. Chongqing also released "Xiangyouyou," described as China's first full-scenario AI platform for rural leisure tourism. The Chongqing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence is developing the "Mingjing" intelligent agent platform, whose core capabilities are expected to be officially launched by the end of this year. Feng Ning, the institute's assistant dean, is quoted saying that general AI's biggest feature is strong autonomy. The platform is intended to draw on natural environment, infrastructure and social data, including tens of millions of anonymized population records, to simulate urban operations and inform decisions on public resources and services.

Chongqing says it has built a three-tier innovation system that includes research institutes, AI-focused future laboratories and enterprise-developed large models. The city reports 53 high-level science and technology innovation platforms, 47 new research and development institutions and four AI industrial innovation complexes. Taken together, the articles present these efforts as a way to drive continued advances in AI and to develop an AI economy spanning low-altitude logistics, embodied robotics and new-generation AI devices. The articles present these developments as ongoing, with the Mingjing platform's launch later this year the next concrete milestone.

Articles.Title: Inside Chongqing’s AI “Testing Ground”: Factories, Hospitals and Hot Pot Restaurants - iChongqing

stories.Headline: Oakley planners approve A.I. data center ban
stories.Summary:
On October 20, the Oakley Planning Commission voted 4-0 with one abstention to recommend that the City Council approve a total ban on data centers. Commissioner Adam Sterud abstained, and the commission also approved several other projects at the same busy meeting. The City Council will make the final decision at a later meeting. The ban would cover both artificial intelligence and non-AI data centers, though small auxiliary server rooms used by businesses would be exempt. Community Development Director Ken Strelo said data centers have grown rapidly amid rising public opposition, and Oakley wanted to act quickly while state and federal rules were still being written.

The City Council passed a 45-day moratorium on April 14 and extended it to one year on May 12. Joint City Council and Planning Commission work sessions were held on July 21 and September 15 to guide staff on drafting the ban ordinance for all zoning districts. Many residents spoke against data centers, though one resident, Jason Lester, argued a ban would cost jobs and let China dominate the field. Lester asked for only a temporary ban, but Commissioner Sean Ireland said a moratorium could last no longer than one year and that a future council could repeal the ban if needed. Also at the meeting, the commission approved the Peixoto Ranch subdivision at 5321 Sellers Avenue, which will divide a 20.1-acre lot into 110 lots along with a stormwater basin, a central park, and a landscaping corridor.

The developer, Meritage Homes, will connect it by road to its Machado subdivision. The commission also approved a General Plan amendment and rezone of 5801 Bridgehead Road to light industrial, which is part of the 164-acre Bridgehead Industrial Project approved by the council in March. An A.I. data center had been a possible use for that space but was withdrawn before approval. The commission gave a design review and conditional use permit 5-0 for a Panda Express and Quick Quack car wash at the southeast corner of Main Street and Neroly Road, one of Oakley's primary gateways. Associate Planner Evan Gorman said the applicant redesigned the project several times at staff's request, adding a stone wall between it and the nearby mobile home park.

Panda Express will operate from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. and Quick Quack from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m., and the operators must control litter and graffiti. The city-owned parcel was once a PG&E maintenance station, and if developed, its sale proceeds would go toward the city's outstanding bond debt and to organizations such as school districts.

Articles.Title: Oakley planners approve A.I. data center ban - thepress.net

stories.Headline: Reed Union schools to develop age-based framework for screens, AI
stories.Summary:
The Reed Union School District board used its first look at a districtwide technology plan to ask whether students from preschool through eighth grade spend too much time on screens. The discussion came four months after the board approved the district's first artificial intelligence policy. Jonathan Weller, the district's director of information systems, educational technology and innovation, told the board on Oct. 13 that a framework setting age-appropriate limits on devices and AI will return to the board in February. Board members raised their concerns during an update on curriculum pilots. They questioned how much learning should rely on technology in the classroom.

Board member Mike Ghaffary said classrooms should use real textbooks and paper and pencil whenever possible. He said the whole world had overrelied on technology. Ghaffary argued it would be hypocritical for parents, teachers and the board to warn students about device addiction outside school while requiring devices in class and for homework at night. His remarks gave the screen discussion its sharpest edge. The article does not record any formal vote on the framework at that meeting.

The Ark reported the story in its Oct. 27 coverage, and the article is written as a single report of the board discussion. The district's plan, as described, will be presented in February and will set limits by age on devices and AI use. The article does not say what those limits will be, how they will be enforced, or whether they will apply to every grade level in the same way. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Reed Union schools to develop age-based framework for screens, AI - The Ark newspaper

stories.Headline: Intuit Unveils Custom Financial AI Tools for Nonprofits and Manufacturers
stories.Summary:
Intuit announced new and expanded financial intelligence tools for the nonprofit, manufacturing and construction sectors on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, according to a press release the company issued. The new capabilities were added to Intuit Enterprise Suite and QuickBooks Online Advanced. For nonprofits, the update builds fund and grant accounting directly into the platform instead of requiring spreadsheets. For manufacturers, it adds workflows for multi-location inventory and production, including pick-pack-ship and multi-level bills of material, while construction businesses receive deeper industry-specific capabilities.

Intuit described the tools as powered by its Intuit Intelligence platform, which combines AI, machine learning, deterministic code, human expertise and permissioned financial data. The announcement came at the company's Intuit Connect event, where Intuit also introduced several other products. These included Agentic Books Close, which automates more of the monthly close process for accountants, along with Firm Playbooks and portfolio intelligence tools. The company also said a ProPartner program would launch in 2027 to offer training, certifications, rewards and client connections.

Intuit Chairman and CEO Sasan Goodarzi was quoted in the release saying the tools let businesses and accountants manage greater complexity and scale with confidence. He said the company is harnessing AI so that businesses can keep pace with what he called the largest technology disruption in the company's history. In an August earnings call, Goodarzi said 75% of Intuit Enterprise Suite users were using the company's AI agents every month. Intuit first introduced Intuit Intelligence in October 2025, describing it as a system that would unify business data and provide a team of AI agents across financial tasks.

Articles.Title: Intuit Unveils Custom Financial AI Tools for Nonprofits and Manufacturers

stories.Headline: AI, Big Tech Regulation Emerges as Selling Point in AG Campaigns
stories.Summary:
Across the United States, roughly $200 million is being spent on state races for attorney general, and in about half of those contests incumbents or challengers are running ads about taking on technology companies. According to a Bloomberg Law analysis of ads and spending compiled by AdImpact, candidates from Nevada to Georgia and Florida to Michigan are using their stance on AI and social media firms as a campaign message. Lawyers quoted in the reporting say the office has grown from handling consumer scams into a role confronting the largest technology companies. The article reports that eight current attorneys general are running for higher office and that a dozen current governors once held the same post.

The central example is a settlement of roughly $18 billion that Meta reached in August with 48 states, which resolved allegations that Facebook and Instagram were designed to addict children. Several candidates in both parties now cite it in their ads, including Connecticut's William Tong and Idaho's Raul Labrador, and nine other incumbents are running similar messages. The article also says that Florida's James Uthmeier is campaigning against OpenAI after a 2025 shooting at Florida State University in which the suspect allegedly used ChatGPT to plan the attack. Florida has asked a court to act as a clearinghouse for frontier AI models, and a bipartisan group of attorneys general has sued to block OpenAI from using recursive self-improvement techniques. Lawyers cited in the article say states have stepped into this gap because Congress has taken little action and President Donald Trump has shown little interest in regulating these companies, and state lawmakers enacted more than 500 AI bills in the last two years.

Party leaders are also investing in these races, with the Republican Attorneys General Association pledging $7 million for 13 states and the Democratic Attorneys General Association pledging $5 million for Florida and $2 million for Georgia. Louis Jacobson of Sabato's Crystal Ball describes the anti-tech message as a way to appeal to voters worried about costs, and he says about 10 states look like toss-ups. Other races are dominated by different issues, such as immigration in Minnesota and culture war themes in Texas, and in Michigan and Nevada candidates are also campaigning on energy costs and data centers. Lawyers at several firms expect state attorneys general to bring more privacy, consumer protection and antitrust cases against technology companies in 2027. Lauren M. Weinstein of O'Melveny & Myers predicts that state antitrust litigation may rival federal enforcement within a few years, citing new state merger review rules and an exodus of talent from federal agencies.

Articles.Title: AI, Big Tech Regulation Emerges as Selling Point in AG Campaigns - Bloomberg Law News
