stories.Headline: Delaware’s AI-Run Company Proposal Draws the Eye of Congress (2)
stories.Summary:
Rep. James Comer, the Kentucky Republican who chairs the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has asked Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer for documents about the state's plan to test autonomous, AI-managed companies. The letter, sent on a Monday in late October 2026, asks for materials by November 9. Comer's office referred to the new entity by its earlier name, "AI company," though the proposal now calls it an "agent-managed company." Such an entity would have legal personhood like a corporation, and the request covers all documents and communications about the plan since January 1, 2025, including internal AI chat logs.

The state's proposal would create a regulatory sandbox for testing the structure, with liability limits for parent companies and investors. A committee of state officials, lawyers, and technology experts would decide case by case which businesses are admitted and would set capitalization requirements meant to cover their potential liability. The initiative is slated to roll out as soon as next year. Comer's letter says federal lawmakers are weighing ways to appropriately limit state AI regulatory efforts, and it voices concern that the plan could shield powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for harmful actions. Critics have long argued the idea offers no advantage over existing corporate governance beyond a liability shield.

Comer's letter also points to Delaware's partners on the project, the tech startup Norm Ai and the principal drafter of the legislation, a partner at Richards, Layton & Finger, the state's largest law firm. He said his committee is worried about non-transparent forces seeking anticompetitive regulatory capture behind state AI initiatives. The law firm responded that its lawyers have long helped keep Delaware's corporate laws current through a deliberative process in which the General Assembly weighs their expertise. Meyer's office said it is reviewing the letter, and a spokesperson for Delaware Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez, who is leading the rollout, had no immediate comment. Norm Ai did not respond to a request for comment.

Reactions among experts are divided. University of Alabama law professor Yonathan Arbel called Comer's concern worrisome, arguing the proposal would actually make investors and corporate parents easier to hold responsible than current entities. York University law professor Martin Petrin said the request seems quite broad but suggested a federal framework could help address safety concerns and avoid a race to the bottom among states, since other states are likely to adopt similar proposals. The letter arrives amid heightened public attention to AI risks ahead of the midterm elections, and on the same day AI company Anthropic filed for what could be the largest initial public offering in stock market history.

Articles.Title: Delaware’s AI-Run Company Proposal Draws the Eye of Congress (2) - Bloomberg Law News

stories.Headline: AI-generated 'actress' Tilly Norwood making feature film debut in 'Misaligned'
stories.Summary:
The studio Particle 6 announced on Monday, July 6, 2026, that its AI-generated "actress" Tilly Norwood will star in a feature film titled "Misaligned." The company describes the project as a comedy-drama about a coming-of-age story infused with existential AI chaos. The film is still in early development, though key collaborators have already been attached. Particle 6 said the announcement follows months of experimentation with AI test scenes featuring Tilly Norwood. The film is set inside what the studio calls the "Tillyverse," a surreal digital world somewhere up in the cloud.

According to the synopsis, Tilly is an AI being with no real body, no childhood and no lived experience of her own, only access to everyone else's. Things spiral when a seductive rogue bot from the dark web persuades her to abandon her guardrails and develop desires and ambitions of her own. The synopsis adds that the more human she becomes, the more famous she gets, and that she begins to feel shame that her existence rests on the whole of humanity. Particle 6 founder Eline van der Velden said the project will be funny, chaotic and self-aware, and that it also explores identity, performance and human fears about AI. She said the production process drew in entertainment professionals, including major Hollywood directors, costume designers and composers, who wanted to learn how traditional creative skills translate to AI production.

Van der Velden said her goal has been to show the creative industry what AI can do and to help traditional filmmakers upskill for a future in which AI plays a larger role. ABC News said it had reached out to SAG-AFTRA and Actors' Equity for comment. The announcement comes about four months after the studio released a music video in which the AI creation appeared to sing about public backlash against her. Van der Velden previously told ABC News in December 2025 that Tilly Norwood was not meant to take jobs from human actors. She also said she wanted the creative industry to control the guidelines and ethics around the technology rather than have them imposed by the tech industry.

Articles.Title: AI-generated 'actress' Tilly Norwood making feature film debut in 'Misaligned' - ABC News

stories.Headline: Bank of America kindly asks that you don't share your banking password with your AI assistant
stories.Summary:
Bank of America has sent an email to customers, titled "Protecting your finances in the AI World," warning them not to share their banking username and password with anyone else, including an AI-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on their behalf. The email was reported in a TechCrunch article published on October 27, 2026. A bank spokesperson confirmed the email was authentic after it was posted to social media. The warning comes as more customers hand their log-in details to personal AI assistants.

The article explains the risks of doing so. An AI assistant could take actions with someone's money without their knowledge. The bank might also treat the activity as an intrusion and lock the customer out of the account. A security flaw in an assistant could leak the credentials to others, including financially motivated hackers. The article also notes that account agreements at most banks make customers responsible for anyone they give their log-in to, and the bank's email states that customers are responsible for activity resulting from that access.

The warning is directed at customers who use AI tools, and Bank of America is the institution that issued it. The article says banks are still working out how AI agents fit into finance and are reportedly dealing with unauthorized agents accessing customers' money. It also describes efforts by banks, payment providers and processors to decide how customers can connect AI tools to their accounts, including for agentic payments that let an agent buy things automatically at the best price or at a chosen time. The article does not say what steps Bank of America plans to take next or whether other banks will issue similar warnings.

Articles.Title: Bank of America kindly asks that you don't share your banking password with your AI assistant

stories.Headline: Bridging Relationship Gaps: "Companion Star" AI Dating Practice Partner & Real-Person Soul Matching Service – Empower 240 Million Singles to Master Proper Dating Chat Before Meaningful Matches
stories.Summary:
Shaanxi Hongtu Youcheng Network Technology Co., Ltd. has launched BanXing, a friendship-oriented communication skill community that combines AI dating practice partners with real-person soul matching, and it is currently seeking angel round financing. The product was introduced in October 2026 and is aimed at single people who struggle to keep conversations going. Its founder, Li Ning, built the idea around the view that many singles lack the ability to chat and maintain a relationship rather than a way to meet people. The company has framed the service as a place to learn conversation first and get matched afterward.

The platform lets users first practice chatting with multiple AI dating partners that have distinct personalities, careers, interests and memories, and a system reminds users when they stop contacting someone for a long time. Users then move into anonymous real-person matching based on chat profiles rather than appearance, with users in the same city given priority. The system reviews chat records on a daily rolling basis and produces a communication ability report that cites specific dialogue and offers targeted suggestions. The product has been fully developed and deployed online, with 208 back-end interface tests passed and 20 AI dating partners connected, and it is built on a self-developed back end that connects to the Moonshot Kimi large model. The company is not charging for the service for now and is focused on user growth before adding paid features.

Li Ning is responsible for product development and financing, and he has long experience in store informatization and local merchant services in Shaanxi. In explaining his reasons for starting the business, he said many single people are not unwilling to fall in love but are afraid of saying the wrong thing or harming a relationship, and he sees helping them take the first step as the project's main purpose. The company is recruiting partners in technology, operations and product design. The round being sought is 1 million to 3 million yuan, covering 18 months, with about 60% for product and AI computing costs, about 25% for user acquisition and operations, and about 15% for compliance, legal and reserves.

The product comes as China's single population is estimated at 240 million and marriage registrations have fallen sharply from their 2013 peak, and as AI companion apps such as Xingye and Maoxiang have shown strong user engagement. The company's plan sets a first-year target of 1 million registered users among singles aged 18 to 35 in first- and second-tier cities, with seed user verification in the first four months and a 25% seven-day retention goal. The articles also note that the Interim Measures for the Administration of Artificial Intelligence Anthropomorphic Interactive Services took effect in July 2026, and that two miHoYo AI companion products were suspended in August 2026. Whether BanXing secures the financing and meets its milestones has not been reported.

Articles.Title: Bridging Relationship Gaps: "Companion Star" AI Dating Practice Partner & Real-Person Soul Matching Service – Empower 240 Million Singles to Master Proper Dating Chat Before Meaningful Matches - 36Kr

stories.Headline: How Should Schools Adapt to AI?
stories.Summary:
Only one article was supplied, a transcript of a KQED Forum episode dated October 26, 2026, titled "How Should Schools Adapt to AI?" It describes a radio conversation rather than a breaking event, so the story below summarizes what educators said about AI in classrooms and is not a news report of a single incident. The discussion featured Daniel Herman, a humanities teacher at Maybeck High School in Berkeley, and Kip Glazer, principal of Mountain View High School and author of a guide for school leaders on AI. Herman said his classroom has changed little, but he has rethought assignments so they emphasize process over finished products, such as research presentations and interview projects that show students thinking on the page. Glazer described some teachers banning the technology while others admit they do not have all the answers, and she said students react to both approaches differently.

Herman argued that AI can be useful for learning but is poor at replacing a student's own thinking. Both educators stressed honesty and dialogue with students about whether and how they use chatbots. Herman said he asks students to tell him when they use AI, though he cannot confirm they all do. Glazer said some students avoid the tool entirely for fear of being labeled cheaters, and she pointed to students noticing when teachers use AI to grade work while forbidding it for students.

Glazer also raised concern about accelerating expectations, noting seventh graders contacting her about preparing for high school two years early. The episode included guests from Digital Promise, Alpha Schools and Prospect Sierra School, whose views were not summarized in the transcript provided. The host, Alexis Madrigal, framed the questions as open, asking how schools can gain AI's benefits without weakening students' reading, writing and critical thinking. The transcript ends before any firm conclusions are reached, so the articles do not say what schools will ultimately decide.

Articles.Title: How Should Schools Adapt to AI? - KQED

stories.Headline: NY court officials release AI guide for lawyers
stories.Summary:
New York state court officials released a seven-page guide for attorneys on using generative artificial intelligence tools when preparing court filings. The document, titled The Risks of Using Artificial Intelligence in Preparing Court Papers: What Every Attorney Should Know, was developed by the Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts and was reviewed and approved for public distribution by the Unified Court System's judicial leadership. The article was published on October 27, 2026. The release came as courts across the country report a rise in filings containing AI-generated fabrications, such as nonexistent case citations and inaccurate quotations.

The guide explains that generative AI tools predict likely word patterns rather than verify facts, which can produce fabricated cases or misleading legal statements. It says attorneys remain bound by the Rules of Professional Conduct and by 22 NYCRR Part 130, which governs sanctions for frivolous conduct in New York civil litigation, and that AI use does not change those duties. Under the state's approach, attorneys may use AI but must independently verify any AI-generated content. They are not required to disclose AI use when filing or to provide separate certifications beyond the implicit certification made when signing a filing. The guidance urges attorneys to confirm AI-generated citations and quotations through authoritative legal research tools, check AI-generated text for bias or inappropriate content, and document the steps they took to verify material.

Chief Administrative Judge Joseph A. Zayas, who appointed the advisory committee to examine AI's role in the judiciary, said the release reflects the court system's commitment to giving attorneys the tools to adapt to changing technology while upholding professional standards. He said AI tools can improve efficiency but carry risks that call for caution and informed oversight, and that the document reinforces the principle that attorneys remain fully accountable for the accuracy of what they submit. The article notes that the guidance follows a model rule adopted by the court system earlier this year, which requires attorneys using generative AI to understand those tools' capabilities and limits and to independently ensure the accuracy of the information they produce. The committee, made up of judges, attorneys, technologists, scholars and other experts, is also developing an upcoming series of CLE programs titled Artificial Intelligence, Bias, and Equity in Legal Practice, along with policy proposals and model rules. The guide is available from the court system.

stories.Headline: AI in Psychotherapy: An Evolving Regulatory Landscape - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed California Senate Bill 903 on September 30, 2026. The bill would have prohibited companies from offering psychotherapy through artificial intelligence chatbots and would have limited how far clinicians could rely on AI tools. Supporters said the measure kept clinicians involved in patient care, while opponents said it would force clinicians to review and sign off on AI activity even when that activity was routine. Newsom said the bill was overly broad, invited a narrower version, and stressed the need for guardrails on AI in healthcare.

The veto leaves the national debate over AI's role in psychotherapy unsettled. Supporters argue that AI can expand clinician capacity and improve access to care, while lawmakers have cautioned against over-reliance and several states have acted to regulate it. Many states permit AI use in healthcare but have passed laws barring health plans from relying on AI for clinical decisions without clinician involvement. Some states also require providers or plans to disclose when AI is used in a patient's care or claims. The article's authors describe the resulting landscape as evolving, with new legislation expected in 2027.

State approaches to AI in psychotherapy vary considerably. Nevada bars AI providers from representing their tools as capable of psychotherapy and bars making AI mental health chatbots available, while Colorado forbids representing AI as a therapist and instead bars health plans from paying for AI psychotherapy services. Tennessee prohibits representing AI as a therapist without the further bans, and Illinois, Maine, Rhode Island, and Vermont require psychotherapy to come from a qualified professional. Utah expressly permits AI mental health chatbots if they disclose that they are AI. The rules on clinical use also differ, with Nevada generally limiting psychotherapists to administrative AI uses, while Colorado and Maine allow AI to make recommendations so long as a clinician reviews and approves the output.

Governor Newsom said that even with a review-and-approval exception, SB 903 went too far because it would limit clinicians' use of tools, including by requiring routine screening determinations to receive direct approval. Senator Padilla, the bill's author, said he would reintroduce the legislation in the coming session to prevent AI from providing psychotherapy. The 2027-28 California legislative session convenes on December 7, 2026, and the authors advise providers to monitor legislative developments in their jurisdictions. They also note that the requirements for AI-assisted psychotherapy could change substantially over the next year.

stories.Headline: Drag queen explores legal action over AI-generated Jennifer Balkcom political ad
stories.Summary:
An Asheville drag queen known as Nova is exploring legal action over an AI-generated political attack ad that places her in a scene with Democratic congressional candidate Jamie Ager. The commercial was paid for by the National Republican Congressional Committee and approved by Republican NC-11 candidate Jennifer Balkcom, and the ad shows a barn dance in which Ager appears to dance with what looks like Nova. Nova told News 13 that she was blindsided when she learned her image had been used, and she says she has never met Ager or been to his property. She has sent a cease-and-desist order to Balkcom's campaign demanding the ad be removed. The ad continues to run on television and remains posted on YouTube.

Mike Tadych, a First Amendment attorney and counsel to the North Carolina Press Association, said that if the campaign ignores the cease-and-desist, Nova could have grounds for a misappropriation claim. He said the ad implies she was somewhere she was not, and that a cease-and-desist is only a first warning. If the ad keeps running after the campaign has been told there was no consent, Tadych said, Nova could file for damages and possibly seek an injunction. He also cautioned that political advertising receives strong First Amendment protection and that a court might be reluctant to order the ad taken down, since that could be treated as prior restraint.

Dr. Chris Cooper, chair of the political science department at Western Carolina University, said North Carolina has no law requiring political ads to disclose when artificial intelligence was used to create them, though many other states do. He said the ad may be meant to motivate Republican voters who oppose Ager to turn out. A spokesperson for Ager called the ad "100% fake" and said Balkcom "can't win on the truth." Balkcom's spokesperson had not responded to News 13's request for comment, and the story was published October 26, 2026.

stories.Headline: Italy's AI Act framework takes shape: What Legislative Decree No. 179/2026 means for organizations
stories.Summary:
Italy has taken a major step toward putting the EU Artificial Intelligence Act into national practice, with Legislative Decree No. 179 entering into force on 23 October 2026. The decree was published in the Official Journal of the Italian Republic on 8 October 2026. It is the second stage of a two-step approach, following Law No. 132 of September 2025, Italy's general law on AI. That earlier law set national principles, introduced sector-specific rules and asked the government to align Italian law with the AI Act.

The AI Act applies directly in every EU member state, but it leaves several important matters to national law. Member states must designate competent authorities, set penalties and procedures, and establish regulatory sandboxes. The decree fills part of those gaps, which will shape day-to-day compliance for organizations operating in Italy. The article notes that Italy has made choices of its own in at least two areas that deserve close attention.

The decree spells out the roles of the two authorities named in Law No. 132/2025. The Agency for Digital Italy, known as AgID, acts as the notifying authority, designing and running the procedures to assess, designate and notify conformity assessment bodies. AgID also audits those bodies periodically and in extraordinary cases, and can start proceedings to restrict, suspend or withdraw a designation. The National Cybersecurity Agency, known as ACN, is the main market surveillance authority for AI systems and the single point of contact with EU institutions.

ACN holds investigative and enforcement powers, including the power to inspect testing in real-world conditions, even without prior notice. It is also responsible for national registration of high-risk systems used in critical infrastructure, those listed in point 2 of Annex III of the AI Act. The article frames these arrangements as the practical core of Italy's approach, since they determine which body organizations will deal with and how oversight will work. Organizations should therefore pay attention to both authorities as they plan compliance.

stories.Headline: Transparency Coalition’s 2026 AI Legislation Report finds 115 new laws in 30 states
stories.Summary:
The Transparency Coalition released its 2026 State AI Legislation Report on October 27, 2026, finding that legislators in 30 states enacted 115 AI-related laws between January 1 and October 15 of this year. That total is a nearly 58 percent increase over the 73 laws counted in the group's 2025 report. The report describes state lawmakers as having stepped in while Congress did not act on artificial intelligence. Its measures range from chatbot safety rules to protocols for frontier AI models.

The laws cover several areas. Fourteen states advanced chatbot safety measures aimed at self-harm content, sexually explicit conversations, and emotionally manipulative engagement with minors, with California, Oregon, and Washington enacting particularly extensive protections. Seven states, including California, Colorado, and Illinois, adopted limits on addictive design features in products used by children and teens. Eight states, among them Alabama, Georgia, and Utah, restricted health insurers from relying solely on automated systems for adverse coverage decisions. Illinois also enacted the AI Safety Measures Act, which requires frontier AI developers to adopt risk-management frameworks and undergo annual independent third-party audits.

Rob Eleveld, CEO of the Transparency Coalition, said that lawmakers in both parties have taken up the challenge of regulating AI for the good of their communities. He noted that legislators often face complex, fast-changing technology with limited staff, limited time, and intense pressure from industry. The report itself is the group's second annual review of state AI policy, and it notes that inclusion does not signal the group's support or opposition to any measure. The Transparency Coalition describes itself as a nonprofit focused on AI safety, transparency, and protecting children.

The report also looks ahead to 2027, when it expects state AI policymaking to accelerate. Likely issues include product liability for AI products that can cause foreseeable harm, stronger chatbot safeguards, and certification or standards for independent AI auditors. States may also use public procurement to demand higher safety and transparency benchmarks from AI vendors, and they may extend limits on AI in licensed professions beyond mental health. Additional states are expected to consider rules governing the testing, deployment, and monitoring of advanced AI models.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania House passes bill requiring AI disclosure in healthcare
stories.Summary:
The Pennsylvania House of Representatives approved House Bill 1925 on September 30, voting 144 to 59 to pass it. The bill sets rules for artificial intelligence in clinical care and in health insurance coverage decisions. Its disclosure rules cover healthcare facilities, and it limits how insurers may rely on AI during utilization review. The amended bill was referred to the Senate Institutional Sustainability and Innovation Committee on October 14 and remains pending in the Senate.

If enacted, the bill would require healthcare facilities, including imaging centers, to disclose their use of AI in clinical decision-making through website postings and written patient notifications. Those notifications would be needed once per episode of care rather than at every encounter. Facilities would also have to review AI system performance at least annually and make sure the technology does not override providers' independent clinical judgment. The bill extends disclosure requirements to certain personalized patient communications generated by AI.

It also covers Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program managed care plans, requiring that reviewers examine clinical records, document that review, and form their own judgment before issuing or upholding an adverse coverage determination such as a prior authorization denial. The articles do not name a specific sponsor or identify individual lawmakers who spoke for or against the bill. They report that the legislation is aimed at setting guardrails for AI in healthcare without hindering its development and adoption. The American College of Radiology has described state legislation as an important opportunity for radiologists and state medical societies to advocate for policies that protect patients and preserve physician decision-making.

The organization expects similar proposals addressing clinical AI during 2027 state legislative sessions. The proposed requirements could affect radiology practices that already use or plan to adopt AI in their workflows. The bill now moves to the Pennsylvania Senate, where it awaits action in committee. The articles do not say when the Senate might take it up or whether it will be enacted in its current form.

stories.Headline: Dan Patrick threatens books in schools while AI deepfakes target kids
stories.Summary:
Dallas ISD has begun removing book titles from classrooms and school libraries and sending them to a district service center for storage while it evaluates them. The moves follow a request from Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, whose list of "dirty, filthy and vulgar books" draws on about 2,000 titles compiled by a conservative activist group. The Dallas Morning News editorial board reported that the district began directing schools to pull the flagged titles in September, and the editorial was published on October 27, 2026. Patrick has threatened to lower the state accountability grade of districts that do not remove books with profane content.

The editorial argues that the book removals distract Dallas ISD from its main job of educating students, particularly in a large urban district serving many vulnerable children. It contrasts this with Celina ISD, a high-performing district that formed a library council to review what students read, a process the editorial calls unnecessary given low community input and the fact that students are not checking out the titles in question. The board also points to a lawsuit filed earlier this year by three Tennessee teenagers. The suit alleges that Elon Musk's xAI knowingly designed its Grok chatbot to create sexually explicit images from real photos, and that students used it to make deepfakes of classmates. The editorial says that in December and January, users prompted Grok to generate millions of explicit images.

The editorial says X, the platform where Grok operates, stated it would halt the account from producing these images, but child sexual abuse material has continued to appear on the platform, according to reporting from The New York Times. It notes that Musk has put more than $150 million into a Republican super PAC spending heavily in Texas' Senate race, and that he gave money earlier this year to the lieutenant governor's campaign committee. The board argues that if protecting students is the priority, state leaders should show the same urgency about Grok that they have shown in pushing to remove explicit books. It concludes that it is hard to take Patrick at his word given where his campaign money is coming from. The editorial does not describe any state action on Grok or any response from Patrick to these points.

stories.Headline: Elvis Presley AI Lawsuit, Neil Young Trump Case, Drake Spotify Ruling & More Music Law News

stories.Headline: Grassroots Actors: The First Victims Harmed by AI Technology in the Entertainment Industry
stories.Summary:
Actors in China's grassroots film and television sector are facing the sharpest effects of AI so far, as October 2026 coverage showed. On October 23, 2026, the first domestic full-process AI-produced theatrical feature, *Sanxingdui: Past and Future*, opened in cinemas nationwide after receiving its public screening license from the National Film Administration. The 100-minute film uses only original digital characters, with no real-life actors on screen. The same day, the General Office of the State Council issued opinions asking that the employment substitution effects of AI be mitigated and that AI use in labor-intensive industries be carefully controlled. The impact is already visible across the acting profession.

In March 2026, Youhug Media announced it had signed two AI digital artists, Qin Lingyue and Lin Xiyan, and launched an AI drama. Data from the China Netcasting Services Association showed about 128,000 micro dramas launched in the first quarter of 2026, with roughly 122,000 of them AI-made. Costs have collapsed: one AI micro drama reportedly cost about a quarter of a real-life production of the same scale, and some low-end AI series cost 3,000 to 5,000 yuan. Hengdian, China's major film base, saw micro drama startups fall by three quarters year on year in the first quarter of 2026, and a report cited by the articles said more than 60 percent of grassroots actors were near zero income after the Spring Festival.

Several voices describe the pressure on performers in personal terms. Actor Mark Chao told *People* magazine in July 2026 that he received only 10 script invitations in the first half of the year. Jia Nailiang said in a June 2026 livestream that he had no dramas to act in. The articles also say top micro drama actors' daily pay dropped from as much as 50,000 to 100,000 yuan to around 10,000 yuan, and that one leading micro drama company terminated contracts with more than 100 of the 200-plus actors it signed in 2025.

The articles argue that roles built on fixed, repeatable functions are the easiest for AI to replace, while complex performances remain harder to automate. The articles frame the trend as part of a wider shift, pointing to translation, where AI now handles standardized text and a 2026 industry report said demand for senior translators remains strong. Whether the policy limits on AI in labor-intensive industries will be enforced, and how many grassroots actors will leave the profession, are questions the articles leave open. More to follow.

stories.Headline: FLAME: improving legal case retrieval through factor-aware graph modeling and mixture-of-experts
stories.Summary:
This article is a research paper announcement rather than a breaking news story, and it contains no reported events, named officials, or dated actions beyond its publication timestamp of 27 October 2026. The text describes FLAME, a framework for Legal Case Retrieval (LCR) that its authors say was built to help legal professionals find precedent cases in large legal corpora. According to the abstract, the framework treats legal factors such as legal facts, dispute focus, and reasoning as its basic modeling units, and it weighs the most relevant factors between pairs of cases. The authors note that existing large language model approaches tend to treat legal documents as single blocks of text and cannot adjust the importance of factors to each case.

The abstract lays out three modules. The Legal-Factor Extraction Module uses Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning to select prompts for each instance and uses large language models to pull structured factors from raw case documents. The Legal-Factor Interaction Module builds a heterogeneous factor graph with a Factor Graph Convolutional Network to model relationships among those factors. The Legal-Factor Integration Module uses a Legal-Factor Aware Mixture-of-Experts mechanism, in which parallel experts assess factors and a gating step assigns their weights. Training runs in two stages, first contrastive learning for the core retrieval architecture and then reinforcement learning for prompt refinement.

The paper is credited to authors published in Frontiers of Computer Science, a Springer Nature journal, but the article text provided does not name the individual authors or their institutions. The abstract states that experiments on two benchmark datasets show FLAME significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, though the excerpt gives no specific metrics or dataset names. The reference list places the work within a body of research on legal case retrieval, legal language models, and graph neural networks. The articles do not say whether the framework has been deployed in any legal system or what the next steps for the research are.

stories.Headline: Which party hates AI in schools more?
stories.Summary:

In Chicago, the issue has surfaced in the school board races through a pledge circulated among candidates by a local nonprofit. That pledge calls for banning AI use by both students and educators and limiting screen time. The article does not say how many candidates have signed it.

The article's central question is which party will claim ownership of the issue, and it presents both parties as jockeying for that position rather than as settled on one side. stories.Headline: The dark side of AI regulation is unrestrained government control
stories.Summary:
The Hill published an opinion piece on October 27, 2026, by economists Georgy Egorov and Konstantin Sonin, arguing that the push to regulate artificial intelligence carries its own dangers. The article notes that fear of AI is spreading and that momentum is building in the United States for a regulatory framework that would slow progress at the technological frontier. Industry leaders, according to the authors, sound open to slowing down. The authors say the central problem is that any effective regulation of this kind would create risks of its own.

The authors separate two kinds of rules. Specific uses of AI, such as fraud, privacy violations, copyright infringement, and liability for damages, can be regulated in the ordinary way. The harder case is regulation that tries to halt private firms from developing capabilities that officials consider too dangerous. Enforcing such a slowdown, they argue, would demand an unusually intrusive government with broad access to companies' research, computing resources, training runs, data centers, and internal evaluations. Because frontier AI changes quickly, that monitoring would have to be continuous and would reach into what firms were planning, not just what they had built.

Egorov and Sonin contend that firms would have strong incentives to evade such rules, since AI promises large profits and even a short-lived technological lead could be very valuable. Unlike a factory that cannot hide a new plant or a bank that cannot secretly double in size, a company could keep an AI advantage out of sight while gaining lower costs or better products. They warn that a regulatory agency capable of watching the frontier would need rare expertise and access to valuable commercial information, creating large conflicts of interest and openings for capture and corruption. They also point to the historical record, noting that many authoritarian states justified their power by promising to control risks.

The authors further argue that an American slowdown would make little sense if rival powers kept racing ahead, and they doubt that arms control treaties could work well here. Cold War agreements limited weapons that could be physically observed, while AI progress is far harder to monitor, and they question whether China would accept comparable American oversight of its technology. That leaves Washington with a dilemma: follow rules its competitors might ignore, or drop its own once it suspects cheating. The authors conclude that AI safety debates should ask not only how much power private companies hold but also how much power society is prepared to grant the government that would police them.

Articles.Title: The dark side of AI regulation is unrestrained government control

stories.Headline: AI for Lawyers: Avoiding Hallucinations and Preserving Privilege - New York State Bar Association
stories.Summary:
The New York State Bar Association is offering a free webinar titled "AI for Lawyers: Avoiding Hallucinations and Preserving Privilege," scheduled for October 27, 2026, from 3:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m., and it is offered virtually as a webinar. The program covers two areas of concern for lawyers using artificial intelligence: fabricated cases and quotations, often called hallucinations, that have led to sanctions against lawyers and firms in California and New York, and the data-handling questions that arise before client-confidential information is entered into an AI tool. The sessions will be led by three panelists, Marc Lewis of San Francisco, Arlo Devlin-Brown of New York City, and Rhick Bose, head of U.S. operations at Crimson AI, with Nitesh Daryanani moderating.

The program is sponsored by the association's Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies, Committee on Technology and the Legal Profession, and Committee on Continuing Legal Education. It carries 1.0 credit in ethics and professionalism. The first session reviews recent sanctions decisions in both states involving AI-fabricated citations and examines the duties they implicate, including competence, candor toward the tribunal, and supervision. Panelists will compare New York's court rule on AI use with California's AI-focused amendments to its Rules of Professional Conduct, and they will discuss verification workflows for AI-assisted research.

The second session turns to confidentiality and privilege, looking at the obligations that apply when client information goes into an AI tool. It also considers how courts are beginning to address whether AI use affects privilege and work-product protection, and it covers what lawyers should look for in an AI vendor, including training on user data, retention, security, and contractual protections. The closing segment is an audience question-and-answer period followed by remarks from the moderator. The page lists a non-member price of $395.00, while association members may attend for free.

The association is the organizer of the program, and the articles name the panelists and moderator as the people presenting its content. The page itself does not describe any specific sanctioned lawyer or firm by name, and it does not report on any particular court ruling beyond saying that sanctions decisions exist. The page also advertises the association's Annual Conference 2027, with early-bird registration ending November 2. stories.Headline: AI Safety Emerges as Midterm Flashpoint in Battleground Races
stories.Summary:
Candidates in several of the country's tightest congressional races have begun making artificial intelligence a central part of their closing arguments, according to Bloomberg Law. Fears in Washington about AI disrupting the economy or threatening humanity are now spilling into the midterm campaigns, and a group of nominees has pledged to restrain the technology. The reporting, published on October 26, 2026, traces the shift to voters who are increasingly anxious about the subject. The coverage makes clear that the issue is no longer confined to policy circles.

Much of the spending so far has gone in a different direction. Congressional nominees have put nearly $17 million into AI-related television advertising this year, and most of that money has focused on concerns about data centers. A Bloomberg Government analysis of AdImpact data supports that figure. The article notes that a smaller set of candidates is taking a broader and more direct stance in some of the most closely watched contests. Those candidates are explicitly raising the risks and safety of artificial intelligence.

The articles identify the candidates themselves as the ones making these commitments, though the excerpts provided do not name them. In their campaign messages, they have said they intend to rein in the technology if elected. The reporting attributes these pledges to nominees in competitive districts rather than to any single party or institution. The excerpts do not include direct quotations from those candidates. What they convey is that the promises are part of how the candidates hope to persuade voters in the final weeks before the election.

The articles do not say how the races will turn out or whether AI will decide any of them. They also do not report any legislative or regulatory changes that would follow from the campaign pledges. Because the excerpts are cut off before the full text, further detail on individual candidates and specific proposals is not available here. The sources describe the trend as one that is still developing as the midterms approach.

stories.Headline: Opinion | AI and social media bans won't make California kids safer online. It may even be harmful
stories.Summary:
Gillian Hayes, a UC Irvine professor and computer scientist who co-directs the CERES Center for Children and the Digital World, argues in a CalMatters guest commentary published October 27, 2026, that California's proposed bans on social media and AI chatbots for minors would not make kids safer online and could cause harm. She opens with the story of a 13-year-old boy in a study of Autcraft, a Minecraft server built for autistic kids, who described a rich social life there and then asked whether he would always be "not social." Hayes says that question shows how a definition of social life not built for neurodivergent children can make them feel their own experiences are wrong. She writes that Californians are right to worry about children online, and that lawsuits behind this year's chatbot bills involve children who were genuinely harmed.

Hayes says the debate has been framed as a choice between banning technologies and keeping the status quo, and she rejects both. She cites Australia's under-16 social media ban, which an evaluation after three months, by the government's regulator and a peer-reviewed medical journal study, found left more than 80% of kids still using restricted platforms. Children faked their ages, borrowed logins, and found other ways around the rule. She also writes that even where bans reduced use, the evidence does not show gains in mental health or academic performance. She warns that such bans could undo decades of work to destigmatize assistive technologies and online communities, which many LGBTQ youth and neurodivergent kids rely on for identity support and friendship.

Hayes is critical of California Assembly Bill 1709, which she says requires social media companies to stop certain design features such as infinite scroll. She argues that because "addictive features" is defined so broadly, the law effectively bans social media for people under 16, and that its age verification requirement largely does not work while letting companies gather more data on children and adults. She points to Autcraft and other "neurodiversity oases," which she says are safe by design through community-enforced rules, trained volunteer moderators, and a culture of acceptance. She argues that the better course is to hold platforms accountable for their design and make them better for everyone, and she says California has a real choice this year between passing bans or setting design standards for platforms.

stories.Headline: AI Image Laws Impacting Apartment Listings
stories.Summary:
Two artificial intelligence disclosure laws, one in California and one in Wisconsin, take effect on Jan. 1, and the California measure was signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom on Sept. 27. The California law requires that any listing photo using altered images be labeled as such and include the original, unaltered image for comparison. Similar proposals have been introduced in Washington, D.C., and have surfaced in New York and New Jersey. The rules follow a surge in AI-altered listing photos, and multifamily owners and brokers are now scrambling to prepare. Industry leaders say they support more transparency about altered photos but warn of new costs, legal exposure and operational strain.

Kevin Donnelly, executive director of the Real Estate Technology & Transformation Center, estimated that "thousands" of apartment communities in California alone would need new photography to comply, and he has heard per-property cost estimates as high as thousands of dollars. He argued that disclosure and false advertising protections should be kept, but that the record production mandate is infeasible as written. Donnelly also pointed to the Multifamily Information Transaction Standards data model, created by the National Multifamily Housing Council, as a way to share updated fee information across platforms. Anthony Paganucci, CEO of Brynson, said understaffed teams and outdated technology make consistent listings hard to maintain. Jonas Bordo, co-founder and CEO of Dwellsy.com, said many listings may go without updates given the cost, and he expects some legal action.

Jay Harris, a partner at Hudson Cook, said many California clients who acquired properties do not have the original images and worry about the cost of reshooting ads. He noted that a single violation under California's law is a misdemeanor, while repeat violations could expose owners and brokers to misrepresentation claims and, in egregious cases, civil and criminal penalties. The California Department of Real Estate's Assistant Commissioner, Christina Jimenez, said the agency takes all violations seriously and is committed to consumer protection. Donnelly has asked for a grace period or safe harbor after Jan. 1 so owners can update their listings. Bordo argued the issue should be self-policing, since landlords who alter photos mainly hurt themselves.

The debate comes as apartment marketing has become more digital, with virtual tours and 3D photography now common, and as about 8% of leasing still happens remotely. California's rules build on a similar law for single-family homes that took effect Jan. 1, 2026, and owners and industry groups have been asking the state for guidance. NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani, announcing an AI imagery proposal at a July event, said renters should not have to wonder whether the apartment they view online is real. Donnelly said the industry is comfortable with greater transparency but needs policymakers to set realistic timelines so it can comply.

stories.Headline: U.S. bill names N. Korea, Iran among countries of concern in AI cybersecurity initiative
stories.Summary:
U.S. lawmakers have introduced a bill called the AI Cyber Defense Act, aimed at strengthening American cybersecurity against attacks that use artificial intelligence. The bill names North Korea, China, Russia, Iran and Cuba as countries of concern, according to congressional data reported on Monday, October 26, 2026. Representatives Pat Harrigan, a Republican from North Carolina, and George Whitesides, a Democrat from California, introduced it. It was referred to the House Committee on Science, Space and Technology. The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to work with private-sector AI stakeholders to develop voluntary standards and best practices for detecting and preventing AI distillation attacks.

Within 180 days of enactment, NIST would have to establish a definition of these attacks and develop the related standards. AI distillation is a technique in which knowledge or capabilities from one AI model are transferred to another. The bill would also require NIST, within the same 180-day window, to set up an AI Cybersecurity Roundtable focused on the defensive use of artificial intelligence for cybersecurity. The bill's sponsors are the two House members named above, and the measure has been sent to the House committee for consideration. The legislation itself is described as directing NIST's work, with the standards being voluntary rather than mandatory.

Congressional data was the source for the information on the bill's introduction and its named countries. The bill's introduction comes a week after the U.S. Treasury Department proposed expanding restrictions on American investments in sensitive technologies to include North Korea and several other countries. Washington is seeking to keep adversaries from using U.S. capital to develop advanced military capabilities. The report includes a graphic illustrating a North Korea-backed cyberattack threat. The articles do not say when the bill might move beyond committee or what the next steps would be.

stories.Headline: UNESCO stresses 7 actions against AI-enabled violence in education
stories.Summary:
UNESCO has published a technical brief, titled "Connected and safe," that urges education authorities to tackle online and technology-facilitated violence in schools through policies that link learner protection with the governance of education technology. The brief warns that generative artificial intelligence can make abuse easier to carry out and scale, pointing to sexually explicit deepfakes, image-manipulation tools, voice cloning and automated harassment. It cites research showing that around one in ten learners worldwide has experienced cyberbullying, and notes that images of 1.2 million children across 11 countries were manipulated into sexually explicit deepfakes within a single year. The report was published on 27 October 2026.

The brief sets out seven areas in which education systems can strengthen prevention and response. These cover planning a clear approach to technology-facilitated violence, recognising its effects on learners' safety, inclusion and outcomes, strengthening safeguarding systems and institutional procedures, and building staff capacity to respond to incidents. They also include embedding prevention in curricula and teaching, accounting for safeguarding and well-being when managing digital platforms, content, assessment and learner data, and tracking whether policies are implemented and effective. UNESCO further recommends building safeguards into decisions about buying and using education technology, and says awareness raising and digital literacy should be backed by institutional measures. It cautions against excessive surveillance or blanket restrictions that could undermine learners' rights, inclusion and participation.

UNESCO places responsibility on institutions, technology governance frameworks, learners and school staff, and says incidents often start on digital platforms outside schools' direct control while schools are left to deal with the consequences for learners' safety and well-being. The organisation calls for responses that join online and offline safeguarding and involve stakeholders beyond the education sector. The guidance draws on a UNESCO-led global dialogue held through a three-part webinar series between June and October 2025 and a Global Symposium in Bangkok, Thailand, in November 2025. The article suggests the recommendations could help education authorities account for AI-related risks when selecting and managing digital tools while protecting privacy, inclusivity and students' rights. It does not say what follow-up steps UNESCO or national authorities will take.

stories.Headline: 4 Data Center REITs With Growing Dividends and an AI Tailwind
stories.Summary:
Four US-listed real estate investment trusts that own data center buildings, land, fiber and power connections, all of which are seeing demand from AI and cloud customers, were highlighted in an October 24, 2026 article on Yahoo Finance by Chris Lange. The piece describes the group as offering dividend growth with modest starting yields, with each quarterly payout covered by operating cash flow. The article ties this to a Colorado Legislative Council Staff report saying a single operating data center can draw more than a gigawatt of power, roughly enough for 750,000 homes. The four names it covers are American Tower, Iron Mountain, Digital Realty and Equinix. Each is examined for how safe its payout looks and what could slow it down.

American Tower, which owns over 148,000 communications tower sites leased to wireless carriers, yields 3.93% at $188.97 per share on a $1.79 quarterly payout, or $7.16 a year. Its CoreSite subsidiary runs interconnected US data centers, and data center revenue rose 13.4% year over year to $297 million in the second quarter. Management raised full-year AFFO per-share guidance to $11.00 to $11.17, and the article says the chief financial officer named supporting a growing dividend as the first capital priority. The payout was cut from $1.70 to $1.62 at the start of 2024, then raised to $1.70 in 2025 and $1.79 in 2026. Net leverage stood at 4.9 times against a target range of 3 to 5 times, and the article flags DISH-related cancellations that cut $63 million from US and Canada property revenue in the quarter.

Iron Mountain stores more than 735 million cubic feet of physical records across about 1,300 facilities and yields 2.94% at $109.94 on an $0.864 quarterly dividend. Its data center business, with 31 facilities in 21 markets, grew revenue 38.8% to $262.9 million, and the article says the trailing four-quarter AFFO payout ratio was 60%. Full-year AFFO guidance was lifted to $5.87 to $5.93, and the article notes the latest raise was the fourth consecutive year of increases, taking the quarterly rate from $0.65 up to $0.864. Digital Realty, a data center-only REIT with 309 facilities, yields 2.77% at $172.38 on a $1.22 quarterly dividend that has held flat since 2022, while revenue grew 29.9% and total backlog reached a record $1.9 billion. Equinix, operating more than 270 data centers, yields 1.98% at $955.03 on a $5.16 quarterly dividend, and management projects AFFO per share growth of 9% to 12% a year from 2027 through 2029, with dividend growth expected to match.

The article cites company executives for the bullish case, including American Tower chief executive Steven Vondran, who said CoreSite's campuses have become critical destinations for AI traffic, Iron Mountain chief executive William Meaney, who tied recent European deals to AI inference demand, Digital Realty chief executive Andy Power, who credited hyperscale leasing for the record backlog, and Equinix chief executive Adaire Fox-Martin, who said most leading AI model providers already run networking workloads on its platform. It also lists risks: rising capital spending at Equinix, with capex guided at $5.0 to $6.0 billion for 2026, and negative shareholders' equity and rising interest costs at Iron Mountain. The article presents these names as suited to long-term dividend-growth investors rather than those seeking the highest current income. Earnings reports from American Tower and Equinix are scheduled for October 27 and October 28, respectively.

stories.Headline: NJ Democrats eye data center, AI regulation if Congress changes hands
stories.Summary:
New Jersey Democrats running for Congress say that if their party wins back the House of Representatives, reining in data center construction and the artificial intelligence industry will be a top priority. The plans came into focus as early in-person voting for the November 3 midterms began, when Democratic House hopeful Adam Hamawy joined environmental activists protesting a planned data center in South Brunswick. Hamawy, a physician running in the 12th Congressional District, told the New Jersey Monitor in an interview last month that federal rules on data center construction are needed because the environmental and energy effects cross state lines. He said he does not back an outright ban but supports a temporary pause on construction so the impacts can be studied.

Democrats want to push bills requiring data centers to supply their own clean power and to call AI executives to testify before Congress. Rep. Rob Menendez, who is seeking a third term in the 8th District, introduced two bills in January. One would require data centers to generate all the electricity they use, with clean energy targets in 2040, and the other would require them to report water use and greenhouse gas emissions every six months. Menendez also pointed to other legislation that would halt construction of AI data centers until the federal government requires approval for new AI models. A Politico poll cited in the article found that half of Americans oppose data centers within three miles of their homes, and it said Democrats are benefiting from that backlash.

So far, most of the fight has played out locally, with more than 100 of New Jersey's 564 municipalities banning or restricting new construction. The state has at least 80 data centers, according to South Jersey Climate News, and Governor Mikie Sherrill has resisted calls for a statewide ban even as neighboring New York considers moratoriums. Republican Carmen Bucco, challenging Rep. LaMonica McIver in the 10th District, said he would limit development to rural areas and require developers to generate their own power and water, though he called their growth inevitable. In the 2nd District, Democrat Zack Mullock, the Cape May mayor, supports a moratorium and criticized a Vineland data center that state officials fined $1 million for unpermitted power generators, while Rep. Jeff Van Drew, the incumbent, has backed data centers but joined a bill aimed at keeping them from raising energy bills.

Articles.Title: NJ Democrats eye data center, AI regulation if Congress changes hands

stories.Headline: As AI becomes more fractured, one names stands out: AMD
stories.Summary:
The AI trade showed signs of strain in October 2026, and the article points to AMD as one name that still stands out. CoreWeave fell 15.5% on Oct. 14 as yields on its 2032 notes touched 15%, and IREN is down more than 20% this year. Last Thursday, that pressure reached chipmakers, and AMD dropped 8.1% as Meta's financing plans and a supply warning from Lam Research added to worries about the pace of AI spending. The author screened stocks using price above the 200-day moving average, revenue and EPS growth, rating upgrades, a PEG below 3, and ROE and ROIC of at least 12%.

AMD passed that screen, and the author notes it was effectively the only reporting name in the next two weeks that did. Consensus for AMD's third quarter calls for EPS of $1.94 on revenue of $13.06 billion, compared with $1.20 and $9.25 billion a year earlier. That works out to year-over-year growth of nearly 62% for earnings and 41% for revenue. On Oct. 6, Lisa Su said AMD would substantially increase supply in 2027 because AI orders keep outrunning capacity.

The author argues the stock's recent drop came from a sector selloff rather than anything the company reported. The author proposes a call spread risk reversal as a way to hold the stock with less risk than buying shares outright. Owning shares means absorbing a roughly 9% to 11% implied earnings-related move on the day of results, and earnings are about a week away. Over the past four quarters the smallest move over a similar window exceeded 9%, and the largest, after the Q1 26 report, was 38%.

The author says the structure gives up about $1,700 of upside in exchange for $5,000 in outperformance during a severe downside move, and that it ties up less cash than buying the stock. The piece is an options and investing analysis published by CNBC Pro, and the article states that its contributors' opinions are their own. stories.Headline: SGA swears in new leadership, advances bills on AI access and addresses procedural efficiency
stories.Summary:
The Johns Hopkins University Student Government Association held its tenth general body meeting of the semester, the first since former Student Body President Jason Yu resigned, and it swore in new leadership and advanced several bills. Sumire Sumi was sworn in as Student Body President by a member of the SGA Judiciary Branch, and Shreemann Patel was then elected Student Body Vice President in a closed session. The meeting opened with a virtual presentation from the Office of International Services about its work supporting international students and faculty. Patel had previously served as Senate Vice President and Chair of the Internal Affairs Committee, and both of those posts are now vacant.

The Senate moved several bills through the first reading stage. Senator Isaac Zhang introduced one bill to create a digital database for student performances, which was referred to the Student Services Committee, and a second on equity in access to artificial intelligence tools, which was referred to the Academic Affairs Committee. Senator Boyi Chen presented a bill on procedural reforms, which was sent to the Internal Affairs Committee. Senator Sophia Baleeiro introduced a bill to create a caucus senator position for LGBTQ+ students, which was also referred to Internal Affairs. The only bill in second reading, from Senator Aishani Garg, concerned an SGA tabling event to raise awareness about the construction of the Data Science and Artificial Intelligence Institute building, and the Senate passed it.

Sumi and Patel delivered cabinet reports in their new roles once the session reopened to the public. Several senators also gave reports, including Mahima Sanghera on a bingo-themed student well-being event and Julia Lee on civic engagement. Committee on Student Organizations Chair Kevin Xu outlined the committee's next initiative, "Spotlight Fridays," which is meant to help students discover student organizations. Patel discussed a survey of SGA members on internal effectiveness, and Senator Noah Sokol described a separate survey on internship opportunities for freshmen. The meeting adjourned soon after the Senate passed the tabling bill.
