stories.Headline: Long Beach Unified Surveys Families on AI as Parents Push for a Moratorium
stories.Summary:
Long Beach Unified School District has opened a survey asking students and families what they think about artificial intelligence and computer screens in classrooms. The survey opened earlier in October and probes how families feel about the effects of classroom technology on learning, well-being, privacy and attention. It closes on November 6. The move comes as parents and students have spent months pressing the district to rein in classroom technology.

The district may develop new technology policies in response to that public pressure, according to Long Beach Post. Groups pushing for limits argue that heavy technology use harms learning and development while draining the budget. The district says it spent $2.5 million on laptops during the 2025-26 school year and projects another $2.5 million for the current year. A district workgroup will review the survey results once the survey closes. The workgroup will include teachers, students, guardians, administrators and industry experts.

Long Beach parents helped start a local chapter of Schools Beyond Screens, a national group that advocates limiting screen use in classrooms. Kim Tashkin, who helps lead that chapter, said she hopes the district passes an AI moratorium as soon as possible. The district adopted a policy in 2025 to curtail phones and personal devices, but some parents say it did not go far enough. At an October 7 board meeting, students told members that unchecked AI use could leave them unable to think independently.

Student surveys and national research point to widespread AI use. A student campaign survey found that 91% of respondents had used, or seen someone use, AI to cheat on assignments, and 85% had seen or heard about teachers using AI in class. A 2025 RAND study found that 54% of students and 53% of teachers reported using AI for school. Long Beach is not alone, since Los Angeles Unified and New York City Public Schools have both passed AI moratoriums. Spokesperson Eric Mitchell said the workgroup's findings may help shape policy recommendations.

Articles.Title: Long Beach Unified Surveys Families on AI as Parents Push for a Moratorium - Hoodline

stories.Headline: The markets are starting to act seriously weird. Blame AI
stories.Summary:
Stocks in the United States have been behaving in unusual ways, and David Goldman, writing in a CNN Business analysis published October 26, 2026, links the strange moves largely to worries about artificial intelligence. On the surface the market looks steady, with stocks near record highs and bonds roughly where they have been for a couple of months, but Goldman says investors are growing nervous beneath that calm. The key signal came on October 22, when the equal-weighted S&P 500 gained 0.5% while the market-value-weighted index fell 1.2%, a divergence that had occurred only twice before since 1995, on April 14, 1999, and March 30, 2000, according to James Reilly of Capital Economics. The same day, the 10-year Treasury yield fell below 5% in its largest single-day drop since March 10, 2023.

Goldman explains that bond yields had been surging for three main reasons: the Iran war and resulting inflation, America's debt, which he puts at $40 trillion with a budget deficit of $2 trillion over the past fiscal year, and heavy AI spending, which runs around $1 trillion a year and is increasingly financed by borrowing. Those pressures have not eased, and the article notes oil prices are at four-year highs and that President Donald Trump has signaled the Iran war may escalate again after the midterms. Even so, investors turned to Treasuries as a safe haven after doubts arose about the AI portion of that picture. The article points to CoreWeave, a debt-funded company renting computing power to AI firms, whose borrowing costs rose to about 15% earlier in October. It also cites a Wall Street Journal report that Anthropic's draft IPO filing showed a loss of nearly $81 billion in the first half of 2026, and says Meta spent $2 billion more cash than it generated in the third quarter, sending its stock down 7% on Thursday.

Goldman writes that these concerns have prompted some traders to question how much value Wall Street places on AI and whether current debt levels are sustainable. Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US, is quoted saying the market shows elevated volatility around something that looks like a bubble. The article notes the Nasdaq has slid about 6% over two weeks, but that similar scares in past earnings seasons were followed by renewed buying of AI stocks. It adds that even if an AI bubble bursts, the broader economy might not follow, because recent sectoral booms and busts have balanced one another in what some economists call a rolling recession. Goldman concludes that it is unclear whether this episode marks the start of something larger or is just another bump in the road.

Articles.Title: The markets are starting to act seriously weird. Blame AI

stories.Headline: Marshall County demands action after nude AI-generated image of daughter
stories.Summary:
A Marshall County mother says two teenage boys used artificial intelligence to create a nude image of her underage daughter, and the school's response has drawn her anger. Ashley Neuschwander said a guidance counselor contacted her on October 2 after the boys used a photo from her daughter's Instagram account to make the image. All the students involved are freshmen at Arab High School. Neuschwander said the two students received five-day suspensions, and that neither she nor her daughter was told when the boys returned to class. She described her daughter as heartbroken and worried that people would believe the image was real.

Neuschwander said the punishment falls short and that the school system needs to show accountability. She told WAFF that five days is not enough and that the response was not about revenge. Her daughter, she said, was concerned about her reputation and did not want people to think she was the kind of student who would do something like that. Neuschwander's comments were reported by WAFF in an article published October 26, 2026.

Marshall County District Attorney Jennifer Bray said she is aware of the incident but cannot comment on it because it involves minors. Bray said that creating, possessing or sharing AI-generated explicit images of minors can carry serious criminal consequences under Alabama law. The Arab City Schools superintendent said the district cannot discuss disciplinary action involving juveniles. The articles do not say whether criminal charges have been filed or whether the school will change its discipline policy.

Articles.Title: Marshall County demands action after nude AI-generated image of daughter

stories.Headline: AI Bot Activity Strains Digital Libraries at Universities
stories.Summary:
AI-driven bot traffic is overwhelming open research repositories, pushing colleges and universities to spend resources sorting different kinds of traffic and protecting access for people who need it. Libraries, archives, museums and research repositories face growing pressure from web traffic automated by artificial intelligence tools, which can slow websites, overload servers and keep resources from reaching their intended audience. The problem was described at the EDUCAUSE Annual Conference earlier this month, where information was shared about a discussion group on AI challenges for digital repositories. Since its start in 2025, that group, run by Fedora and the nonprofit Invest in Open Infrastructure, has drawn 143 participants from 109 institutions.

The strain is measurable at individual campuses. Before AI bots, the University of North Carolina Library system typically handled about 100 simultaneous searches during busy periods such as finals week, but in December 2024 it saw 500 or more at a time, which overwhelmed servers and periodically shut out students, faculty and staff, according to a June 2025 university story. A 2025 survey by the GLAM-E Lab, which studies galleries, libraries, archives and museums, found that 39 of 43 people maintaining online collections had seen traffic rise over the previous year. Experts say the older defenses no longer work well, since robots.txt files that once steered crawlers away from restricted areas are often bypassed by bots that disguise their addresses. As a result, many institutions now spend more time checking IP addresses and blocking bots than maintaining collections and helping researchers.

Program manager Arran Griffith of Fedora, who helps coordinate the discussion group, said staff should not have to watch logs for bot activity as a regular duty. He also warned that inflated traffic can distort the usage statistics administrators rely on to justify funding, making collections appear far more used than they are. Lauren Collister, research engagement manager at Invest in Open Infrastructure, said that repository managers used to read access patterns to judge who was using a collection, but automated requests are now harder to tell apart from human activity. Griffith also said institutions worry that the people who created and catalogued material may not be credited, and that openly collected work could later be sold back in commercial products or licensed content. The articles do not describe any formal rule or policy that these institutions are required to adopt.

Some institutions have responded with commercial web application firewalls, open-source tools that challenge automated requests, rate limiting that caps how many requests a system accepts in a given period, and services that classify incoming traffic. Collister said she values efforts to identify which bots are harvesters or scrapers and to distinguish them from agents working for students or research labs. Griffith cautioned that these approaches are not guaranteed to hold, because bots keep evolving and what works today may fail tomorrow. The articles do not say what further steps the discussion group plans to take.

Articles.Title: AI Bot Activity Strains Digital Libraries at Universities

stories.Headline: IBM Integration Intelligence Hub gives AI the context to act, not just access
stories.Summary:
IBM has published an article describing its new Integration Intelligence Hub, which is designed to give AI coding assistants and agents the enterprise context they need before they act on integration assets. The piece, dated 26 October 2026, argues that letting an AI agent reach a tool is not enough, because the agent also needs to know what integrations already exist, which ones are current and endorsed, what depends on them, who owns them, and what the agent is permitted to change. IBM frames this as the gap between access and understanding, and says the Hub is meant to close it. The Hub combines three capabilities that the article names as Asset Explorer, Skills and IBM DataPower Interact Gateway. Asset Explorer gives the agent context about integration assets, including what they mean, how they connect, who owns them and which are trusted.

Skills act as runbooks written for AI, giving assistants a repeatable way to follow practices that are often held in documentation or by experienced specialists. Interact Gateway serves as the policy enforcement point for identity, access, audit and approved actions, and higher-risk actions can stay subject to human oversight. The article also describes progressive disclosure, in which an assistant starts with a few entry tools and receives only the skills and tools relevant to the task at hand. The article is written by IBM's own product staff, Jiri De Jagere, a Product Manager for Strategy and AI, and Jigdesh Sampath, a Product Marketing Manager, and it presents the Hub as part of a broader set of AI capabilities across IBM Integration. It names FlowPilot, which brings MCP tools and agent skills into development environments, and says the Hub builds on these as well as on Interact Gateway's governed traffic handling.

IBM also states that it plans to introduce the Hub initially as a SaaS capability within IBM Integration, with wider product and deployment coverage to follow over time. The article offers a worked example, a purchase-order integration using SAP and Kafka, to show how the assistant with enterprise context identifies a dependent B2B process and pauses before deleting a flow. The piece places the Hub within a wider shift the article describes, in which gateways, integration platforms and agentic orchestration are converging as enterprises seek more consistent ways for AI to interact with their systems. It does not report any independent evaluation, customer results or pricing, so the claims about the Hub's benefits rest on IBM's own description. IBM says it will expand the Hub's product and deployment coverage over time, but the article gives no timetable for that expansion.

Articles.Title: IBM Integration Intelligence Hub gives AI the context to act, not just access

stories.Headline: Republican candidate defends AI-generated ad targeting Iowa governor rival
stories.Summary:
Republican Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn released an advertisement featuring an AI-generated likeness of his opponent, Democrat Rob Sand, according to a report by KCCI published October 26, 2026. The ad includes the line "He was a European model for real" and says Sand called himself extremely liberal in college. Some voters reportedly saw what appeared to be Sand, though the figure was an artificial likeness created with AI. The ad carries a disclaimer in its bottom right-hand corner telling viewers that it contains AI-generated content.

Lahn has said he stands by the ad and defended its accuracy, pointing to the disclaimer as proof he disclosed the use of AI. He argued that the central question is whether the ad's content is true, and said the content is accurate regarding positions Sand has supported, including on transgender books and classrooms and gun control. Lahn's position is that the substance of the claims, rather than the method of presentation, should determine whether the ad is fair. The reporting makes clear that this is his stated defense and does not independently verify the claims in the ad.

Sand's campaign responded sharply to the advertisement. In a statement, the campaign said Lahn was using AI to try to trick Iowans into believing Sand is someone he is not, and it predicted the tactic would fail. The campaign's response frames the ad as a deception rather than a legitimate comparison of records. The exchange places the disputed ad at the center of the race's closing stretch, with each side presenting the other as misleading voters.

Articles.Title: Republican candidate defends AI-generated ad targeting Iowa governor rival

stories.Headline: NVIDIA's DSX POD Pushes AI Factory Construction Toward the Assembly Line
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA has unveiled a factory-integrated data center model called DSX POD, announced October 21 at GTC Berlin and built around its Vera Rubin platform. The reference design packages computing, networking, rack-level power and liquid cooling into standardized modular containers that partner manufacturers would integrate, cable and test before shipment. NVIDIA says this could cut deployment time at a prepared site from six months to as little as 14 days, with partner deliveries beginning in early 2027. NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang said an AI factory creates value once it starts producing tokens rather than when construction ends. The move responds to pressure on operators to bring power-dense AI infrastructure online while facing labor shortages and long build schedules.

The announcement is part of a wider push by infrastructure partners toward repeatable, factory-made AI capacity. Armada and Johnson Controls plan a distributed sovereign AI program targeting 500 MW in 2027, with modules built at Armada's Galleon Forge facilities in Gilbert, Arizona, and Dublin, Ireland. Armada CEO Dan Wright said the race in system integration will not be won by whoever pours concrete fastest. Schneider Electric and Compass Datacenters also released a time study finding that prefabricated IT pods cut measured onsite installation time from 75.5 hours to about 15 hours per pod, an 80 percent reduction. The companies stress that this figure covers one installation portion, not total construction time.

Responsibility for the design and its rollout sits with NVIDIA, which has built a large partner ecosystem including Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo, Foxconn, Schneider Electric, Vertiv, Eaton, Crusoe and others. The partners are preparing manufacturing capacity, and Crusoe has opened a modular manufacturing facility in Colorado. Vertiv has also worked on a 41 MW deployment in Norway. The DSX POD design extends NVIDIA's earlier DSX AI Factory architecture, introduced in March, into physical manufacturing rather than replacing site and facility systems. The articles also flag that the two-week timeline depends on prepared sites, reliable component supplies and energy infrastructure that can take years to build, so the claims remain untested at commercial scale.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA's DSX POD Pushes AI Factory Construction Toward the Assembly Line

stories.Headline: Virtual session to discuss how hospitals put AI governance into practice
stories.Summary:
The West Health Accelerator at the American Hospital Association's Health Research & Educational Trust is hosting a virtual session on October 29 at 2:30 p.m. Eastern Time. The event is set to examine how hospitals are putting artificial intelligence governance into practice. The session was announced in an AHA News item published October 26, 2026. Its agenda covers how large and small hospitals are evaluating AI solutions, setting guardrails, and handling real-world adoption.

Presenters are expected to highlight resources from DiMe and the American Heart Association's AI Torch program. The articles do not describe any new requirement or policy that the session would impose. They frame it as a discussion of practical steps hospitals are taking. Registration details and speaker names are not included in the material provided.

The session is organized by the West Health Accelerator, which operates within the AHA's Health Research & Educational Trust. The AHA also has been active on AI policy, according to other items in the same news feed. On October 19, the AHA sent recommendations to the Food and Drug Administration on possible regulatory frameworks for generative AI-enabled medical devices. On October 7, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality announced a two-part Super Intelligence for Healthcare Improvement Initiative focused on AI in medical evidence reviews and data.

Other recent items point to a wider debate. An AHA blog posted October 5 responded to a Blue Cross Blue Shield Association report that linked hospitals' use of AI documentation tools to higher healthcare costs. The AHA also submitted comments on AI-related cyberattacks to a Senate Homeland Security subcommittee on September 30. The articles do not say what outcome, if any, will follow the October 29 session.

Articles.Title: Virtual session to discuss how hospitals put AI governance into practice

stories.Headline: AI Bubble Bursts in China, Wiping $480 Billion: Is America Next?
stories.Summary:
China's AI stock rally has collapsed, wiping out about $480 billion as the STAR50 index of AI and chip companies fell 40% from its July high. US AI stocks have taken a much smaller hit so far, with the Nasdaq sitting about 6% below the record it set three weeks ago. Analysts have pointed to stretched prices, tax bills, and the risk of US bans on Chinese data-center equipment as contributing factors. The damage is broad, since according to Goldman Sachs, AI stocks make up 42% of China's market value and 57% of its trading. The broader CSI 300 index of China's biggest companies recently entered a bear market.

A Beijing-based fund manager, Dong Baozhen, was cited by Reuters as saying the market had turned into a speculative bull run before the bubble burst. Even after the crash, the STAR50 trades at about 100 times past earnings, compared with roughly 30 times for the Nasdaq 100. Morgan Stanley expects offshore Chinese stocks to fall another 10% to 15% before China's market bottoms. The article notes that US AI stocks have so far held up far better than their Chinese counterparts. The key question for the US is whether that gap will hold.

This week's Big Tech earnings will be the test. Microsoft and Alphabet report Wednesday after the market closes, hours after the Federal Reserve's rate decision, and Amazon follows on Thursday. Alphabet expects to spend $195 billion to $205 billion on chips and data centers in 2026, while Amazon expects about $220 billion. Microsoft has guided for 44% to 45% growth at Azure, its cloud unit, and Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges expects investors to focus on Azure's return on invested capital. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said even its higher spending will not meet all demand this year.

Investors are watching these reports closely because all three companies have trailed the S&P 500's 11% gain this year heading into results. Alphabet fell 7.1% after its July report despite beating profit estimates, which shows how sensitive the stock is to spending figures. The article does not say what the companies will report or how markets will react. It also does not confirm whether the US market will follow China's downturn. The outcome of this week's earnings is expected to show whether investors still back the US AI trade.

Articles.Title: AI Bubble Bursts in China, Wiping $480 Billion: Is America Next?

stories.Headline: Duolingo slapped with class-action lawsuit alleging AI efforts, relentless ads hurt user growth
stories.Summary:
A class-action securities fraud lawsuit was filed earlier this month against Duolingo, the language-learning app, in US District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania by the law firm Levi & Korsinsky, LLP. The suit covers investors who bought Duolingo shares between May 2, 2025, and Feb. 26, 2026, and those investors are eligible to file as claimants. It accuses the company's executives of hiding from investors how aggressively they were pushing paid subscriptions and of rolling out low-quality AI features that they allegedly knew would frustrate customers. The Post reported the lawsuit on October 27, 2026.

The complaint says free users were forced to watch unskippable ads after each lesson, with some spending as much or more time on ads than on lessons. It also says Duolingo replaced its old Hearts system with an Energy system that drains energy on every answer, right or wrong, so that users can refill it by watching more ads, waiting until the next day, or paying for a premium tier. According to the suit, the real goal was to create friction that would push free users into subscribing. The lawsuit names no specific individuals as defendants in the portion summarized here, and it describes executives' statements to investors rather than any formal findings.

The suit says CEO Luis von Ahn told investors that the company's main focus was boosting user engagement and that it would smooth out sources of frustration, while calling daily active user growth probably the most important metric in the company. The lawsuit accuses executives of misleading investors on these points, and it says the company described its AI features as improving quality rather than cutting costs. The complaint also points to a drop in daily active user growth to 36 percent in November 2025, followed by a preliminary figure of 30 percent in January 2026 and a February report confirming the slowdown would continue through 2026. Duolingo did not immediately respond to The Post's request for comment, so the company's position is not yet known.

Duolingo was founded in 2011 at Carnegie Mellon University by von Ahn and a graduate student, and it teaches more than 40 languages along with subjects such as math and chess. Its paid tiers, Super and Max, cost roughly $12.99 and $30 a month, respectively, before annual discounts, and the stock was last trading near $138.60 a share, down more than 20 percent so far this year. The stock fell 25 percent after the November 2025 user growth report and dropped further after the January and February announcements, including the departure of chief financial officer Matthew Skaruppa. Further developments in the case were not described in the articles.

Articles.Title: Duolingo slapped with class-action lawsuit alleging AI efforts, relentless ads hurt user growth

stories.Headline: Hong Kong's urban renewal body to set up HK$100 million 'AI-first' tender assessment subsidiary
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong's Urban Renewal Authority will spend up to HK$100 million to set up a subsidiary that will check tender applications using automated AI systems. The move comes after accusations of corruption linked to the deadly Tai Po fire. The sum is a third of the HK$300 million the government allocated to the authority in its 2026-27 Budget. The funds are meant to reform the authority's Smart Tender scheme.

The Smart Tender system was launched in 2016 to give property owners an electronic platform for recruiting contractors. Its design anonymises the tender process, which is meant to prevent interference and encourage competition. However, the system cannot control who takes part in a tender exercise or who withdraws from one. The new subsidiary would bring in a professional team and build an automated workflow for deeper data verification and analysis. The authority said the approach would be "AI-first".

The authority's managing director is among those who have spoken on the plan, which is described as a direct response to the corruption concerns. According to the article, the director explained that the start-up money will go toward the new unit and its staff. The reporting quotes the director's account of the scope of the work, though the excerpt available is cut short. Further details on who else is accountable were not included in the material provided.

The plan sits within a broader government effort to restore public confidence after the Tai Po fire, which was deadly and which prompted questions about how renewal contracts were awarded. The articles provided do not say when the subsidiary will begin operating or how its performance will be measured. They also do not give a timeline for the wider reform of the Smart Tender scheme. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Hong Kong's urban renewal body to set up HK$100 million 'AI-first' tender assessment subsidiary - Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

stories.Headline: AI is knocking on banks’ doors — are defenses ready?
stories.Summary:
Recent cyberattacks on Korean financial institutions showed signs of artificial intelligence involvement, and some customer information was compromised. According to an analysis by a U.S. cybersecurity company, attackers connected an AI-powered security testing tool called Artex to multiple AI models. The article notes that the exact intrusion methods and the AI's role at each institution still need further investigation. Previously, hackers had to gather information, write programs and adjust their methods by hand after failures, but AI can now handle repetitive tasks such as identifying targets and testing weaknesses.

The author, a former president of KAIST, describes three technological shifts behind this change. The first is agentic AI, which receives an objective, uses tools and carries out multistep tasks rather than only answering questions. The second is the spread of open AI models and automation tools that can be downloaded and run independently. The third is that the same techniques serve both security researchers and attackers, so banks often can see only traces of activity, such as login records and program execution, rather than the instructions attackers gave their systems.

The author stresses that humans directed the attacks, so responsibility rests with those people, though developers and financial institutions should still be examined for their safeguards. The author proposes three responses. AI developers should treat safety as a basic product requirement, restrict permissions for risky actions and require human approval for potentially damaging steps. Banks should adopt Zero Trust defenses, which means segmenting internal systems, limiting access to what each person needs, and scrutinizing even legitimate accounts that pull unusually large amounts of data in short periods.

Governments should build systems for rapidly sharing information about attack methods and cooperate internationally to pursue cybercriminals who operate across borders. The article places these recommendations within a broader historical pattern, comparing AI rules to traffic lights and seat belts that followed earlier technologies. The author argues that AI cannot be governed by prohibition alone and that regulation should keep its benefits while limiting its risks. The article does not describe specific regulatory steps already scheduled, so what happens next remains unspecified beyond these calls for action.

Articles.Title: AI is knocking on banks’ doors — are defenses ready?

stories.Headline: Inside Henkel's Korean factory making adhesives for AI chips
stories.Summary:
Henkel, the German chemicals company, is producing semiconductor adhesives at its factory in Songdo, Incheon, South Korea, and the Korea Herald published a feature on the plant on October 26, 2026. The adhesives hold chips together, protect delicate connections and help dissipate heat, tasks that grow more demanding as AI requires more powerful processors and more complex packaging. The Songdo site, completed in 2022 after an investment of about 35 million euros ($39.2 million), is the only one of Henkel's four Korean factories that makes these materials. The facility covers 10,144 square meters and can produce up to 250 metric tons of semiconductor adhesive a year.

The plant operates under tight controls, with workers in cleanroom suits, temperature and humidity regulation, and ultraviolet light filtered out of some rooms to prevent unwanted chemical reactions. Its broader range covers more than 500 adhesive solutions for packaging, electronic components and device assembly. Production runs through seven stages, from raw material checks to mixing, testing and filling syringe-style containers, with about 100 barrel and cap combinations offered to customers. Henkel plans a new technical center in Seoul's Gasan Digital Complex, tentatively scheduled to open in March 2027, to expand its research work and coordinate with the Songdo plant. The company also says it is widening its portfolio for AI and high-performance computing, including its recently introduced Loctite Ablestik CDF900 series of thermally conductive die-attach films.

Hendrik Kohleick, Henkel's regional president for Asia-Pacific operations, described the Songdo plant as one of the company's major production sites for advanced packaging in the semiconductor industry and said it will strengthen cooperation with customers. Chang Ho-jun, president and head of Adhesive Technologies at Henkel Korea, said customers want adhesives that flow more easily and form thinner layers as chips shrink. Kim Young-mi, president of Henkel Korea, said the plant's role will grow in importance given the expansion of the global AI market and the strength of Korea's chip industry. The article notes that the site is near Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, that Incheon International Airport is about 30 minutes away, and that Henkel's Adhesive Technologies business generated about 10.7 billion euros in sales last year, compared with about 9.8 billion euros for Consumer Brands, which includes Persil.

Articles.Title: Inside Henkel's Korean factory making adhesives for AI chips

stories.Headline: Pa. law doesn't regulate AI-generated candidates in election ads, but some hope to change that
stories.Summary:
A recent campaign ad in Pennsylvania has renewed questions about whether artificial intelligence deepfakes are legal in political advertising. Republican gubernatorial challenger Stacy Garrity's campaign released an AI-generated video depicting her Democratic opponent, incumbent Governor Josh Shapiro, as the midterm elections approached less than a week away. The ad opens with a figure resembling Shapiro in the governor's office, and the synthetic Shapiro refers to sexual harassment scandals before pointing to a real New York Times headline. The video contains no watermark or on-screen text disclosing its artificial origin, and the fake Shapiro does not reveal that he is not the real candidate until about 45 seconds in. Near the end, the synthetic figure says the ad was created with AI, crediting "big beautiful data centers."

A spokesperson for the real Shapiro called the ad "cheap" and "dishonest" in a statement to Axios. Garrity told KDKA-TV that she stands by the ad. Under current Pennsylvania law, there is no prohibition on deepfakes in political ads and no requirement for a disclaimer. State Sen. Lisa Boscola announced in May that she planned to introduce legislation barring AI-generated or AI-altered video, audio or images of a candidate during the 90 days before an election, but that bill had not yet been introduced. A separate bill to regulate deepfakes in campaign ads passed the state House last year but did not clear the state Senate.

The reporting places the issue in a broader regional context, noting that several neighboring states, including Delaware, Maryland and New York, have laws that either prohibit election deepfakes or require a disclosure that content is AI-generated. Pennsylvania, by contrast, currently has neither. The article does not say whether Boscola's proposal or any other measure will advance before the election. It also does not indicate what penalties, if any, the Garrity ad could face under existing law.

Articles.Title: Pa. law doesn't regulate AI-generated candidates in election ads, but some hope to change that

stories.Headline: Meta Aims to Raise $95 Billion to Pursue New AI Opportunities
stories.Summary:
Meta has said it plans to raise $95 billion to support its artificial intelligence efforts. The company announced the fundraising plans on Monday, October 26, 2026. It intends to raise $35 billion through underwritten public equity offerings and another $60 billion through an at-the-market program. Meta says the investments will support continued momentum in its core business and in emerging AI opportunities.

The company pointed to its Family of Apps, where Facebook and Instagram have seen record engagement, which it credits to strong growth in video. It also highlighted its Muse AI model, which drew more than 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada in its first weeks. Meta additionally sees chances to serve high-margin inference demand from business customers through the Meta Enterprise Platform and its advanced models, including Muse Wonder. Mark Zuckerberg has positioned Muse as the foundation for shopping, advertising, enterprise software and smart glasses.

On the company's recent earnings call, he said more than 25% of Muse users are daily users, and that early engagement ran more than twice the level Threads reached at launch. He described Muse as the product form of his vision for personal superintelligence. The report also notes that Meta spent $34.9 billion on capital expenditures in the quarter while reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion. Those costs have pressured the company.

Zuckerberg said Meta needs more than a tenfold improvement in compute efficiency over the next year to make the economics work at scale. Meta has postponed a global Muse rollout partly because of these costs, and it expects to monetize Muse earlier than usual. The company has not disclosed its current per-user operating cost, and it reported $64.6 billion in quarterly revenue, up 26%, with advertising helping to fund the effort. Whether Muse can generate enough revenue to justify the spending remains unproven.

Articles.Title: Meta Aims to Raise $95 Billion to Pursue New AI Opportunities

stories.Headline: China's industrial profits rise 15.5% in first nine months of 2026, driven by high-tech manufacturing, AI integration
stories.Summary:
Profits at China's major industrial firms rose 15.5 percent year on year in the first nine months of 2026, according to official data released on Tuesday. Firms with annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan ($2.8 million) reported combined profits of 6.03 trillion yuan from January to September. The National Bureau of Statistics said profits grew 14.4 percent in September alone. Industrial production stayed steady, and cumulative profit growth has remained in double digits this year. The electronics industry was the main driver, with its profits doubling year on year over the period and adding 9.6 percentage points to the overall gain.

Demand for artificial intelligence computing power and advanced memory technologies helped push up earnings, with electronic specialty material manufacturing up 220 percent and semiconductor device manufacturing up 51.7 percent. Optoelectronic component and electronic circuit manufacturing rose 69.8 percent and 62.5 percent. High-tech manufacturing profits jumped 52 percent, accounting for 25.5 percent of total industrial profits, up 6.2 percentage points from a year earlier. Optical fiber and optical cable manufacturing profits surged 570 percent and 110 percent, respectively, as computing infrastructure and data center construction expanded.

Raw materials manufacturing also contributed, with profits climbing 44.9 percent and adding 5.9 percentage points to overall growth. Strong demand for copper, aluminum and other metals from AI and new-energy industries lifted nonferrous metals profits by 79.7 percent. Mining profits rose 38.2 percent and manufacturing profits increased 17 percent across the broader sector. Chen Xi, a researcher at the Academy of Macroeconomic Research under the National Development and Reform Commission, said large-scale equipment upgrades, the integration of AI into manufacturing and tax policy support have helped firms cut costs and improve efficiency.

He also credited China's comprehensive industrial supply chains and quick response to market demand. The National Bureau of Statistics said it will focus on expanding domestic demand, improving supply and accelerating the shift from traditional to new growth drivers. The agency framed these goals as ways to strengthen the economy's internal momentum and advance high-quality industrial development. The articles do not specify further policy measures or timelines beyond these stated aims.

Articles.Title: China's industrial profits rise 15.5% in first nine months of 2026, driven by high-tech manufacturing, AI integration - Global Times

stories.Headline: Bullies created AI images of student, and ACA allowed it, lawsuit says
stories.Summary:
A lawsuit filed September 9 in Buncombe County Superior Court accuses Asheville Christian Academy, a private Christian school in Swannanoa, North Carolina, of failing to stop students from bullying and hazing a 13-year-old boy identified only as "John Doe." According to the complaint, the boy began at the school in August 2023 at age 11, and the bullying escalated in fall 2025. The suit alleges that other students created AI-generated, sexually explicit images and videos of him and circulated them among the student body. It also says administrators who learned of this did nothing to discipline those involved.

The complaint describes a pattern of physical and sexual abuse, including hazing in the shower after gym class, a locker room assault in which students beat him with a belt, and students taking his emergency medication while he was weak. It further alleges that one student, described as the ringleader, contacted a convicted pedophile in the area, tried to set up a relationship with that person in the boy's name, and sent the man the boy's home address. The lawsuit accuses the school of negligence and seeks an unspecified amount of damages. The boy, who has medical issues, no longer attends the school.

The school has denied the allegations in an emailed statement issued October 27, saying its investigation led it to believe the claims are without merit and that it intends to defend itself vigorously. The school declined further comment. The Buncombe County Sheriff's Office told the Citizen Times that it received a report of hazing at the school, which did not involve AI-generated images, and that an investigation into possible hazing is ongoing. Attorney Bobby Jenkins, who represents the boy, said the case is not a "boys will be boys" situation and invited any witnesses to come forward.

Articles.Title: Bullies created AI images of student, and ACA allowed it, lawsuit says

stories.Headline: Stacy Garrity talks AI, skill games and measles in Pennsylvania's governor race
stories.Summary:
Republican Pennsylvania Treasurer Stacy Garrity sat down with KDKA-TV reporter Josh Taylor ahead of the November 3 election for governor. In an interview published October 27, 2026, she answered questions for about 30 minutes about artificial intelligence, skill games, affordability, federal cuts to SNAP and Medicaid, and a measles outbreak in the state. The interview covered her campaign against incumbent Democrat Josh Shapiro. It also included a discussion of a political ad about Shapiro that was made with AI.

Garrity defended the AI-generated ad, saying its content was accurate and that the ad states up front that it was made with AI. When asked whether it was ironic to use AI in an ad given growing criticism of the technology, she pointed to Shapiro's campaign finances, saying he had received $5.7 million from data center developers and used that money to run ads against her. She also said Shapiro's ads against her were false. On skill games, she criticized the state for letting an October 13 deadline pass without a resolution, which forced American Legion posts, VFW halls, fire halls, gas stations, convenience stores and some pharmacies to remove the machines.

Garrity said the games supported thousands of jobs and returned millions of dollars to local communities, and she argued that a real leader would have acted before the deadline. On federal cuts to SNAP and Medicaid, she said the state should lower its error rate so taxpayers pay less, and she said that benefits should go to pregnant mothers, single parents, caretakers and people with disabilities. On measles, the Pennsylvania Department of Health has reported nearly 1,300 cases along with the state's first measles-related deaths in years. Garrity said Shapiro ran to a camera before he had the facts, and she said a leader should first console families and then gather facts and be transparent.

KDKA invited Shapiro to sit for a one-on-one interview before Election Day, but according to the report he has not accepted. The article does not indicate any response from Shapiro's campaign to Garrity's specific criticisms. The report notes that the interview was part of local coverage of Pennsylvania's gubernatorial race. It does not describe further steps in the race beyond the November 3 election date.

Articles.Title: Stacy Garrity talks AI, skill games and measles in Pennsylvania's governor race

stories.Headline: AI medical device regulation after approval: What NHS trusts should set up now - Health Tech World
stories.Summary:
On 6 October the UK government accepted all 44 recommendations of the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare, shifting the focus from a single moment of approval toward how AI-enabled medical devices perform across their working life. The Commission's report was published on 10 September. The MHRA has committed to draft guidance by December 2026 on managing changes to AI-enabled devices as they adapt and improve. A consultation on qualifying and classifying these devices will begin next year, and a full implementation roadmap with timelines and responsibilities is promised by spring 2027, overseen by a new Programme Board.

The article argues that this direction matters most to NHS trusts already running these tools, since evidence of safety after go-live can only come from the hospitals that use them. A procurement file built for a one-off decision may say little about what will be measured months later, who will review it, and what happens if performance drifts. The author suggests starting with one deployed tool, choosing two or three measures that would reveal deterioration, and recording changes to inputs such as imaging protocols or software updates alongside the figures. Trusts should also ask suppliers how they will notify them of retrained or modified models, and agree internally who has authority to accept an update. The MHRA has also opened applications for Phase 3 of its AI Airlock sandbox, which focuses on post-market surveillance, with first participants due to be chosen in November.

The author, Rafael Patron, president of the Scientific-Technical Committee of the Italian Association of Artificial Intelligence Professionals (AIPIA), frames monitoring as a matter of professional conduct as well as regulation. The AIPIA code of ethics asks members to keep systems explainable and auditable and to keep consequential decisions under human oversight. Patron suggests NHS teams should set this expectation with suppliers now, so that the people behind a model can explain what changed and show it still works. The government has also said it will explore staged pathways that let promising AI tools into NHS use earlier under close supervision while more real-world evidence is gathered. The article's central point is that the detailed rules will take shape over coming months, but the data needed to test them is being produced on NHS wards now.

Articles.Title: AI medical device regulation after approval: What NHS trusts should set up now - Health Tech World

stories.Headline: AI Governance Is Not a Checkbox: Five Practical Lessons for Organizations
stories.Summary:
The article is a Law.com opinion piece by Christine Chasse of Spencer Fane, published October 27, 2026, arguing that responsible use of artificial intelligence is an ongoing risk-management discipline rather than a one-time technology decision. It notes that AI is already embedded in everyday business work, from email and research to clinical decision support, and that adoption often outpaces governance. The piece frames governance as requiring visibility, accountability, testing, and documented oversight. The excerpt available here cuts off before the five lessons are laid out, so the specific steps and their details are not available from this text.

The central point is that governance cannot be treated as a box to tick once. Organizations that deploy AI tools need to know where those tools are being used, assign clear responsibility for their outcomes, test them before and during use, and keep records showing that someone is overseeing them. The article presents these as continuing obligations, not a single compliance event. Because the full text is behind a subscription wall, the article does not specify timelines, thresholds, or named regulatory requirements in the portion visible here.

The author is Christine Chasse, identified in the byline as a lawyer at Spencer Fane. The article's stated view is that adoption tends to run ahead of governance, and that closing that gap takes sustained discipline. The related coverage listed alongside it includes a piece on smaller, sovereign AI for law firms and a report that the Fifth Circuit reassigned a case after a judge relied on AI to draft a ruling containing errors, which illustrates the risks the governance argument addresses. The visible text does not say what further steps the author recommends beyond the general principles above.

Articles.Title: AI Governance Is Not a Checkbox: Five Practical Lessons for Organizations

stories.Headline: Newsom Signs Law Requiring Disclosure Of AI-Generated Performers In Ads 09/18/2026
stories.Summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom signed a California law this week requiring ads that use AI-generated "synthetic" performers to clearly disclose that those figures were created by artificial intelligence. The article, written by Wendy Davis and dated September 17, 2026, reports that the bill, SB 1050, was backed by the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists. Newsom said on Thursday that the bill takes bold action against the growing risks of AI, including protecting workers. The statute itself states that the disclosure mandate is needed to prevent deceptive or misleading advertising. The law defines synthetic performers as AI-generated digital figures or voices that appear human but are not recognizable as a particular person.

The disclosure rule applies only when these characters are featured prominently, which the bill describes in three situations. The first is when a synthetic performer appears in the foreground demonstrating or illustrating the product or service. The second is when the digital performer narrates an ad, and the third is when the character illustrates or reacts to narration. Ads for movies, TV shows, video games and similar programs are exempt, provided the use of AI characters matches how they appear in the program or game being promoted. The measure also requires media outlets to stop distributing ads that a court has found to violate the disclosure law.

Major advertising trade groups opposed the bill and urged a veto in a September 4 letter. The Association of National Advertisers, the American Association of Advertising Agencies, the American Advertising Federation and the Digital Advertising Alliance argued that the bill imposes an overbroad labeling regime, exposes businesses to opportunistic lawsuits and burdens ordinary commercial speech. They also contended that the rule would apply even when a synthetic performer is used for background or thematic purposes and is unlikely to mislead consumers about a material claim. Santa Clara University law professor Eric Goldman told MediaPost that the requirement for online publishers to remove violating ads appears inconsistent with Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. He said he does not know how publishers would respond to such court orders, but that the provision looks like a Section 230 violation in the abstract.

Articles.Title: Newsom Signs Law Requiring Disclosure Of AI-Generated Performers In Ads 09/18/2026 - MediaPost

stories.Headline: Impact of Artificial Intelligence, budget bill and lobbying laws on the agenda
stories.Summary:
The House and Senate committees have a busy schedule on October 26, 2026, with a range of reviews that touch on artificial intelligence, federal spending and lobbying rules. The Status of Women committee will begin a self-initiated review of how AI is affecting women, girls and 2SLGBTQIA+ individuals, hearing at 11 a.m. from Digital Moment CEO Indra Kubicek and representatives of the Canadian Council of Innovators and Women's Health Collective Canada. Later that afternoon, the Subcommittee on International Human Rights will examine the global effects of AI on human rights movements, with witnesses from the Institute on Resilience and Urban Innovation, ControlAI and UN Special Rapporteur Gina Romero. Those hearings are scheduled to take place at 3:30 p.m.

The Finance committee has set aside one hour, starting at 5:15 p.m., to hear from Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon. Members are continuing to review the details of Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne's omnibus plan, which would roll out additional measures from last year's budget. The Access to Information, Privacy and Ethics committee will also resume its statutory review of federal lobbying laws at 11 a.m., receiving a briefing from Lobbying Commissioner Nancy Bélanger. Separate sessions cover the opioid epidemic and toxic drug crisis at the Health committee, Canada's nuclear future at Natural Resources, and the effectiveness of international institutions at Foreign Affairs.

Several other committees have set their own agendas for the day. Public Safety and National Security will begin reviewing Conservative MP Dane Lloyd's backbench proposal to treat refusal to disclose the location of bodies or remains as an aggravating factor in sentencing, with Lloyd and fellow Conservative MP Michael Cooper slated to speak alongside the Federal Ombudsperson for Victims of Crime. Public Accounts will revisit the 2024 and 2025 public accounts with William Robson of the C.D. Howe Institute, while National Defence will continue its look at modernizing the Canadian army. Veterans Affairs will explore how civilian recognition of military skills works, and Fisheries and Oceans will receive an update on Atlantic salmon populations. On the Senate side, Secretary of State for Defence Procurement Stephen Fuhr is scheduled to describe Canada's procurement strategy and overall defence spending at 4 p.m., with Defence Investment Agency CEO Doug Guzman also expected to attend.

stories.Headline: Latham & Watkins Lends Lawyer Funds Expertise for Harvey AI Tool

Latham & Watkins has agreed to work with the legal AI startup Harvey to design an artificial intelligence tool aimed at private funds work. The plan was announced on a Tuesday, and the article is dated October 27, 2026. stories.Headline: Meta reverses losses to rise as investors weigh $35 billion AI funding plan
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms, the parent of Facebook and Instagram, launched roughly $35 billion in equity offerings to help fund its artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, and its shares initially fell as much as 4% on the news before recovering to rise about 1%. The offerings, reported on October 26, 2026, comprise $22.5 billion in Class A common stock sold through forward sale agreements and about $12.5 billion in mandatory convertible preferred stock. Meta also outlined a separate program of roughly $60 billion in Class C nonvoting shares, expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027, though it has not yet entered into an agreement for that program. The preferred shares are expected to convert automatically into common stock around August 15, 2029, and Meta intends to seek a Nasdaq listing for the depositary shares under the ticker METAM. Underwriters also have a 30-day option to buy up to $3.375 billion in additional Class A stock.

The company said it will use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, including AI infrastructure investment, as it forecasts capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion for 2026. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs are leading the offerings. Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have expressed non-binding interest in buying up to $5 billion in aggregate of the Class A shares, on the same price and terms as other investors. Meta generated $97 billion in operating cash flow in the first nine months of 2026 and held about $82 billion in cash and marketable securities at the end of September. Free cash flow nonetheless turned negative in the third quarter as capital spending rose.

Meta's management, including CEO Mark Zuckerberg, is behind the plan, and the articles indicate the nonvoting share issuance would let the company raise equity while preserving the voting control of Zuckerberg and other existing voting shareholders. The articles describe the move as part of a broader shift in which the AI investment race is changing financing decisions even for highly profitable technology firms. Analysts and investors, according to the coverage, are weighing the potential long-term returns from AI against the costs and possible dilution from financing the expansion. The articles do not say what comes next beyond the planned Class C program in 2027 and the preferred conversion in 2029.

Articles.Title: Meta reverses losses to rise as investors weigh $35 billion AI funding plan

stories.Headline: Law Commission pitches laws, frameworks for AI use in criminal justice
stories.Summary:
The Law Commission of Ontario has recommended new provincial legislation and governance and risk management frameworks for artificial intelligence used in the criminal justice system. Its final report on "AI in Criminal Justice," published on October 26, 2026, is described as the first in Canada to examine the uses, benefits and risks of putting AI systems into criminal justice. The report sets out 29 recommendations aimed at helping police, Crowns, courts and other institutions use AI responsibly. The article notes that no Canadian government has yet enacted laws or regulations governing police or court use of AI. The commission wants a governance framework that gives governments, police, courts, Crowns, defence counsel and legal aid clear legal and policy guidance.

That framework should require public disclosure of AI use in criminal justice, a dedicated impact assessment for each such system, continuous auditing and evaluation, and guarantees for judicial independence. It also urged the Ontario government to amend the Enhancing Digital Security and Trust Act, 2024, or pass complementary laws. Those laws would apply a precautionary principle and require AI systems to comply with the Charter, criminal procedural fairness, privacy and human rights law, criminal common law and judicial independence. The commission also proposed mandatory risk categories and yearly public reports on police AI use, prepared by the province's Inspector General of Policing and Law Enforcement Complaints Agency. The report was written by Ryan Fritsch, counsel who leads the LCO's Criminal AI Project, and Nye Thomas, the LCO's executive director.

In the executive summary, the authors said AI tools such as predictive policing, facial recognition and generative AI can improve public safety, investigations and efficiency, but carry proven risks to human rights, criminal procedure, privacy and access to justice. They said those risks fall most heavily on racialized and low-income communities. The commission also called for a joint federal-provincial committee to recommend safeguards for AI evidence rules in criminal matters. It asked Ontario's Ministry of the Attorney General to increase funding for Legal Aid Ontario so defence counsel can respond to AI evidence, and proposed that Legal Aid Ontario create an AI Centre of Excellence to provide training, set competence standards and support test cases. The articles do not say when or whether the government will act on these recommendations.

Articles.Title: Law Commission pitches laws, frameworks for AI use in criminal justice - Law Times

stories.Headline: AI rules in courts, tribunals an ‘unholy mess’, senator says

What is clear is that the criticism concerns the lack of a consistent approach across different bodies. Shoebridge's remark, as reported, points to the fact that different courts and tribunals have adopted different rules on generative AI use rather than a single common standard.

The available text does not say which rules are in place, what they require of lawyers or litigants, or when they took effect. stories.Headline: How Are Schneider Electric, Nscale and Start Campus Using NVIDIA Digital Twin Technology to Develop AI Data Centers?
stories.Summary:
Emerald AI released results from a pilot run with Nvidia and Nscale at Nscale's data center in Iceland, with the figures shared during Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin in the week of October 23, 2026. According to the companies, Emerald AI's Emerald Conductor platform, working together with Nvidia's DSX power-management technology, cut the power use of the AI server racks by about 25 percent. The reduction was held for 30 minutes before the site returned to normal operations. It was the first time Emerald Conductor had been fully integrated with DSX, which is designed to get as much computing as possible out of every watt of energy. It was also the seventh test Emerald AI has carried out, following three in the US, in Santa Clara, Phoenix and Chicago, and one in the UK with National Grid.

Separately, Schneider Electric said on October 23 that it is launching new prefabricated power modules and power skids. They are based on a reference design developed jointly with Nvidia for its GB300 NVL72 AI server system, and they support power densities of up to 142 kilowatts per rack while integrating power management and liquid cooling controls. The modules use Schneider's Galaxy VXL uninterruptible power supply technology and come in three capacities, 2MW, 2.25MW and 2.5MW. The 2.5MW version is the company's largest single-container prefabricated power solution so far. Prefabrication means the equipment is built and tested at a factory before installation, which shortens construction time and lets operators add capacity module by module.

Varun Sivaram, founder and CEO of Emerald AI, said access to power has become the main constraint on Europe's AI build-out. He argued that the fastest way to ease it is to make AI factories flexible enough to use grid capacity that already exists, which also helps keep energy affordable for local communities. In his view, the pilot shows that AI computing can lower its power use on request, which utilities need to see before they can connect such sites faster. Emerald Conductor acts as a go-between for the grid and data centers, orchestrating AI workloads in real time so that sites can adjust their consumption while keeping compute performance acceptable. Schneider will build its new products at its facility near Barcelona, Spain.

On the wider picture, Emerald AI announced its first commercial project in October, with its software to be deployed at Nvidia's under-construction 96MW Aurora data center in Manassas, Virginia. The company raised a further $150 million in Series A funding in August, and earlier raised $25 million in seed extension funding. It belongs to Nvidia's Inception program for startups and is backed by Google's chief sustainability officer, Kate Brandt. Schneider plans to launch its power modules first in Europe, then in North America later in 2026, before expanding sales to the Asia-Pacific region. A commentary on Nscale put its contracted backlog at $103.4 billion against first-half 2026 revenue of $140.6 million and a net loss of about $1.02 billion, with Anthropic and Microsoft the main customers, and it raised the question of whether the company is overleveraged.
